sections.heading: Select the method from the question and data
breadcrumb: Select the method from the question and data
sections.text: Methods are complementary—not interchangeable Method Best fit Important caution Descriptive only Very few independent heats or severe confounding Do not report inferential p-values. OLS / GLM One-level independent observations; choose Gaussian, logistic, count, or ordinal family to match Y Invalid when residuals remain clustered or repeated. Heat-level aggregation Simple heat-level association with adequate heats Loses pipe/specimen detail; weighting needs justification. Weighted least squares Aggregated means with meaningfully different, estimable precisions Weights must represent inverse variance—not merely larger row counts. Fixed-effects / blocked model Within-group contrasts while absorbing stable group differences Cannot estimate a predictor that is constant within the absorbed group. Cluster-robust SE Population-average association with many independent clusters Use an appropriate finite-sample correction; not a cure for few heats. GEE Marginal or population-average effects Requires enough clusters and a chosen working correlation. Mixed-effects model Nested variance, cluster-specific effects, unbalanced data Check convergence, singularity, and random-effect support. Generalized mixed model Binary, count, or ordinal outcomes with nested or crossed dependence Choose the link and distribution from the response—not convenience. Longitudinal / repeated model Ordered measurements over time or position Exchangeable correlation may be wrong; inspect lag and time structure. Crossed-effects model Factors such as lab, operator, machine, or batch cross multiple groups Do not force crossed factors into a false nesting hierarchy. Bayesian hierarchy Complex hierarchy or sparse cells with defensible priors Report prior sensitivity and posterior predictive checks. GAM / nonlinear hierarchy Engineering-supported curvature or thresholds Control flexibility and validate on unseen groups. Survival / frailty model Time-to-failure outcomes with censoring and clustering Ordinary regression of observed failure times mishandles censoring. Cluster bootstrap Interval sensitivity check with a reasonable number of heats Resample whole heats; bootstrapping cannot create missing information.

sections.text: Assume the fitted three-level variance model estimates heat ICC = 0.38. The average cluster contains 13.5 specimens because 486 ÷ 36 = 13.5. Design effect DE = 1 + (13.5 − 1)(0.38) = 5.75 Information-equivalent row count n eff ≈ 486 ÷ 5.75 = 84.5 rows This approximation shows how correlation erodes the apparent information in 486 rows. It does not turn 84.5 into the sample size for Ca. Because Ca changes only between heats, the Ca association is supported by 36 independent Ca-bearing units.

sections.text: Aggregate to one row per heat and fit: Mean Charpy h = β₀ + β₁(Ca h ) + β₂(S h ) + β₃(Mean exit temperature h ) + ε h There are 36 rows and four estimated parameters, including the intercept, so the residual degrees of freedom are: Residual df 36 independent heats − 4 estimated parameters = 32 Reproducible heat-level sensitivity result from the supplied fictional dataset Term Estimate SE Approx. 95% CI Engineering reading Ca, per 1 ppm −1.03 J 0.34 −1.72 to −0.33 10 ppm higher Ca corresponds to about 10.3 J lower mean energy. S, per 1 ppm −2.39 J 0.48 −3.36 to −1.42 Association is conditional on Ca and mean exit temperature. Mean exit temperature, per 1°C −0.26 J 0.14 −0.55 to 0.03 The interval includes zero; important effects in either direction must be judged against engineering limits. Why not celebrate the p-values? The data are synthetic and the coefficients were embedded for teaching. In real historical data, model form, overlap, confounding, measurement error, influential heats, and selection processes determine whether such precision is credible.

sections.text: Defensible example statement: “Within this fictional 36-heat dataset, and after adjustment for sulfur and heat-mean exit temperature, a 10 ppm higher calcium value was associated with an estimated 10.3 J lower heat-average Charpy energy. The approximate 95% interval for the 10 ppm contrast was 3.3 to 17.2 J lower. This is an observational between-heat association within the 12–36 ppm Ca range; it does not establish that changing calcium would cause the predicted energy change.” Before using the statement operationally, confirm that grade, product dimensions, rolling practice, test temperature, slab thickness, specimen size, orientation, and production period either overlap sufficiently, are controlled appropriately, or define a deliberately restricted population. Three-heat mini-example: three heats can demonstrate the hierarchy, but an intercept plus Ca and S uses all three heat-level degrees of freedom and leaves zero residual degrees of freedom. It cannot support standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values, ICC claims, or a dependable cluster bootstrap. Interactive laboratory

sections.text: Convert the specimen table to an Excel Table with Ctrl+T ; name it CharpyData . Keep explicit identifiers: Heat_ID , Pipe_ID , Specimen_ID . Never infer nesting from row order. Excel functions used in this lesson Purpose Example formula What to verify Heat mean =AVERAGEIFS(CharpyData[Charpy_J],CharpyData[Heat_ID],A2) Response definition and exclusions are consistent. Specimen rows per heat =COUNTIFS(CharpyData[Heat_ID],A2) Do not call this the number of independent chemistry observations. Unique pipes per heat =COUNTA(UNIQUE(FILTER(CharpyData[Pipe_ID],CharpyData[Heat_ID]=A2))) Available in Microsoft 365. sections.heading: Minitab Navigation
sections.text: Minitab: mixed-effects workflow Open the long-format dataset with one row per specimen. Store Heat and Pipe as categorical identifiers; store Ca, S, temperatures, OD, and gauge as numeric columns. Verify nesting with Stat → Tables → Cross Tabulation and Chi-Square : each Pipe ID should map to one Heat ID. Explore the response with Graph → Boxplot → One Y, With Groups . Graph Charpy by Heat and then by Pipe. For a mixed model, use Stat → ANOVA → Mixed Effects Model → Fit Mixed Effects Model . Menu wording can vary by release. Enter Charpy_J as the response. Add scientifically justified fixed terms such as centred Ca, centred S, centred exit temperature, and required product controls. Specify Heat and Pipe-within-Heat as random terms only if the design supports their variance estimation. Do not add random slopes for heat-level Ca because Ca does not vary within a heat. Under Graphs , request four-in-one residual plots and residuals versus relevant predictors. Under Results , request the model summary, fixed-effect table, and variance components. Review warnings first. Then inspect variance components, fixed-effect contrasts with confidence intervals, residual plots, and unusual observations. Use Predict only for combinations represented by the fitted design. State whether prediction is for a new observation, pipe, or heat. Output fields that matter: convergence status, variance components, fixed-effect estimate and interval for a meaningful contrast, residual degrees of freedom method, residual diagnostics, and any unusual observations. A low p-value does not override a singular fit or confounded design.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
sections.text: ASQ and real-work connection: identify the experimental unit before selecting a method, distinguish replication from repeated measurement, and never let a large row count disguise a small number of independent groups. On an exam, these cues point to blocking, nested factors, repeated measures, or a hierarchical model; at work, they determine whether the uncertainty and engineering conclusion are defensible. Python: complete analysis skeleton import pandas as pd import statsmodels.formula.api as smf df = pd.read_csv("hierarchical_charpy_practice.csv") required = {"heat_id","pipe_id","charpy_j","ca_ppm","s_ppm","exit_temp_c"} assert required.issubset(df.columns) # Verify heat-level predictors are constant within heat. assert df.groupby("heat_id")["ca_ppm"].nunique().max() == 1 assert df.groupby("heat_id")["s_ppm"].nunique().max() == 1 # Heat-level sensitivity model: one independent row per heat. heat = df.groupby("heat_id", as_index=False).agg( charpy_mean_j=("charpy_j", "mean"), ca_ppm=("ca_ppm", "first"), s_ppm=("s_ppm", "first"), pipes=("pipe_id", "nunique")) heat_fit = smf.ols("charpy_mean_j ~ ca_ppm + s_ppm", data=heat).fit() # Marginal sensitivity: cluster-robust covariance by heat. robust = smf.ols( "charpy_j ~ ca_ppm + s_ppm + exit_temp_c", data=df ).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={ "groups": df["heat_id"], "use_correction": True }) # Random heat intercept plus pipe-within-heat variance component. # pipe_id must be globally unique, as it is in the practice dataset. mixed = smf.mixedlm( "charpy_j ~ ca_ppm + s_ppm + exit_temp_c", df, groups="heat_id", re_formula="1", vc_formula={"pipe": "0 + C(pipe_id)"} ).fit(reml=True) print(f"rows={len(df)}, heats={df.heat_id.nunique()}, " f"pipes={df.pipe_id.nunique()}") print(heat_fit.summary()) print(robust.summary()) print(mixed.summary()) R: nested mixed model and checks library(readr) library(dplyr) library(lme4) library(lmerTest) d <- read_csv("hierarchical_charpy_practice.csv") stopifnot(max(tapply(d$ca_ppm, d$heat_id, function(x) n_distinct(x))) == 1) m <- lmer(charpy_j ~ ca_ppm + s_ppm + exit_temp_c + (1 | heat_id/pipe_id), data = d, REML = TRUE) summary(m) isSingular(m) plot(m) qqnorm(resid(m)); qqline(resid(m)) # Leave one entire heat out at a time. loo <- lapply(unique(d$heat_id), function(h) { fit <- update(m, data = filter(d, heat_id != h)) c(omitted_heat = h, ca = fixef(fit)["ca_ppm"]) }) do.call(rbind, loo) Correct cluster-bootstrap pattern # Each sampled heat occurrence receives a NEW bootstrap cluster ID. import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(42) heat_ids = df["heat_id"].unique() boot_coefs = [] for b in range(2000): sampled = rng.choice(heat_ids, len(heat_ids), replace=True) pieces = [] for instance, heat_id in enumerate(sampled): part = df.loc[df.heat_id.eq(heat_id)].copy() part["boot_heat_id"] = f"b{instance}" # preserves multiplicity pieces.append(part) boot = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True) bh = boot.groupby("boot_heat_id", as_index=False).agg( charpy_mean_j=("charpy_j", "mean"), ca_ppm=("ca_ppm", "first"), s_ppm=("s_ppm", "first")) if bh[["ca_ppm", "s_ppm"]].drop_duplicates().shape[0] > 3: fit = smf.ols("charpy_mean_j ~ ca_ppm + s_ppm", bh).fit() boot_coefs.append(fit.params["ca_ppm"]) print(np.quantile(boot_coefs, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975])) Decision language

sections.heading: When you see this, it means this
breadcrumb: When you see this, it means this
sections.text: Interpretation guide When you see this It means this Action High heat ICC Results from the same heat are strongly correlated. Model heat clustering; do not count specimens as independent chemistry replicates. Singular mixed-model fit The proposed random structure may exceed what the data support. Simplify with engineering justification; do not hide the warning. Large leave-one-heat-out change One heat strongly influences the conclusion. Investigate data quality and report sensitivity. OLS and mixed-model SE differ Clustering or variance structure affects uncertainty. Use the design-respecting result. No overlap across practices Practice and chemistry effects are confounded. Restrict conclusions or collect better-balanced data. Interval includes zero but excludes large harm No clear direction, yet practically important harm may be unlikely. Discuss engineering bounds, not only “not significant.” Random-row accuracy exceeds grouped-by-heat accuracy The original validation leaked heat-specific information. Use grouped folds and report new-heat performance. Random heat variance is near zero After fixed effects, little additional heat-level variance was estimated. Check singularity and whether the random term is supported; do not conclude heats are identical. Ca coefficient changes sharply after adding practice The unadjusted result was sensitive to practice composition. Show both models, inspect overlap, and narrow the claim. Confidence interval is narrow but outside historical range The numerical prediction is extrapolation despite apparent precision. Do not use it as validated evidence; collect supporting data. Reporting template: “After controlling for product dimensions, test temperature, and rolling practice, a 10 ppm increase in heat-level Ca was associated with an estimated X J change in average Charpy energy (95% interval Y to Z J). This is a heat-level observational association and does not establish causation.” Failure prevention

sections.heading: Common mistakes, warning signs, and corrections
breadcrumb: Common mistakes, warning signs, and corrections
sections.text: Calculation error: using specimen count as heat-level n Why wrong: repeated Ca and S values do not create independent chemistry contrasts. Recognize it: the same predictor value appears on many rows with the same Heat ID. Prevent it: count distinct heats, show the hierarchy, and use cluster-aware inference. Interpretation error: association becomes causation Why wrong: grade, practice, dimensions, and time may jointly influence chemistry and Charpy. Recognize it: words such as “caused,” “improved,” or “reduced” appear in an observational result. Prevent it: use “was associated with” and state the design limits. Assumption error: bootstrap will rescue three heats Why wrong: resampling cannot create new independent information. Recognize it: thousands of bootstrap draws are used to disguise a single-digit cluster count. Prevent it: keep the analysis descriptive or collect more heats. Software-output error: ignoring convergence or singular-fit warnings Why wrong: parameters may sit on a boundary or be poorly identified. Recognize it: warnings, near-zero variances, correlations near ±1, or unstable estimates. Prevent it: inspect warnings first and simplify with engineering justification. Weighting error: calling inverse-variance WLS automatically optimal Why wrong: estimated variances can be noisy and may weight large clusters in unintended ways. Recognize it: weights are applied without a variance model or sensitivity check. Prevent it: define the estimand, justify weights, and compare unweighted and defensibly weighted results. Data error: mixing ppm, wt%, and mass fraction Why wrong: unit errors change a value by factors of 100 or 10,000. Recognize it: a column called “Ca” contains decimals without units. Prevent it: use names such as Ca_ppm . Remember: 22 ppm = 0.0022 wt% = 0.000022 mass fraction. Engineering error: mixing incompatible Charpy definitions Why wrong: base metal, weld, fusion line, HAZ, orientation, specimen size, and test temperature represent different populations. Recognize it: the same response column silently combines them. Prevent it: standardize or stratify definitions before modeling. Validation error: splitting specimen rows at random Why wrong: specimens from one heat can enter both training and validation sets, leaking heat-specific information. Recognize it: unusually strong validation performance that drops on a new production period. Prevent it: group cross-validation by Heat ID. Exam trap: random intercept versus random slope A heat-level Ca value cannot support a within-heat Ca slope because Ca does not vary inside a heat. A random Ca slope by heat is therefore not identified from this design. Random slopes require within-cluster predictor variation. Apply the workflow

sections.heading: Model answer
sections.text: 1. Experimental unit: Heat, because Ca and S vary only between heats. 2. Residual degrees of freedom: 5 heats − 3 parameters (intercept, Ca, S) = 2 residual df. Adding more heat-level predictors would reduce this further. 3. Why p = 0.002 is suspect: specimen-level OLS treats correlated rows as independent and repeats the same Ca and S values dozens of times. The nominal standard error is therefore likely too small. 4. Defensible current analysis: display the five heat means, chemistry values, within-heat distributions, and confounding table. Treat any regression as descriptive and explicitly avoid inferential or causal claims. A mixed model may describe variance but cannot make the chemistry effect well-supported with five heats. 5. Better data: collect more independent heats spanning the Ca range with overlap across sulfur, grade, practice, dimensions, slab thickness, and production period. Preserve multiple pipes and specimens to estimate lower-level variation, but prioritize new heats for the heat-level chemistry question. Take it to work

sections.heading: You built the model.Then what?
sections.text: Fitting a regression, a response surface, or a CatBoost model in Minitab, Excel, or Python is the middle of the job, not the end. A model is a mathematical stand-in for your process — it only earns its keep when you use it to decide or act . sections.heading: A model is a means, not a deliverable
breadcrumb: A model is a means, not a deliverable
sections.text: Nobody ships a model. They ship a decision : a mill reduction schedule, a dryer operating window, a soft-sensor readout, a control-plan setpoint. The model is the tool that lets you answer a question cheaply — in silico — instead of running another 30 heats. So the honest way to ask "then what?" is to ask what question are you trying to answer . Each question routes you to a different next step. Here's the whole menu on one plate; the rest of the lesson takes each item in turn. "What will Y be if I set X here?"

sections.heading: Predict — and pick the right interval
breadcrumb: Predict — and pick the right interval
sections.text: The simplest use: plug new settings into the fitted equation and read off \(\hat{Y}\). For a yield-strength model that's predict(reduction=18%, C=0.06, Nb=0.035, coil_temp=560) . The number itself is the easy part. The part people get wrong — and the part that changes decisions — is how much to trust it . The one distinction that trips everyone Confidence interval (CI) = uncertainty about the average Y at those settings. Prediction interval (PI) = uncertainty about a single next observation. The PI is always wider because it carries both the model's uncertainty and the process's own scatter. Decision rule: if you're setting policy about the process on average ("does grade X70 clear 355 MPa on average?"), the CI is your tool. If you're making a call about the next pipe or next heat ("will this heat pass?"), you owe the customer a PI. Quoting a CI where a PI belongs is how a process that looks capable on paper ships nonconforming product. $$\hat{Y}_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-p}\; s\sqrt{\underbrace{x_0^\top (X^\top X)^{-1} x_0}_{\text{mean: CI}} \;+\; \underbrace{1}_{\text{new obs: PI}}}$$ That lone +1 under the root is the entire difference between the two intervals. Drop it and you have a CI; keep it and you have a PI. As sample size grows the CI term shrinks toward zero, but the +1 never does — the PI can't get narrower than the process's own noise. The widget below lets you feel that.

sections.heading: Connection between them
breadcrumb: Predict — and pick the right interval
sections.text: Strip away the regression machinery and the same logic shows up in the simplest possible case — a plain sample mean, no model at all. For a mean \(\bar{X}\) with sample standard deviation \(S\) and \(t = t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\): Confidence interval — for the process average $$\bar{X} \;\pm\; t\,S\,\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n}}$$ Prediction interval — for a single next observation $$\bar{X} \;\pm\; t\,S\,\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{n}}$$ Notice the prediction interval carries \(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n}}\) where the confidence interval only has \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}\). Since \(1 + \frac{1}{n} > \frac{1}{n}\) for every sample size, the prediction interval is always wider . And as \(n\) grows the \(\frac{1}{n}\) term melts toward zero — the CI can shrink to a point, but the PI can't drop below \(\bar{X} \pm tS\), because that leading 1 is the process's own scatter. It is the exact same role the +1 plays inside the regression formula above.

sections.heading: Real problems have competing responses
sections.text: You almost never optimize one thing in isolation. On a roughing-mill reduction schedule you want strength up , toughness held , roll load and energy down , all at once — and the setting that maxes one degrades another. Two standard ways to handle it: Desirability functions (Derringer–Suich). Convert each response to a 0–1 desirability \(d_i\) (0 = unacceptable, 1 = ideal), then combine into one composite \(D=(d_1 d_2 \cdots d_k)^{1/k}\), optionally weighted by importance. The optimizer maximizes \(D\). Because it's a geometric mean, any \(d_i = 0\) forces \(D=0\) — one violated response kills the whole setting. That's the behavior you want. Overlaid contour plots. Draw each response's spec contour on the same factor axes; the region where all of them are simultaneously satisfied is your operating window. This is precisely the deliverable behind an "operating-window optimization" — you're not handing over a single point, you're handing over the feasible zone plus a recommended center.

sections.heading: Which knobs actually move Y
sections.text: Before optimizing, know your leverage. From a designed experiment: the Pareto of standardized effects and the normal/half-normal plot separate the vital few from the trivial many. From a fitted regression: standardized coefficients. From a tree model like your CatBoost yield-strength work: SHAP values and partial-dependence plots, which show not just how much a factor matters but which direction and where it bites. Why bother before optimizing? Because it tells you where to spend control effort. A factor with huge leverage needs tight tolerances at the setpoint; a factor with near-zero effect is free real estate — loosen its tolerance and buy back cost or throughput. 4 · Robust design

sections.heading: The best mean can be a fragile place to sit
breadcrumb: The best mean can be a fragile place to sit
sections.text: The peak of a response surface is often on a steep slope — great average, but a small drift in a noisy input sends Y tumbling. Robust design asks a different question: where is the surface flat? A slightly lower mean on a plateau beats a higher mean on a cliff, because the plateau transmits less variation from the noise you can't control. Taguchi robust parameter design — deliberately separates control factors from noise factors and finds settings that minimize the noise's effect. Dual-response surface — model the mean and the variance, then optimize for on-target mean with minimum variance. Propagation of error — use the model's slopes to predict how much input scatter shows up in output scatter; steep slope = high transmitted variation.

sections.heading: A point estimate hides the risk; a distribution shows it
breadcrumb: A point estimate hides the risk; a distribution shows it
sections.text: Your optimizer hands back a single setpoint and a predicted mean. But every input has real variation — tundish weight drifts, chemistry ranges, coil temperature swings. Monte Carlo pushes those input distributions through the model thousands of times to produce the distribution of Y. From that you read the predicted defect rate and predicted Cpk — capability, estimated before you commit a single trial heat. This is the natural bridge from "the model says the mean will be 372 MPa" to "the model says 98.6% of heats clear 355 MPa with the current input tolerances." One is a number; the other is a business decision.

sections.heading: Confirm — reality gets a vote
sections.text: The model is a hypothesis about the process. Before you roll a new schedule to production, you test the hypothesis : run confirmation trials at the predicted optimum and compare what actually happens to what the model promised. Pass Actual results land inside the prediction interval from item 1. The model generalizes; you've earned the right to deploy. Note that "inside the PI" is the right bar — not "exactly equal to the point prediction," which never happens. Fail Results fall outside the PI . Don't tune the setpoint and try again — that's fitting to noise. Loop back: check for a missing term or interaction, a curvature you didn't model, extrapolation, or a lurking variable that shifted between the design runs and now. The most common way good analyses go bad Skipping confirmation. A response surface optimized on 20 runs will always report an impressive optimum — that's what optimizers do. Whether that optimum survives contact with the real process is a separate, empirical question. In DMAIC this is a gate, not a formality: no confirmed result, no Control phase.

sections.heading: Deploy & monitor — hold the gains
sections.text: A confirmed optimum that isn't held drifts back to baseline within a quarter. Deployment is what turns a one-time improvement into a permanent one, and it's where the model often gets a second life as an operational asset. Lock the setpoints into the control plan. The optimized settings become documented operating parameters with tolerances — tightest on the high-leverage factors from item 3, loosest where you have slack. Put SPC on the vital few. Control charts on the key X's and the Y catch drift before it becomes scrap. This is the "hold" mechanism — signal vs noise, tampering vs missed shifts. Run the model as a soft sensor. If Y is slow, expensive, or destructive to measure (Charpy, tensile) and the X's are cheap and fast, the model predicts Y in near-real-time from routine inputs — an inferential measurement between physical tests. Score new data in a pipeline. Batch or streaming, the fitted model becomes a step in production: new heat → predict → flag if predicted Y approaches spec. Monitor for drift. Models decay as equipment wears, feedstock shifts, seasons change. Track the residuals (actual − predicted) on a control chart of their own; a trend or a widening spread is the model telling you it's going stale and needs a refit. The quiet killer "Set and forget." A model deployed with no drift monitoring is a liability with a shelf life — it keeps returning confident predictions long after the process has moved out from under it. Budget for periodic revalidation the same way you budget for gauge R&R.

sections.text: Stat ▸ Regression / DOE Once you've run Fit Regression Model (or a DOE analysis), Minitab stores the equation and every option below operates on it. The three you'll reach for after fitting map straight onto the menu you already know — Predict, Factorial Plots, and Response Optimizer — and they cover items 1, 3, and 2 of the menu above. Read this before you click Predict A model can post a healthy R-sq and still be useless for prediction. Check R-sq(pred) in the model summary first: an R-sq of 76% next to an R-sq(pred) of 0.00% means the model explains the data you already have and predicts nothing new — every Predict output from it would be fiction. R-sq(pred) is the gatekeeper for this whole section. Predict — item 1

sections.heading: Multiple responses, one desirability, draggable setpoints
breadcrumb: Multiple responses, one desirability, draggable setpoints
sections.text: The Response Optimizer is Minitab's desirability engine (the composite D from the optimize widget, run for real). You state a goal and importance for each response; it returns the factor settings that maximize composite desirability and an optimization plot with red vertical lines you can drag to explore trade-offs live. Real problem: set the roughing schedule so strength hits target, toughness stays acceptable, and roll load stays under the mill's limit. RESPONSE OPTIMIZER — Goals 3 responses Response Goal Lower Target Upper Weight Import Strength Maximize 355 420 — 1 1 Toughness Target 80 120 160 1 1 Roll load Minimize — — 9.5 1 1 Solution Reduction = 16.4% Carbon = 0.058% Composite Desirability D = 0.87 Predicted: Strength 401 MPa Toughness 118 J Roll load 9.1 MN D = 0.87 (not 1.0) is honest: no single setting is perfect for all three, and the geometric mean would have collapsed to 0 if any response were out of bounds. Drag a setpoint in the real optimization plot and every predicted response — and D — recomputes instantly. Why Contour / Surface / Overlaid were greyed out Those three need two or more continuous predictors in the fitted model to have a surface to draw. Add a second factor and they wake up — and Overlaid Contour Plot becomes your operating-window deliverable: every response's spec contour on one pair of axes, with the feasible region shaded where they all overlap. sections.heading: Excel functions
sections.text: Function Syntax Purpose When to use it TREND =TREND(known_ys, known_xs, new_xs) Fit a linear least-squares model and return the fitted Y at one or more new X values. Fast point predictions straight from historical X/Y columns, no separate model object. FORECAST.LINEAR =FORECAST.LINEAR(x, known_ys, known_xs) Predict Y at a single new X on the fitted line. A one-off point prediction with a single predictor (successor to the legacy FORECAST). LINEST =LINEST(known_ys, known_xs, TRUE, TRUE) Array result: coefficients, their standard errors, R², F, residual df, and s. When you need the coefficients and s to build confidence / prediction intervals by hand or for several predictors. SLOPE / INTERCEPT =SLOPE(ys, xs) · =INTERCEPT(ys, xs) Return b₁ and b₀ of a simple linear fit. Rebuild the prediction equation in a cell so Goal Seek, Solver, or a Data Table can push values through it. STEYX =STEYX(known_ys, known_xs) Standard error of the estimate, s . The process-spread term that sets prediction-interval width. T.INV.2T =T.INV.2T(alpha, df) Two-tailed Student-t critical value. The multiplier for a CI or PI at confidence 1−alpha (e.g. alpha = 0.05 for 95%). NORM.DIST =NORM.DIST(x, mean, sd, TRUE) Cumulative normal probability up to x. Fraction of heats below an LSL (yield loss) or above a USL; feeds DPMO. NORM.S.INV =NORM.S.INV(probability) Inverse standard normal (z-score). Convert a target yield to a z, or build z-based capability estimates. Cpk (manual) =(mean−LSL)/(3*sd) One-sided lower capability index. Turn a simulated mean and sd into predicted capability before committing to runs. Array note: modern Excel spills LINEST automatically; in older versions enter it as an array with Ctrl + Shift + Enter . The optimisation and What-If tools (Solver, Goal Seek, two-variable Data Table) are covered in the In Excel section above.

sections.heading: Excel use cases
sections.text: Point prediction: put the fitted equation =290+4.6*B1+320*(B2-0.05) in a cell with reduction in B1 and carbon in B2 . At R = 16.4% , C = 0.058% it returns about 368 MPa . Prediction interval: with s from STEYX (≈ 11) and t = T.INV.2T(0.05, n−2) , a single-heat 95% PI is roughly fit ± t·√(s² + SE_fit²) . Quote the lower bound when you promise a heat clears 355 MPa. Confidence interval: same t but only SE_fit (drop the s² term) — the narrower band for the average heat, not a single one. Predicted capability: after a Monte-Carlo Data Table, compute =(mean−355)/(3*sd) for Cpk and =1−NORM.DIST(355, mean, sd, TRUE) for the fraction clearing spec.

sections.heading: Minitab navigation
sections.text: Fit the model: Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model . From a designed experiment use Stat → DOE → Factorial → Analyze Factorial Design or Stat → DOE → Response Surface → Analyze Response Surface Design . Predict with CI & PI (item 1): Stat → Regression → Regression → Predict . Enter the factor settings; the table returns Fit, SE Fit, 95% CI, and 95% PI side by side. DOE alternative: Stat → DOE → Response Surface → Predict . Choose Predict (not a fitted-line plot) when you need the numeric interval table for specific settings. Optimize (item 2): Stat → DOE → Response Surface → Response Optimizer (or the Factorial equivalent) for multi-response desirability. For a feasible operating window rather than one point, use Stat → DOE → Response Surface → Overlaid Contour Plot . Rank drivers & interactions (item 3): Stat → DOE → Factorial → Factorial Plots (Main Effects and Interaction) and the Pareto of standardized effects from the analysis dialog. Capability from the prediction (item 5): Stat → Quality Tools → Capability Analysis → Normal . Monitor residuals (item 7): Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → I-MR on the actual−predicted residuals. Exam tips CI vs PI is a classic trap. On the ASQ CSSBB and CQE exams, remember the prediction interval is always wider because it adds the individual-observation spread; a question that asks about a single future unit wants the PI. The confidence interval is for the mean response. Improve-phase content. Response-surface optimization and desirability sit in the CSSBB Improve body of knowledge; capability indices (Cpk / Ppk) and control-chart monitoring map to CSSBB Control and to the CQE statistics and SPC sections. Expect items on choosing the Response Optimizer vs an overlaid contour plot. Real-world discipline. Never extrapolate beyond the design space, confirm at the predicted optimum before deploying, and watch residuals for drift — the same sequence the consoles above rehearse. Cheat sheet

sections.heading: Traps between "model built" and "value delivered"
sections.text: Trap What it costs you Extrapolating past the design space The equation returns confident numbers that may be physically meaningless. Guard your input ranges. Quoting a CI where a PI belongs Process looks capable on average while individual units fail. Use PI for any per-unit decision. Optimizing one Y, breaking another Strength up, toughness gone. Use a composite objective or overlaid contours across all responses. Optimizing the mean, ignoring variance You land on a cliff. A flatter, slightly-lower setpoint transmits less noise and holds better. Skipping confirmation runs An in-silico optimum that never touched the real process. No confirmation, no rollout. Chasing R² instead of prediction error A model that fits the training data and predicts poorly. Judge on hold-out RMSE / MAE. Deploy and forget Silent decay. Chart the residuals; refit when they trend or spread. Treating hierarchical rows as independent Pseudoreplication inflates significance. Aggregate to the right level (slab / heat) before you model or predict.

sections.heading: The one-screen recap
sections.text: A model is a surrogate for a decision — building it is the middle of the job. Predict with the right interval: CI for the mean, PI for the next unit. Never extrapolate. Optimize across all responses at once — desirability or overlaid contours give an operating window, not a fragile point. Rank, robustify, simulate — know your leverage, sit on a plateau not a cliff, and predict the spread and Cpk before committing. Confirm against reality; land inside the PI or loop back. Deploy & monitor — control plan, SPC, soft sensor, and watch the residuals for drift.

sections.heading: In this lesson
sections.text: Evaluation is the discipline of asking, honestly, “would this model still be right on data it has never seen?” Tuning is the discipline of improving it without lying to yourself in the process. sections.heading: What is your model actually predicting?
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
sections.text: Before you can judge a model, you have to know what it is trying to do. Almost everyone’s first misunderstanding is the same one: they think a regression predicts the exact value. It doesn’t — and that gap is where every evaluation metric lives.
sections.excerpt: Before you can judge a model, you have to know what it is trying to do. Almost everyone’s first misunderstanding is the same one: they think a regression predicts the exact value. It doesn’t — and that gap is where every evaluation metric lives.

sections.heading: The confusion, stated plainly
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
sections.text: “When people say OLS regression predicts the average , I get confused, because I thought it predicts the actual value of y.” This is the single most common stumbling block in modeling, and it is worth clearing up completely. The weight analogy If I ask you to guess the weight of a person you have never met, your safest single guess is the average weight of everyone in the room. OLS regression does exactly this — just with more information. When you give it an input, it doesn’t know the random quirks that made one specific real value what it is; it gives you the average outcome for cases like this one .

sections.heading: It predicts the “conditional mean”
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
sections.text: When you plug an x into the model, OLS looks at how the target behaves for that kind of input and returns the average — the mean of y conditional on x. The goal is to predict the actual value; the reality is that the best possible guess for any specific case is the average of similar cases.

sections.heading: The error is the leftover
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
sections.text: For any single data point: Actual = Predicted + Error . The error (also called the residual ) is the part OLS cannot predict — the random noise it can’t see. The model hands you only the “Predicted” part, which is the average behavior at that x.

sections.heading: Why a straight line still works
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
Why a straight line still works
sections.text: Real data has scatter, so a straight line cannot touch every point. By minimizing the squares of the errors, the line settles right in the middle of the cloud of points — which is precisely why it behaves like a line of averages. The decomposition every metric is built on y i = ŷ i + e i where ŷ i = predicted (conditional mean) · e i = residual (what’s left) The reframe Stop reading “line of best fit” and start reading “ line of averages .” OLS predicts what y would be on average for a given x — which is, statistically, your most accurate single guess for the actual value. Quick check Your steel-process model predicts 512 kWh for a slab, but the slab actually used 505 kWh. Did the model fail? No. 512 kWh is the model’s estimate of the average energy for slabs with those settings. The 7 kWh gap is the residual — random, slab-specific variation the model was never trying to capture. You judge the model by the pattern of residuals across many slabs, not by any single miss. Try it Predicted mean vs. the actual slab The blue line is the model — a line of averages . Pick a process setting to see the predicted mean, then sample a real slab and watch the residual appear. Sample a few: the actuals scatter around the line, never on it. Process setting 50 Move the slider to a setting, then sample an actual slab to reveal its residual.

sections.heading: Not every model predicts the mean
breadcrumb: What is your model actually predicting?
Not every model predicts the mean
sections.text: This matters because it decides which metrics are even valid. Ordinary regression predicts the mean. Quantile regression deliberately predicts a chosen slice of the distribution instead — say the 90th percentile of energy use, the level you’ll stay under 90% of the time. Because it is not aiming at the mean, mean-based metrics like R² and RMSE measure the wrong target. We return to its special metrics in Module 4. Why this leads the lesson Every downstream choice — which metric, which diagnostic, what “good” looks like — depends on knowing what the model estimates. Get this wrong and you will happily optimize a number that means nothing. Module 02 · Validation

sections.heading: Validate: train, holdout & cross-validation
sections.text: A model that is graded on the same data it studied is like a student who saw the exam in advance. To know if it truly learned, you must test it on material it has never seen. That is the entire idea behind the three R² values you will see printed in modeling code. The core danger A flexible model can memorize its training data — capturing not just the real signal but the random noise. It then looks brilliant in training and collapses in the real world. This is overfitting , and validation exists to catch it.

sections.heading: Cross-validation R² — CV R²
breadcrumb: The three R² values, in order of trust
sections.text: cv_scores = cross_val_score(...) The model is trained and tested several times on different splits of the data, and the scores are averaged. You get both a central estimate and a spread. The number to trust How k-fold cross-validation works The data is cut into k equal folds (5 is common). Each fold takes a turn as the test set while the other four train the model. Average the five scores for a robust estimate, and read the spread as a stability check. Fold Train Test 1–5 (each) 80% 20% 5-fold CV R²: 0.68 ± 0.05 → average predictive power 0.68, split-to-split variation 0.05. Reading the three together Metric Data used Purpose In-sample R² Training data Fit quality Holdout R² 20% unseen Generalization test CV R² Many unseen splits Robust performance Rule of thumb Use CV R² as your main metric. Training R² is a diagnostic, holdout R² is a quick check, CV R² is the true performance estimate.

sections.heading: Two signatures you must recognize
sections.text: Healthy What good looks like Metric Value Training R² 0.78 Holdout R² 0.74 CV R² 0.72 ± 0.03 Training slightly higher than the rest; holdout and CV are close; the spread is small. The model learned the signal. Overfit What trouble looks like Metric Value Training R² 0.96 Holdout R² 0.42 CV R² 0.38 ± 0.10 A huge drop from training to test, and a large, unstable spread. The model memorized noise. Use case · the steel-process dataset The energy model groups rows by SlabID . Using GroupKFold , every measurement from one slab stays together — all in train or all in test, never split across both. So CV R² answers the question that actually matters on the plant floor: “How well can the model predict energy for completely new slabs it has never seen?” That is the most realistic measure you can get. The leakage trap If the same slab appears in both train and test, the model can “recognize” it and post an inflated score that evaporates in production. Grouped splitting is not a nicety here — it is the difference between an honest number and a fantasy. Compare The three-R² signature Toggle a scenario and read the shape of the three bars — the same at-a-glance diagnosis you'll make on real output. — Training R² — Holdout R² — Cross-val R² — — Quick check A model reports Training R² = 0.94, Holdout R² = 0.51, CV R² = 0.47 ± 0.12. What is your diagnosis, and what is your next move? Overfitting. The 0.94 → 0.51 collapse plus the wide ±0.12 spread are the classic signature. Next move: reduce model complexity (simpler model, fewer/less-correlated features, or regularization) and re-check with grouped cross-validation — covered in Module 3. Module 03 · Tuning

sections.heading: Tune: bias, variance & hyperparameters
sections.text: Validation tells you whether a model generalizes. Tuning is how you make it generalize better — dialing the model’s complexity to the sweet spot between too simple and too clever. The whole art is doing this without secretly cheating on your final test.
sections.excerpt: Validation tells you whether a model generalizes. Tuning is how you make it generalize better — dialing the model’s complexity to the sweet spot between too simple and too clever. The whole art is doing this without secretly cheating on your final test.

sections.heading: The bias–variance trade-off
sections.text: Every model’s total error on unseen data splits into two competing parts. Push one down and the other tends to rise; good tuning finds the balance. High bias · Underfit The model is too simple to capture the real pattern. It is wrong even on the training data. Signature: low R² everywhere — training, holdout, and CV all mediocre. High variance · Overfit The model is too flexible and chases noise. It is brilliant on training data and poor on new data. Signature: high training R², big drop to holdout/CV, wide spread. The sweet spot Enough complexity to catch the signal, not so much that it memorizes noise. Signature: training a touch higher than holdout/CV, all three close together. Explore The overfitting explorer Drag model complexity and watch the fit. The same training data is scored on held-out test points. Training R² only ever climbs — but test R² peaks, then collapses. That peak is the sweet spot tuning is hunting for. Training R² — Test / CV R² — — Model complexity (polynomial degree) 1 —

sections.heading: Search efficiently
sections.text: Grid search tries every combination — thorough but expensive. Random search samples combinations — usually finds a near-best setting far faster when the space is large.
sections.excerpt: Grid search tries every combination — thorough but expensive. Random search samples combinations — usually finds a near-best setting far faster when the space is large.

sections.heading: Lock it in, then test once
breadcrumb: Lock it in, then test once
sections.text: Pick the winning hyperparameters, retrain on all your training data, and evaluate a single time on the untouched test set. The tuning trap — do not skip this If you tune your hyperparameters against the test set , you have quietly turned it into a training set. Your final number becomes optimistic and dishonest. Keep three roles: train (fit), validation / CV (tune), and a held-back test set (report once, at the very end). Nested cross-validation formalizes this when data is scarce. Regularization — a tuning lever with a bonus Ridge and Lasso regression add a penalty (λ) that shrinks coefficients toward zero. Turning λ up fights overfitting and stabilizes a model suffering from multicollinearity — which is exactly the “condition number” problem you will meet in Module 5. Lasso can also zero out weak predictors, doing feature selection for you. Quick check · steel model You are tuning the maximum depth of a tree on the steel data. Depth 3 gives CV R² 0.61, depth 8 gives 0.73, depth 20 gives training R² 0.98 but CV R² 0.55. Which depth do you ship, and why? Depth 8. It has the best cross-validated score. Depth 3 underfits (0.61 everywhere). Depth 20 overfits — the gorgeous 0.98 training score with a 0.55 CV score is memorization. You always tune to the CV number, not the training number. sections.text: A metric is a lens. The wrong lens can make a bad model look great. The metric must match three things at once: the type of problem , what the model predicts , and which mistake actually costs you . Decide Which metric should I use? The right metric depends on the problem type and what an error costs you . Pick both — the recommendation updates live. Problem type What matters most

sections.heading: Regression metrics — when the target is a number
breadcrumb: Regression metrics — when the target is a number
sections.text: Metric What it measures Behaviour Use it when MAE Mean Absolute Error The average size of the errors, ignoring sign. Treats all errors equally; robust to outliers. You want a plain, honest “typical miss” in original units. MSE Mean Squared Error The average of the squared errors. Punishes large mistakes far more heavily than small ones. Big misses are especially costly and must be discouraged. RMSE Root Mean Squared Error The square root of MSE. Same penalty as MSE but back in the target’s units. You want MSE’s sensitivity with a number you can read. R² Coefficient of determination The share of variance in the target the model explains. Ranges toward 1.0 for a strong fit; can be misleading alone. Communicating overall fit; comparing to a baseline. The three regression errors, side by side MAE = 1 n Σ |y − ŷ| · MSE = 1 n Σ (y − ŷ)² · RMSE = √MSE MAE vs RMSE in one line If a few huge errors should hurt a lot, use RMSE. If every error should count the same, use MAE. RMSE ≥ MAE always, and the gap between them tells you how much your errors vary in size.

sections.heading: Classification metrics — when the target is a class
breadcrumb: Classification metrics — when the target is a class
sections.text: These all come from the confusion matrix : counts of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), and false negatives (FN). Metric Plain meaning Formula Use it when Accuracy Share of all predictions that are correct. (TP+TN) / all Classes are balanced. Misleads on imbalance Precision Of the cases flagged positive, how many really are. TP / (TP+FP) False positives are costly (false alarms). Recall (sensitivity) Of the real positives, how many you caught. TP / (TP+FN) Missing a positive is dangerous. F1-score The balance point between precision and recall. harmonic mean You need both and the data is imbalanced. ROC-AUC Ability to separate classes across all thresholds. See the interactive curve ↓ area under ROC Ranking quality; threshold-free comparison. Use case · defect detection A vision system flags defective parts. Here a missed defect (a false negative) ships a bad part to a customer — expensive and dangerous — while a false alarm just triggers a re-inspection. So you optimize Recall , accepting some precision loss. Flip the costs (say, a fraud filter that freezes innocent customers’ accounts) and you would optimize Precision instead. The metric follows the cost. The accuracy illusion If 99% of parts are good, a model that blindly says “good” every time scores 99% accuracy — and catches zero defects. On imbalanced data, accuracy is the metric that lies most confidently. Reach for precision, recall, F1, or ROC-AUC. Try it Move the threshold — watch precision fight recall Each dot is a part the model scored 0→1 for “defect.” Slide the decision threshold : everything to its right is flagged. There is no free lunch — catching more defects (recall) means more false alarms (precision). Tap a chip to show or hide its curve — leave all three on to compare them at once, or narrow it down to just one. Drag the threshold and every visible curve gets a marker at that operating point, moving together. Decision threshold 0.50 Strong model 0.95 Excellent Fair model 0.76 Fair Weak model 0.58 Poor The dashed diagonal is a random guesser (AUC = 0.5). The dot at the top-left corner is a perfect classifier (AUC = 1.0) — every real curve lives somewhere between the two. Probability view What AUC actually means AUC also equals the probability that a randomly picked defect scores higher than a randomly picked good part — for whichever model you last tapped above. Draw pairs and watch the running estimate close in on its AUC. Ranges −1 to +1; higher means denser, better-separated groups. You have no ground truth and want to judge how clean the grouping is. sections.heading: Quantile-regression metrics — when you predict a percentile
breadcrumb: Quantile-regression metrics — when you predict a percentile
sections.text: Recall from Module 1 that quantile regression aims at a slice of the distribution, not the mean. So mean-based metrics measure the wrong thing. Two purpose-built metrics take their place. Pinball loss (quantile loss) The primary error metric. Unlike MSE, it is asymmetric — it penalizes over- and under-predictions differently depending on the target quantile τ. τ = 0.5 (median): penalties are equal both ways — this is exactly MAE. τ = 0.9 (90th pctl): under-predicting is penalized 9× more than over-predicting, which forces the line to sit above ~90% of the points. Pseudo R² The goodness-of-fit measure, in the spirit of R². It compares your model’s pinball loss to that of a null model (no predictors — it just guesses the sample quantile). Like R², it runs 0→1; higher means your predictors beat the baseline. This is McFadden’s pseudo R², in the Koenker–Machado form for quantile regression. Feature OLS regression (mean) Quantile regression (τ) Primary loss Mean Squared Error Pinball (quantile) loss Error metric RMSE / MAE Mean pinball loss (= MAE if τ=0.5) Fit metric R² Pseudo R² Quick check You’re predicting hospital readmission (rare, ~5% positive). Someone reports 95% accuracy. Are you impressed? Not yet — maybe not at all. A model that predicts “no readmission” for everyone already scores 95% and helps no one. Ask for recall (are we catching the readmissions?), precision , and ideally ROC-AUC . On rare-event problems, accuracy is close to meaningless. Module 05 · Diagnostics

sections.heading: Diagnose: reading the regression output
sections.text: Metrics tell you how accurate a model is. Diagnostics tell you whether you are even allowed to trust it — whether its assumptions hold and its coefficients are stable. A model can predict well and still fail its diagnostics, and vice versa. Read both. When you fit an OLS model in statsmodels , the summary prints a block of diagnostics beneath the coefficients. Here is that block, decoded, using the real values from the steel-process energy model. Diagnostic What it tests for Benchmark Steel value Verdict Omnibus p Overall normality of residuals (skew + kurtosis together) > 0.05 = normal 0.000 ✘ ignore (large N) Jarque–Bera p Normality of residuals (a second test) > 0.05 = normal ~0 ✘ ignore (same reason) Skew Symmetry of the residual distribution ≈ 0 −0.21 ✔ good Kurtosis Tail heaviness / outliers in residuals ≈ 3 2.61 ✔ good Durbin–Watson Autocorrelation — are residuals independent? ≈ 2 1.57 ⚠ mild autocorrelation Condition Number Multicollinearity / numerical stability < 100 (ideally < 30) 7,500 ✘ needs attention AIC Fit vs complexity trade-off (prediction focus) Lower is better (relative only) ~917,400 ⚠ compare models only BIC Fit vs complexity, with a stronger penalty Lower is better (relative only) ~917,400+ ⚠ compare models only The large-N trap — the most important lesson here With tens of thousands of rows, the Omnibus and Jarque–Bera normality tests almost always “fail” (p ≈ 0) , because they are powerful enough to flag microscopic, harmless departures from perfect normality. That is why both are marked “ignore” above even though the residuals are actually fine. Trust the skew (−0.21 ≈ 0) and kurtosis (2.61 ≈ 3) values and a residual plot instead of the p-value. This single misread sinks a lot of otherwise-good analyses. Self-check Diagnostic triage — act or ignore? Before you read the verdict, decide for yourself: is each number a real problem, or a distraction? Tap to reveal. Omnibus p = 0.000 tests: normality of residuals Tap: act or ignore? With 60k rows this test flags microscopic, harmless departures from normality. Judge normality by skew & kurtosis instead — not this p-value. ✗ Ignore Jarque–Bera p ≈ 0 tests: normality (second test) Tap: act or ignore? Same large-N trap as Omnibus. Two failing normality p-values here mean nothing on their own at this sample size. ✗ Ignore Skew = −0.21 tests: symmetry of residuals Tap: act or ignore? Essentially symmetric (target ≈ 0). This is the value you actually trust for normality — and it says the residuals are fine. ✓ Fine Kurtosis = 2.61 tests: tail heaviness Tap: act or ignore? Close to the normal benchmark of 3, slightly light-tailed. No outlier problem in the residuals. ✓ Fine Durbin–Watson = 1.57 tests: independence of residuals Tap: act or ignore? Below the ideal 2 → mild positive autocorrelation. Check row ordering / grouping; consider robust standard errors. ⚠ Watch Condition No. = 7,500 tests: multicollinearity Tap: act or ignore? Far above 30. Predictors are nearly collinear, so individual coefficients are unstable. Drop/combine features or use ridge. ✗ Act AIC / BIC ≈ 917k tests: fit vs complexity Tap: act or ignore? Only meaningful compared to another model fit to the same data. The absolute number says nothing on its own. ⚠ Relative VIF (per predictor) tests: collinearity per variable Tap: act or ignore? VIF > 10 (some say 5) flags a predictor tangled with the others — the per-variable companion to the condition number. ⚠ Check

sections.heading: What to do when a diagnostic fails
breadcrumb: What to do when a diagnostic fails
sections.text: High condition number / VIF → multicollinearity Your predictors overlap, so coefficients become unstable and their signs can flip. Fix: drop or combine correlated predictors, standardize the inputs, prune by VIF, or apply ridge regression (Module 3). Durbin–Watson far from 2 → autocorrelation Residuals aren’t independent — common with time-ordered or grouped data. Fix: check the ordering, add lag terms, model the group structure, or use autocorrelation-robust standard errors. At 1.57 the steel model shows only mild positive autocorrelation. Non-normal residuals With large samples the central limit theorem protects your inference, so mild non-normality is usually fine. Real problems are strong skew or heavy tails driven by outliers — investigate those points, consider a transform. AIC / BIC look enormous Their absolute size is meaningless — they only matter relative to another model on the same data. Lower wins; BIC penalizes extra predictors harder, so it prefers simpler models. The mental model Metrics answer “is it accurate?” Diagnostics answer “is it trustworthy ?” The steel model is a perfect example: its residuals are well-shaped (good skew and kurtosis), but a condition number of 7,500 warns that its coefficients are riding on multicollinearity and should not be interpreted one-by-one until that is fixed. Quick check A colleague rejects a 60,000-row model because the Jarque–Bera p-value is 0.000, declaring “the residuals aren’t normal, the model is invalid.” Are they right? Almost certainly not. At 60,000 rows JB will reject on trivial departures from normality. Point them to the skew and kurtosis (near 0 and 3 = fine) and a residual histogram. The p-value is being driven by sample size, not by a real problem. Module 06 · Statistics Implementation

sections.heading: Excel functions
sections.text: Function Syntax Purpose When to use it RSQ =RSQ(known_y, known_x) R² of a simple linear regression. Quick fit measure for one predictor. LINEST =LINEST(y, x_range, TRUE, TRUE) Full regression: coefficients, standard errors, R², F, and residual df (array-entered). Multiple regression, or when you need SEs and R² together. SLOPE / INTERCEPT =SLOPE(y,x) · =INTERCEPT(y,x) The b and a of the fitted line. Reporting or hand-computing predictions. TREND / FORECAST.LINEAR =FORECAST.LINEAR(new_x, y, x) Predicted y (ŷ) for new inputs. Generating the predicted column for error metrics. STEYX =STEYX(known_y, known_x) Standard error of the estimate (Minitab’s “S”). Typical prediction error in the target’s units. SUMXMY2 =SUMXMY2(actual, predicted) Σ(actual − predicted)² — the SSE, the building block of MSE/RMSE. Manually computing MSE and RMSE. DEVSQ =DEVSQ(actual) Σ(actual − mean)² — the total sum of squares (SST). Manually computing R² = 1 − SSE/SST. CORREL / PEARSON =CORREL(a, b) Pearson correlation r between two variables. Screening relationships and collinearity. SKEW / KURT =SKEW(residuals) · =KURT(residuals) Skewness and kurtosis of residuals. Checking residual shape (see caveat below). COUNTIFS =COUNTIFS(actual,1,pred,1) Counts TP / FP / TN / FN cells of a confusion matrix. Building precision, recall, accuracy, F1 by hand. Caveat that trips people up Excel’s KURT returns excess kurtosis, so a normal distribution reads ≈ 0 — whereas the statsmodels output in Module 5 reports raw kurtosis, where normal ≈ 3 . Same shape, two conventions. Add 3 to Excel’s value to compare.

sections.heading: Exam tips — ASQ CSSBB / CQE
sections.text: R² vs adjusted R²: the exam expects you to know that plain R² only ever rises when you add predictors, while adjusted R² penalizes useless ones — use it to compare models with different numbers of terms. “S” (standard error of the estimate) is the exam’s favourite “typical prediction error” value — smaller is better, and it is in the response’s units. Know it maps to Excel’s STEYX . VIF > 10 is the classic multicollinearity flag on the exam; the recommended remedies (remove/combine predictors, collect better data) are frequently tested. Residual analysis — independence (Durbin–Watson ≈ 2), constant variance (no funnel in the residual plot), and normality (probability plot) — is core CSSBB Analyze/Improve content. Expect to interpret a residual plot, not just compute a number. Match the metric to the question: regression → MAE/RMSE/R²; classification → precision/recall/F1 and the cost of each error. The exam rewards choosing recall when a miss is dangerous and precision when a false alarm is costly. The large-N caveat — that normality tests over-reject on big samples — is exactly the kind of interpretation nuance CQE questions use to separate rote memorizers from real analysts. Reference

sections.heading: When you see this, it means this
breadcrumb: When you see this, it means this
sections.text: Tap any card to flip it — front is the symptom you'd spot in output, back is the diagnosis and the fix. Training R² ≫ holdout / CV R² Tap: what it means → Means: Overfitting — the model memorized noise. Do: Simplify, cut correlated features, add regularization; re-check with grouped CV. BAD All three R² values low Tap: what it means → Means: Underfitting — the model is too simple. Do: Add signal: better features, interactions, or a more flexible model. WARN Wide ± spread on CV R² Tap: what it means → Means: Instability — performance depends on the split. Do: Get more data, reduce complexity, confirm the split fits the data's structure. WARN 95%+ accuracy on a rare event Tap: what it means → Means: The accuracy illusion — 'always negative' scores high. Do: Switch to recall, precision, F1, or ROC-AUC. BAD Normality p ≈ 0 on a huge dataset Tap: what it means → Means: Usually the large-N trap, not a real problem. Do: Judge by skew (≈0), kurtosis (≈3), and a residual plot. GOOD Condition number in thousands / VIF > 10 Tap: what it means → Means: Multicollinearity — coefficients unstable. Do: Drop or combine predictors, standardize, or use ridge regression. BAD Durbin–Watson well below 2 Tap: what it means → Means: Positive autocorrelation — residuals not independent. Do: Check ordering/grouping, add lag terms, or use robust SEs. WARN R² reported for a quantile model Tap: what it means → Means: Wrong metric — it assumes a mean prediction. Do: Use pinball loss and pseudo R² instead. BAD Traps

sections.heading: Where people go wrong
sections.text: Trap Judging on the training score Why wrong: a model can memorize its training data. Avoid it: report cross-validated performance on unseen data. Trap Tuning on the test set Why wrong: it quietly turns the test set into training data and inflates your final number. Avoid it: tune with CV, keep one untouched test set. Trap Leaking groups across the split Why wrong: the same slab in train and test lets the model “recognize” it. Avoid it: use GroupKFold to keep whole groups together. Trap Trusting accuracy on imbalanced data Why wrong: the majority class dominates the score. Avoid it: use precision, recall, F1, or ROC-AUC. Trap Chasing a normality p-value on big data Why wrong: the test over-rejects at large N. Avoid it: read skew, kurtosis, and plots. Trap Interpreting coefficients under multicollinearity Why wrong: a high condition number makes individual coefficients unstable and their signs unreliable. Avoid it: fix collinearity first, then interpret. Trap Comparing AIC/BIC across different datasets Why wrong: their scale has no absolute meaning. Avoid it: compare only across models fit to the same data. Trap Trusting a model because the software ran Why wrong: software executes instructions; it doesn’t validate the question or the assumptions. Avoid it: check inputs, metrics, and diagnostics in context. Practice

sections.heading: The evaluation mindset
sections.text: A regression predicts the conditional mean — the average outcome for cases like this one. The residual is the part it can’t and isn’t trying to predict. Judge a model on data it has never seen. Training R² is a diagnostic, holdout R² is a quick check, cross-validation R² is the truth. A big train→test gap and a wide CV spread mean overfitting ; low scores everywhere mean underfitting . Tuning navigates the bias–variance trade-off between them. Tune with cross-validation, never on the test set. Keep one untouched test set for a single, honest final number. Match the metric to the problem and the cost of errors: recall when a miss is dangerous, precision when a false alarm is costly, RMSE when big misses hurt, and never accuracy alone on imbalanced data. Diagnostics test trustworthiness , not accuracy. Beware the large-N normality trap; act on high condition number / VIF and on Durbin–Watson far from 2. With grouped data, split by the group (SlabID) so the score answers the real question: can it predict something brand new? Remember this Predict → Validate → Tune → Measure → Diagnose Decision rule Never trust a single number. Read fit and generalization together, match the metric to the decision, and let the diagnostics tell you whether you’re even allowed to believe the coefficients. breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Thirty years on shop floors and mine sites taught me one thing: every dataset has a troublemaker. Your job isn't to exorcise it — it's to interrogate it. We'll use blast-furnace temperatures, tensile tests, ore grades, and a runaway conveyor to learn four detection methods and, more importantly, what to do once you've caught your suspect. Why this matters: delete a genuine high-grade ore pocket and you throw away the best day the pit ever had. Keep a mis-keyed tensile reading and you ship steel on a lie. Outlier handling is a judgment skill, not a delete key.

sections.heading: Learning objectives
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: Define an outlier and distinguish measurement error, data error, and genuine extreme values. Calculate the Z-score, Modified Z-score (MAD-based), IQR/Tukey fences, and Grubbs' test statistic by hand and in Excel. Select the right detection method based on sample size, distribution shape, and data sensitivity. Investigate a flagged point using a disciplined root-cause procedure before deciding what to do with it. Explain masking and swamping, and why deleting outliers without investigation is a data-integrity risk. Execute the full workflow in both Excel and Minitab, and connect it to ASQ CSSBB/CQE exam expectations.

sections.heading: What exactly is an outlier?
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Here's the definition I've used since my first plant assignment: an outlier is an observation that is inconsistent with the bulk of the data , given some assumed model of how the data should behave. That's it. Statistics gives you tools to flag candidates — it does not tell you why a point is weird. That part is still your job, and it's the part most courses skip. In thirty years of chasing weird numbers through blast furnaces, rolling mills, and open pits, every flagged point eventually sorted itself into one of four buckets:

sections.heading: 1. Z-score

sections.heading: 4. Grubbs' test (ESD, one-sided or two-sided)
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: G = max|xᵢ − x̄| s Reject (flag as outlier) if G exceeds the critical value G crit , which depends on n and your significance level α (typically 0.05) via the t-distribution. Assumes the data are approximately normal. Note: Grubbs' test formally checks only the single most extreme point. To check for more than one outlier, use an iterative approach (remove, retest) or the Generalized ESD test — but iterate carefully, since removing points changes your critical value each round.

sections.heading: Regression / multiple variables
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Check leverage, Cook's distance, and Mahalanobis distance — a point can be unremarkable on each variable alone and still be a multivariate outlier. My rule of thumb after 30 years: run at least two methods. If the Z-score, Modified Z-score, IQR fences, and Grubbs' test all agree, you have real confidence. If they disagree, that disagreement is itself information — usually about masking.

sections.heading: Step-by-step investigation procedure
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Plot it first. Boxplot, individual value plot, or run chart — before any formula. Your eyes catch things statistics miss. Screen with a distribution-free method. IQR fences work regardless of shape and cost nothing to compute. Confirm with a formal test if needed. Grubbs' test if approximately normal; otherwise document the IQR/Modified-Z flag. Investigate the root cause before touching the data. Pull the calibration log, the sample log, the shift log, the material certs. Talk to the operator. Classify it. Measurement error, data error, genuine process shift, or genuine rare event — pick one, with evidence. Decide and document. Correct (if the true value is known), exclude with a documented reason, Winsorize/trim for a specific analysis, or keep it as-is. Never delete silently. Re-run the analysis both ways. Report how the conclusion changes with and without the point — this transparency is what separates rigor from cherry-picking. The cardinal sin: deleting a point because it "ruins the story" or fails a normality test, with no investigation and no documentation. An auditor — or an ASQ exam question — will find this every time.

sections.heading: Worked example: the furnace mystery
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Problem: Sixteen consecutive hot-metal temperature readings (°C) from a blast furnace: 1494, 1502, 1497, 1508, 1499, 1505, 1496, 1501, 1503, 1498, 1500, 1506, 1495, 1504, 1499, 1612. Is 1612°C an outlier, and what should we do about it? Plot it. Fifteen readings cluster tightly around 1500°C; 1612°C sits well clear of the pack on a boxplot. Screen with IQR. Q1 = 1497.75, Q3 = 1504.25, IQR = 6.5. Upper fence = 1504.25 + 1.5(6.5) = 1514.0°C. 1612°C is far beyond it. Confirm with Grubbs. Mean ≈ 1507.44, s ≈ 28.17, G ≈ 3.71. For n = 16 at α = 0.05, G crit ≈ 2.59. Since G > G crit , we reject the null — 1612°C is a statistical outlier. Investigate. The maintenance log shows the thermocouple was replaced two readings later after failing a calibration check — it had drifted high after a furnace reline. Classify and decide. This is a measurement error . We exclude the reading from the process-capability calculation, log the reason (thermocouple drift, confirmed by maintenance record), and flag the sensor for more frequent calibration. Payoff: excluding this one documented point drops the calculated standard deviation from ≈28.2°C to ≈4.2°C — the furnace was never actually running that wild. Reporting 28.2°C as "typical" variation would have triggered an unnecessary and expensive process investigation.

sections.heading: Interpretation guide
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: When you see this, it means this. When you see this It means this What to say / do All four methods flag the same point Strong, convergent evidence of a genuine outlier. Proceed to root-cause investigation with confidence. Z-score misses it, but Modified Z and IQR flag it Classic masking — the outlier has inflated the mean and SD enough to hide itself from a plain Z-score. Trust the robust methods (median/MAD, IQR) over the Z-score here. Grubbs' test says "not significant" on skewed data Grubbs assumes approximate normality; a skewed shape can violate that assumption. Check a probability plot first; fall back to IQR fences if normality is doubtful. A cluster of points near the fence all get flagged Possible swamping — legitimate points crowded by a genuinely shifted subgroup. Investigate whether a real process shift (not individual point errors) occurred. The flagged point has a confirmed calibration failure Measurement error. Exclude from analysis, document the reason and evidence, fix or replace the instrument. The flagged point matches a known process/material change Genuine special cause. Keep it, but segment the analysis; investigate and correct the process, not the data. The flagged point has no assignable cause after real investigation Possibly a genuine rare event from natural variation. Keep it in the primary analysis; consider reporting a robust statistic (median/IQR) alongside the mean/SD.

sections.heading: Excel Functions
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Functions used to detect and characterize outliers in Excel. Function Syntax Purpose When to use it AVERAGE =AVERAGE(range) Sample mean, x̄ Baseline center for the Z-score method. MEDIAN =MEDIAN(range) Robust center, x̃ Foundation for the Modified Z-score and MAD; unaffected by the outlier itself. STDEV.S =STDEV.S(range) Sample standard deviation Denominator of the Z-score and Grubbs' G, for a sample (n − 1 divisor). STDEV.P =STDEV.P(range) Population standard deviation Only when your data is the entire population, not a sample — rare in process work. STANDARDIZE =STANDARDIZE(x, mean, sd) Computes a Z-score directly Fast one-cell Z-score without building the subtraction/division yourself. QUARTILE.INC =QUARTILE.INC(range, quart) Q1 (quart=1) and Q3 (quart=3), inclusive method Standard, most-taught method for building IQR/Tukey fences. QUARTILE.EXC =QUARTILE.EXC(range, quart) Q1/Q3, exclusive method Use when your course or standard specifically calls for the exclusive definition; gives slightly different fences on small n. PERCENTILE.INC =PERCENTILE.INC(range, k) Any percentile Cross-checking quartiles or building custom fences (e.g., 5th/95th percentile). ABS =ABS(number) Absolute value Core building block for MAD, Modified Z-score, and Grubbs' numerator. AVEDEV =AVEDEV(range) Average absolute deviation from the mean Note: this is not MAD. Don't substitute it for the median-based MAD formula. MAD (array formula) =MEDIAN(ABS(range-MEDIAN(range))) Median Absolute Deviation Enter as an array formula (Ctrl+Shift+Enter in older Excel, or automatically in dynamic-array Excel/365). Required for the Modified Z-score. LARGE / SMALL =LARGE(range,1) / =SMALL(range,1) Extreme values by rank Pull the most extreme value to feed Grubbs' numerator, max|xᵢ − x̄|. T.INV.2T =T.INV.2T(probability, deg_freedom) Two-tailed inverse t critical value Computes the t value needed inside the Grubbs' critical-value formula. T.DIST.2T =T.DIST.2T(x, deg_freedom) Two-tailed p-value from a t statistic Convert a Grubbs-derived t statistic back into a p-value for reporting. COUNT =COUNT(range) Sample size, n Needed everywhere — Grubbs' critical value depends heavily on n. IF / AND =IF(ABS(z)>3,"Flag","OK") Flagging logic Turn any of the above statistics into a pass/fail column for review.

breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: Building a Z-score column (data in A2:A17, mean in D1, SD in D2): =(A2-$D$1)/$D$2 , filled down, then flag with =IF(ABS(B2)>3,"Flag","") . Building the Modified Z-score: with median in D3 and MAD in D4 (array formula above), =0.6745*(A2-$D$3)/$D$4 , flag at |M| > 3.5. Building IQR fences: =QUARTILE.INC($A$2:$A$17,1) and =QUARTILE.INC($A$2:$A$17,3) in two cells, then =Q3-Q1 for IQR, and =Q1-1.5*IQR / =Q3+1.5*IQR for the fences. Assembling Grubbs' critical value: with n in D5, α = 0.05: =T.INV.2T(0.05/D5, D5-2) gives the t value, then =((D5-1)/SQRT(D5))*SQRT(t^2/(D5-2+t^2)) gives G crit . Compare against G = =MAX(ABS(A2:A17-$D$1))/$D$2 (entered as an array formula). Caution: Excel has no single built-in "Grubbs' test" function — you assemble it from T.INV.2T, exactly as shown above. Don't confuse this with a simple Z-score screen.

sections.heading: Exam tips
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: ASQ CSSBB / CQE exam connections: outlier detection sits under the Measure phase / basic statistics domain. Expect questions that (1) ask you to compute a Z-score, IQR fence, or interpret a Grubbs' test result by hand or from output; (2) test whether you know Grubbs' test requires an approximate normality assumption while IQR fences do not; (3) present a scenario and ask what you should do before removing a point (the answer is almost always "investigate and document," not "delete"); and (4) distinguish an outlier from a point that is merely influential in a regression context. In real-world capability studies, always report whether outliers were included or excluded and why — an auditor will ask.

sections.heading: Practice activity
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: A rolling mill logs 12 coil widths (mm): 1250, 1248, 1252, 1251, 1249, 1253, 1247, 1250, 1252, 1249, 1251, 1310. Using the IQR method, is 1310 mm an outlier? (Q1 = 1249.00, Q3 = 1252.00.) IQR = 1252.00 − 1249.00 = 3.0 mm. Upper fence = 1252.00 + 1.5(3.0) = 1256.5 mm. 1310 mm is well above 1256.5 mm, so yes, it is flagged as an outlier by the IQR method — and by a wide margin. Conclusion: before removing it, check whether this reading came from a different gauge, a different coil altogether, or a genuine mill excursion. Don't just delete it because it's inconvenient.

sections.heading: Final summary
breadcrumb: Dealing with Outliers: A Steel & Mining Detective's Guide
sections.text: An outlier is a point inconsistent with the bulk of the data — not automatically an error. Four core detection tools: Z-score, Modified Z-score (MAD-based), IQR/Tukey fences, and Grubbs' test — each with different assumptions and blind spots. Masking (an outlier hiding itself or another) and swamping (flagging good points near a real cluster) are real failure modes — cross-check methods. Detection is step one. Investigation — instrument logs, sample logs, operator interviews — decides what a flagged point actually is. Never delete a point without a documented, investigated reason; report results with and without the point when in doubt. Excel builds each method from AVERAGE/MEDIAN/STDEV.S/QUARTILE.INC/T.INV.2T; Minitab's Outlier Test, Boxplot, and I-MR chart give the same answers with far less manual formula work. Decision rule: screen with IQR fences (always works) → confirm with Grubbs' test if approximately normal → investigate root cause before any exclusion → document the decision either way. Remember this: statistics finds the suspect. Investigation finds the verdict. Suggested next lesson: Chebyshev vs. the Empirical Rule .
