sections.text: Measures whether, as X increases, Y tends to increase (or decrease) consistently Best for ordinal data, monotonic-but-curved relationships, and questions about rank association If the relationship is monotonic but visibly curved — for example, a rank of defect severity vs. customer complaints — use Spearman. Rank each variable separately. The smallest X gets rank 1, the next smallest rank 2, and so on; tied values share the average of the ranks they would have occupied. Do the same for Y. Run an ordinary Pearson correlation on the two rank columns. That result is ρ.

sections.heading: What it measures
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Association based on concordant vs. discordant pairs . Take every possible pair of observations. If the pair agrees on ordering — the one with the bigger X also has the bigger Y — it's concordant . If they disagree, it's discordant . Kendall's tau is built directly from that tally. \[\tau_b = \frac{C-D}{\sqrt{(C+D+T_x)(C+D+T_y)}}\] \(C\) and \(D\) count concordant and discordant pairs. \(T_x\) and \(T_y\) count pairs tied only on \(X\) and only on \(Y\), respectively. Pairs tied on both variables are excluded from all four counts. With no ties, the denominator is \(n(n-1)/2\), where \(n\) is the number of observations. If the denominator is zero, the coefficient is undefined.

sections.heading: Practical decision rule
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Are the data quantitative, and is linear association the question of interest? → Use Pearson ; inspect the scatterplot and check inferential assumptions separately. Is the relationship monotonic but not linear? → Use Spearman . Is the sample small, or are there many tied ranks? → Use Kendall . Always look at the scatterplot before trusting any single number. All three coefficients can look “reasonable” while completely missing a non-monotonic (e.g., U-shaped) relationship — none of the three is designed to detect that.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Correlation is not causation. Any of the three coefficients can be large because of a lurking (confounding) variable, not because X drives Y. A single outlier can dominate Pearson. Two extreme points can swing r dramatically while barely moving Spearman or Kendall — try the “Outliers present” preset above. Zero correlation does not mean no relationship. All three coefficients can sit near zero for a strong but non-monotonic (curved both ways) pattern. Ties need the right formula. Skip the shortcut Spearman formula when ranks are tied; use the rank-then-Pearson approach or the tau-b version of Kendall instead. A big r does not certify a good regression. Linearity, constant variance, and independence still need to be checked separately before fitting a line.

sections.heading: Excel Functions
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Functions used across this lesson's Excel workflow Function Syntax Purpose When to use it CORREL =CORREL(array1,array2) Pearson correlation coefficient between two ranges. Use directly on raw values for Pearson r; use on two rank columns to get Spearman ρ. PEARSON =PEARSON(array1,array2) Mathematically identical to CORREL ; older function name kept for compatibility. Either function is fine — most analysts default to CORREL . RSQ =RSQ(known_ys,known_xs) Returns the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient (r²). Use to report the proportion of variance explained when discussing r in a simple-linear-regression context. RANK.AVG =RANK.AVG(number,ref,[order]) Ranks a value within a range, averaging tied ranks. Use to build the rank columns that Spearman (and a manual Kendall check) both depend on. Prefer this over the legacy RANK , which does not average ties. SIGN =SIGN(number) Returns −1, 0, or +1. Use on pairwise differences to classify a pair as concordant, discordant, or tied when building Kendall's tau by hand. SUMPRODUCT =SUMPRODUCT(array1,array2,...) Multiplies arrays element-wise and sums the result. Use with SIGN across a helper pairwise grid to tally concordant/discordant pairs for Kendall's tau (Excel has no native KENDALL function). T.DIST.2T =T.DIST.2T(x,deg_freedom) Two-tailed p-value from the t-distribution. Use to test whether a Pearson r is significantly different from zero: t = r√((n−2)/(1−r²)), then =T.DIST.2T(ABS(t), n-2) . FISHER / FISHERINV =FISHER(x) / =FISHERINV(y) Fisher z-transformation and its inverse. Use to build an approximate confidence interval for Pearson r: transform r with FISHER , build a normal-based interval on the z-scale, then convert the endpoints back with FISHERINV .

sections.heading: Minitab Navigation
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Menu paths for correlation in Minitab Task Menu path Notes Pearson or Spearman correlation Stat → Basic Statistics → Correlation Enter two or more numeric columns; the dialog's Method option lets you choose Pearson (default) or Spearman rank correlation, plus a significance test for each pair. Check linearity/monotonicity first Graph → Scatterplot Alternative/companion step. Always view the scatterplot — with or without a fitted line — before trusting a correlation number, since Minitab will compute r or ρ on any pair of columns whether or not the relationship is actually well-suited to it. Kendall's tau between two variables No dedicated menu item in standard Minitab Basic Statistics Be transparent about this limitation: Minitab's built-in Correlation dialog covers Pearson and Spearman only. For a two-variable Kendall's tau, either compute it manually from ranks (as shown above) or use software with native support (e.g., R's cor(method="kendall") or Python's scipy.stats.kendalltau ). Do not confuse this with Minitab's separate Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance , which measures agreement across multiple raters and is a different statistic. Which option should you choose? Start from the decision rule, not the menu: run Stat → Basic Statistics → Correlation with Method set to Pearson when linear association between quantitative measurements is the question of interest, switch the same dialog's Method to Spearman when the relationship is monotonic but not linear or the data are ordinal, and fall back to a manual or external Kendall's tau calculation for small, tie-heavy samples. Assess the assumptions of any significance test or confidence interval separately.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Correlation ≠ causation, every time it's tested. ASQ CSSBB/CQE items frequently plant a high r and ask what conclusion is defensible — the answer is rarely “X causes Y.” Match the measure to the question before picking a formula. Ordinal or ranked engineering data (defect severity tiers, inspector scores) suggest Spearman or Kendall. Skewness alone does not rule out Pearson. Know why r can mislead. Exam scenarios love the “one extreme outlier” setup precisely because it shows Pearson's sensitivity — if the question hinges on a couple of unusual points, expect Spearman/Kendall to be the more defensible answer. Connect r to regression. r² (via RSQ ) is the proportion of variance in Y explained by a simple linear fit on X — a common bridge question between correlation and regression topics. Ties matter for both real analysis and exam wording. If a scenario mentions repeated or tied ranks, that's the cue for Kendall's tau-b or a rank-based Spearman calculation, not the tie-naive shortcut formula. Statistical significance is not practical significance. A statistically significant correlation in a huge dataset can still be too weak to act on; always weigh the coefficient's size against engineering tolerances and cost of action. Remember: Pearson asks “is it a straight line?”, Spearman and Kendall ask “is it a consistent direction?” — choose the question that actually matches your data before you trust the number.

sections.heading: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
sections.text: Every process wobbles . Here's how to measure it. Variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation and its cousins, covariance, and correlation are usually taught as separate formulas to memorize. They're really one idea, asked several different ways: how far do things drift from where we expect them, and do two things drift together? Drag the slider below to feel it before we name it. relationship strength: 0.70 as you drag, watch the dots snap from a cloud to a line — that snapping-into-a-line is what correlation measures. Part 1 of 6

sections.heading: CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
sections.text: CV isn't the only way to express spread "relative to something." Four more live in the same family, each built from a different raw material — the full range, just the middle 50%, average distance instead of squared distance, or CV itself renamed for a lab bench. Where they disagree is how much a single wild reading can shake them . coefficient of range — spread relative to the total scale quartile coefficient of dispersion — spread of just the middle 50%, ignores the tails coefficient of mean deviation — average distance, not squared distance, relative to the average relative standard deviation — CV, renamed for the lab bench Identical math to CV — just always expressed as a percentage.

sections.heading: The clogged nozzle
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
sections.text: Twelve syringes off Fill Line 7, target 10.00 mL. Then the nozzle catches for one cycle and overfills a single syringe to 13.80 mL. Toggle it in and out and watch which numbers flinch. Include the clogged-nozzle syringe (13.80 mL) fill volume (mL) min / max — Q1 / Q3 — mean — mean deviation — coefficient of range — sensitive quartile coeff. of dispersion — robust coefficient of mean deviation — moderate RSD — sensitive That ordering isn't a coincidence. Quartile coefficient of dispersion only looks at Q1 and Q3 — the middle 50% of the data — so one extreme syringe usually doesn't even change which readings sit at those positions. Coefficient of mean deviation averages every distance once, so the outlier counts, but only once. Coefficient of range and RSD both key off the single most extreme reading (or its squared distance, for RSD) — exactly the reading that just broke. When to reach for which: use the quartile coefficient of dispersion when you know the data has (or might have) outliers and you don't want one bad reading to dominate the story — audits of skewed cycle-time or cost data are a classic case. Reach for RSD/CV when the data is reasonably well-behaved and you want the standard, widely-recognized metric. Coefficient of range is quick and intuitive but inherits the raw range's weakness: it only ever looks at two points. Part 4 of 6

sections.text: Variance multiplies each deviation by itself . Covariance multiplies the deviation of X by the deviation of a second variable, Y , at the same moment. If they tend to be above their means together (or below together), the products are positive. If one's up while the other's down, the products are negative. covariance — and variance is just this with Y = X

breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation

sections.text: Measure Pallets (raw) Pins (raw) Pallets (relative) Pins (relative) Std dev / CV 30.21 kg 0.346 mm 3.73% 6.88% Range / Coef. of range 100 kg 1.1 mm 6.17% 10.89% IQR / QCD 37.5 kg 0.475 mm 2.31% 4.74% Mean dev. / CoMD 25 kg 0.3 mm 3.09% 5.97% RSD — (same as CV, just ×100%) 3.73% 6.88% Every single raw measure says "pallets." Every single relative measure says "pins." Both are computed correctly — they're just answering different questions. The general rule: a raw spread measure (variance, standard deviation, range, IQR, mean deviation) is only comparable between two datasets that share the same units and a similar scale. The instant you're comparing across different units, different scales, or even the same units at very different magnitudes, switch to the relative version — CV, coefficient of range, quartile coefficient of dispersion, or coefficient of mean deviation. That's the entire reason this family of measures exists. Statistics Implementation

sections.text: Stat → Basic Statistics → Display Descriptive Statistics — gives mean, StDev, and variance together; check "Statistics…" to add CoefVar (Minitab computes CV for you, unlike Excel). Stat → Basic Statistics → Correlation — correlation matrix with an option to display p-values; use this over hand-calculating r whenever you have more than two variables to compare pairwise. Which option to use and why: Descriptive Statistics is the right first stop for any single-variable spread question (variance, StDev, CV, and quartiles all live there together). sections.heading: Exam tips (CSSBB / CQE)
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
Running these in Excel and Minitab
sections.text: Sample vs. population: if the question describes measuring "all units produced" or a defined finite lot, use population formulas (n divisor). If it describes a sample pulled for inspection — the overwhelming majority of exam scenarios — use sample formulas (n−1 divisor). Using n instead of n−1 is the single most common calculation trap. Correlation ≠ causation: a classic distractor answer treats a high r as proof that X causes Y. The exam will reward "there is a strong linear association" over "X causes Y" unless the question describes a controlled experiment. CV shows up in Measurement Systems Analysis and reliability questions as a way to compare variability across different gauges or different-scaled processes — if a question compares consistency across two different units of measure, CV (not raw StDev) is almost always the intended tool.

sections.text: All three intervals share one shape: centre \(\pm\) multiplier \(\times\) spread . The centre is always \(\bar{x}\). What changes is the multiplier, and that is the whole story.

sections.heading: 1. Confidence interval for the mean
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
sections.text: When the population standard deviation is unknown (the usual case), use the \(t\) distribution: \[ \bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \] where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean, \(s\) is the sample standard deviation, \(n\) is the sample size, \(\alpha = 1 - \text{confidence level}\), and \(t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\) is the \(t\) value with \(\alpha/2\) of the area above it and \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. The term \(s/\sqrt{n}\) is the standard error of the mean. If the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is truly known, swap \(t\) for \(z\): \[ \bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \] where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the standard normal value with \(\alpha/2\) of the area above it (1.960 for 95%).

sections.heading: Why the extra "1"?
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
2. Prediction interval for one new observation
sections.text: A new fish differs from our sample mean for two reasons: the new fish varies around the true mean, and our sample mean is itself a bit off. Those two errors are independent, so their variances add: \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}\left(X_{\text{new}} - \bar{X}\right) &= \sigma^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \\ &= \sigma^2\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \end{aligned} \] where \(X_{\text{new}}\) is the next observation and \(\sigma^2\) is the population variance. The "1" is the fish-to-fish scatter. It does not depend on \(n\), so it never goes away. That is the PI's floor.

sections.heading: 3. Two-sided tolerance interval (normal data)
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
sections.text: \[ \bar{x} \pm k_2\, s \] where \(k_2\) is the two-sided tolerance factor . It depends on three things: the sample size \(n\), the coverage \(p\) (the share of the population to capture), and the confidence level \(1-\alpha\). Minitab and published tables solve for the exact \(k_2\) numerically. A very good hand formula is Howe's approximation: \[ k_2 \approx \sqrt{\frac{(n-1)\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) z^2_{(1-p)/2}}{\chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-1}}} \] where \(z_{(1-p)/2}\) is the standard normal value with \((1-p)/2\) of the area above it (2.576 for \(p = 0.99\)), and \(\chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-1}\) is the chi-square value with \(\alpha\) of the area below it and \(n-1\) degrees of freedom (10.117 for \(\alpha = 0.05\), 19 df).

sections.heading: What happens with an infinite sample?
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
What happens with an infinite sample?
sections.text: As \(n \to \infty\), \(\bar{x} \to \mu\), \(s \to \sigma\), and \(t \to z\). Each interval settles at a different limit: Interval Half-width as \(n \to \infty\) Plain words CI \(t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \to 0\) You eventually know the mean exactly. PI \(t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\, s\sqrt{1+\tfrac{1}{n}} \to z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma\) The next fish still varies: the floor is \(\pm 1.96\sigma\) at 95%. TI \(k_2\, s \to z_{(1-p)/2}\,\sigma\) It becomes the true population percentiles: \(\pm 2.576\sigma\) for 99% coverage. Going further: intervals around a regression line The same CI-versus-PI idea appears in regression. At a chosen predictor value \(x_0\), with fitted value \(\hat{y}_0\): CI for the mean response: \[ \hat{y}_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\, s_e\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}} \] PI for one new response: \[ \hat{y}_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\, s_e\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}} \] where \(s_e\) is the standard error of the regression (the residual standard deviation), \(\bar{x}\) is the mean of the predictor, and \(S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\). Again the PI carries the extra "1", so its band is always wider, and both bands flare out as \(x_0\) moves away from \(\bar{x}\).

sections.text: Here we play the river. We know the truth: salmon weights follow a normal distribution with \(\mu = 5.5\,\text{kg}\) and \(\sigma = 0.8\,\text{kg}\). Each click draws a fresh random sample, builds all three intervals, then checks each one against its own target. Interval Counts as a hit when… CI it contains the true mean \(\mu = 5.5\) PI one brand-new fish, caught after the sample, lands inside it TI it actually holds at least the chosen coverage (for example 90%) of the whole population Sample size \(n\) 10 Confidence level TI coverage Show on the picture CI PI TI The big misconception: a 95% CI does not contain 95% of the data. In the simulator, look at the CI rows: they are far too narrow to hold most fish. The 95% is about the method : in the long run, 95% of intervals built this way capture \(\mu\). Any one interval either contains \(\mu\) or it does not.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
sections.text: Judging parts against a spec with a CI. A narrow CI only says the average is well known. Individual parts can still fall out of spec. Use a TI for spec decisions. Saying "95% of the data is inside the CI." That describes a tolerance interval (and then only with confidence attached), not a CI. Expecting more data to shrink a PI to nothing. It cannot. The floor is the process's own variation. To narrow a PI, reduce variation. Mixing up confidence and coverage. In a 95/99 TI, 95% is how sure you are; 99% is how much of the population is inside. Using the normal-theory formulas on clearly non-normal data. The PI and TI lean hard on normality because they describe individual values. Check a normal probability plot first. Minitab's tolerance interval tool also reports a nonparametric interval for this case. Using \(z\) instead of \(t\) with a small sample. Unless \(\sigma\) is truly known, use \(t\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.

sections.heading: Excel functions
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals

It has no built-in prediction or tolerance interval for a single sample, so you build those from the critical-value functions below. sections.heading: Exam tips (ASQ CSSBB and CQE)
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
sections.text: Read the target first. "Average", "mean", or "true value" points to a CI. "Next", "a single", or "one more" points to a PI. "Percentage of the population", "proportion of units", or "specification" points to a TI. Know the multiplier pattern. CI uses \(1/\sqrt{n}\), PI uses \(\sqrt{1+1/n}\), TI uses a table factor \(k\). Exam questions often hand you the \(k\) value or a table; you just apply \(\bar{x} \pm k s\). \(t\) or \(z\)? Use \(z\) only when \(\sigma\) is given as known. Otherwise use \(t\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. A small \(n\) with \(s\) is a strong hint for \(t\). Width ranking. At the same confidence level the CI is always narrower than the PI. Expect "which interval is widest?" questions; the TI is usually the answer, but check the coverage. Sample size effect. Quadrupling \(n\) roughly halves the CI width. It hardly changes the PI. This "diminishing returns" idea appears in sample-size questions. Interpretation traps. Watch for answer choices that say "95% probability that \(\mu\) is in this interval" or "95% of the data lie in the CI". Both are wrong. On the job: capability and spec-setting decisions call for tolerance intervals; customer quotes on the next shipment call for prediction intervals; process-change and mean-shift questions call for confidence intervals.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: Confidence vs Prediction vs Tolerance Intervals
sections.text: CI pins down a parameter (usually the mean). It shrinks to zero with enough data. PI brackets one future value. It has a floor set by the process's own scatter. TI brackets a stated share of the whole population with stated confidence. It is the right tool for specs and capability claims. All three are \(\bar{x} \pm (\text{multiplier}) \times s\). Learn the three multipliers and you know the lesson.

lessons.title: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
lessons.description: See how the normal connects to the Weibull, lognormal, t, binomial and more — with a live Central Limit Theorem simulator.

sections.heading: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Statistics Intermediate 20 minutes Interactive The bell curve doesn’t live alone. It sits at the centre of a whole family of distributions — Weibull, lognormal, Student’s t, binomial, exponential — connected to it by transformations, limits, and one remarkable theorem. In this lesson you’ll simulate the Central Limit Theorem live, morph a Weibull curve into a near-bell, and learn to pick the right distribution for the job. Why this matters: real data is often not normal — failure times, repair durations, defect counts, incomes. Knowing how these distributions relate to the normal tells you when the bell-curve toolkit still applies (thanks to the Central Limit Theorem), and which specialist distribution to reach for when it doesn’t. This is core territory for Six Sigma, reliability engineering, and quality certification exams.

sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Explain the Central Limit Theorem and why averages become normal even when raw data is not. Calculate the standard error of a mean and use it in z-score problems about averages. Interpret the Weibull shape parameter (β) and connect it to failure behaviour, the exponential distribution, and near-normal shapes. Identify when the lognormal and Student’s t distributions are the right relatives to use. Apply the rule-of-thumb conditions (np and n(1−p) ≥ 10) for approximating a binomial with a normal. Select an appropriate distribution for a dataset using shape, boundaries, and data type.

sections.heading: The family map in plain English
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
The family map in plain English
sections.text: Think of the normal distribution as the busiest junction in the world of probability. Other distributions connect to it in three distinct ways: 1. Convergence — “becomes normal in the limit.” Several distributions turn into a bell curve as some quantity grows. The binomial (counts of successes in n trials) looks more and more normal as n increases. The Poisson (counts of rare events) does the same as its mean grows. Student’s t — a bell with heavier tails used for small samples — merges into the normal as the sample size climbs. And the granddaddy of them all: by the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) , the average of many independent measurements is approximately normal no matter what distribution the raw data follows . This is why the bell curve is everywhere: nature loves averaging. 2. Transformation — “normal in disguise.” Some skewed distributions are a normal wearing a costume. If data X is lognormal (repair times, incomes, particle sizes), then ln(X) is exactly normal — take logs and the whole bell-curve toolkit comes back. Squaring and summing z-scores produces the chi-square distribution, the engine behind variance tests and goodness-of-fit tests. 3. Flexible cousins — “can imitate the normal.” The Weibull distribution, the workhorse of reliability engineering, has a shape parameter β that lets it impersonate other distributions: β = 1 makes it exactly the exponential distribution (constant failure rate), while β ≈ 3.6 makes it look strikingly like a normal. That flexibility is why Weibull is the default model for time-to-failure data. What this map does not say: it does not mean everything is secretly normal. Raw skewed data stays skewed — the CLT rescues averages , not individual values. Choosing a distribution is a modelling decision that should be driven by the data’s shape, boundaries, and physical story, and checked with plots or goodness-of-fit tests. The normal distribution as a hub: some relatives converge to it, some are transformations of it, and some can imitate it.

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Terms you’ll meet in this lesson Term Plain-language meaning Technical meaning Practical interpretation Sampling distribution The pattern you’d see if you repeated your study many times and kept the statistic each time. The probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. the sample mean) over repeated samples. It describes your average , not your raw data — the CLT is a statement about this distribution. Central Limit Theorem (CLT) Averages become bell-shaped, whatever the raw data looks like. For independent, identically distributed data with finite variance, the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal as n grows. Justifies using z-scores and normal tables on means, even for skewed processes. Standard error (SE) The typical wobble of an average from sample to sample. SE = σ / √n, the standard deviation of the sample mean. Quadruple the sample size and the average becomes twice as precise. Weibull distribution The go-to model for “how long until it fails.” A distribution on positive values with shape β and scale η; its hazard (failure) rate rises, falls, or stays flat depending on β. β < 1: early-life failures. β = 1: random failures (exponential). β > 1: wear-out. β ≈ 3.6: nearly normal shape. Exponential distribution The waiting time for a purely random event. A Weibull with β = 1; memoryless, with a constant hazard rate. Time between random arrivals or failures — the past tells you nothing about the future. Lognormal distribution Data whose logarithm is bell-shaped. X is lognormal if ln(X) is normal with parameters μ and σ (on the log scale). Right-skewed, strictly positive data — repair times, incomes, concentrations. Log it, then use normal tools. Student’s t distribution A bell curve with fatter tails for small samples. The distribution of a standardised mean when σ is estimated from the sample; indexed by degrees of freedom (df). Use instead of the normal when n is small; by df ≈ 30 it is nearly identical to the normal. Degrees of freedom (df) How much independent information the sample carries. For a one-sample mean, df = n − 1. Low df → heavier t tails → wider intervals; high df → back to the normal. Continuity correction A half-unit adjustment when a smooth curve stands in for a staircase. Adding/subtracting 0.5 when approximating a discrete distribution (binomial, Poisson) with the continuous normal. P(X ≥ 20) for counts becomes P(X > 19.5) under the normal curve.

sections.heading: 1. The standard error of a mean (the CLT’s working part)
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
1. The standard error of a mean (the CLT’s working part)
sections.text: SE( x̄ ) = σ √ n and z = x̄ − μ σ / √ n x̄ the sample mean (average of your n measurements, in original units) μ the process (population) mean; σ the process standard deviation n the sample size (number of independent measurements averaged) SE the standard error — the standard deviation of the average , same units as the data Plain-language interpretation: averages wobble less than individual values, and the wobble shrinks with the square root of the sample size. The CLT adds the punchline: for reasonably large n (a common rule of thumb is n ≥ 30, less if the data is already symmetric), that wobble follows a normal distribution — so the z-score above works even when raw data is skewed. Assumptions: observations are independent and come from the same process with finite variance. Do not use when: data points are strongly correlated (trends, autocorrelation), the process shifts mid-sample, or n is small and the raw data is heavily skewed.

sections.text: f ( t ) = β η · ( t η ) β−1 · e −( t /η) β for t ≥ 0 t time to failure (hours, cycles, kilometres — any positive quantity) β the shape parameter (dimensionless): controls how the failure rate changes over time η the scale (characteristic life), same units as t: by this time about 63.2% of units have failed Plain-language interpretation: β is the personality, η is the size. With β = 1 the formula collapses to the exponential distribution (constant failure rate); β < 1 means failures concentrate early (infant mortality); β > 1 means failures build up with age (wear-out); and around β ≈ 3.6 the curve is so symmetric it is often mistaken for a normal. Use for: time-to-event and strength data. Not for: data that can be negative, or counts.

sections.heading: What goes on the y-axis?
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Before we start comparing distributions on the same axes, it’s worth being precise about the vertical axis. Whenever you draw a distribution — a histogram of real data, or a smooth curve like the ones in this lesson — you have four common choices for what the height means, and they matter as soon as you try to overlay a theoretical curve on a histogram (which every tool below does). The surprising part: for a fixed dataset and bin width, all four produce the exact same shape. Changing the y-axis only relabels and rescales the height; it never bends the curve. Four ways to label the vertical axis (for a fixed dataset and bin width, the shape is identical) Y-axis Each height is… Depends on Total under it Best for Frequency the count of observations in the bin sample size and bin width area = n × bin width “how many” — raw, intuitive counts Relative frequency count ÷ n (a proportion) bin width heights sum to 1 the fraction of data in each bin Percentage 100 × count ÷ n bin width heights sum to 100 the same, expressed in % Density relative frequency ÷ bin width nothing — it’s normalised area = 1 matching theory; comparing distributions The heights are all constant multiples of each other: frequency = n · w · density, relative frequency = w · density, and percentage = 100 · w · density, where w is the bin width. Same outline, different ruler. Why density is the special one. Three properties fall out of that normalisation: Area = 1, always. Only density integrates to 1 — the defining property of a probability distribution. Every theoretical curve in this lesson (normal, Weibull, lognormal, t) is a density, so density is the only y-axis on which you can honestly lay one of those curves over a histogram. Bin-width invariance. Double your bin width and the frequency, relative-frequency, and percentage bars roughly double in height (each wider bin catches more data). Density divides that width back out, so its heights stay put — which is why the binomial checker and family explorer later work in density units. Height is not a probability. On a density axis the height is a probability per unit of x , not a probability, and it can even exceed 1 for a narrow curve. Probability is the area, never the height. This applies to the skewed distributions here too: a Weibull or lognormal histogram can be drawn on any of these axes, but you can only overlay the fitted curve in density units. Move the controls below and watch the shape hold while the axis (and the numbers on it) change. Y-axis shows Bin width: 10 Sample size n: 1000 Histogram bars Fitted normal density Method: a normal population (μ = 100, σ = 15) is split into bins of the chosen width; each bar’s expected count is n × the probability of that bin. The plot always rescales to fill the panel — that is exactly the point: the shape is fixed, only the y-axis numbers change. The dashed normal density is drawn only in density mode, because that is the one axis on which the smooth curve and the bars share a scale.

sections.heading: Two views of the same distribution: PDF and CDF
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Two views of the same distribution: PDF and CDF
sections.text: Every distribution in this lesson — normal, Weibull, lognormal, t, exponential — comes as a matched pair. The curves you have been drawing are probability density functions , or PDFs , written f ( x ): the height is a density and the area is probability. Each one has a partner, the cumulative distribution function , or CDF , written F ( x ), which answers a running question: “what is the probability of a value at or below x ?” It climbs smoothly from 0 to 1, tracing an S-shape. (When we ask software for “the probability of failure by time t” or “the percentile of a score,” we are asking for a CDF value.) The two are tied together by the two basic operations of calculus. In plain terms: the CDF accumulates area under the PDF, and the PDF is the slope of the CDF. F ( x ) = ∫ x −∞ f ( t ) d t — integrate the PDF to accumulate the CDF f ( x ) = d F d x = F ′( x ) — differentiate the CDF to recover the PDF Read the first line as “sweep from the far left up to x , adding up density as you go — the total area so far is F ( x ).” Read the second as “how fast is that area piling up right here? That rate is the height of the PDF.” Where the bell is tall (near the mean), probability accumulates fast and the CDF climbs steeply; out in the flat tails, the CDF barely moves. Drag the point x below and watch the coupling: the shaded area in the top panel is exactly the height of the dot in the bottom panel, and the steepness of the orange tangent line in the bottom panel is exactly the height of the dot in the top panel. Drop σ below about 0.4 to see the PDF peak climb past the dashed “1.0” line — proof that a density is not a probability. Point x: 0.70 Spread σ: 1.00 density f(x) = slope of CDF 0.31 shaded area = F(x) = P(X ≤ x) 0.760 right tail P(X > x) 0.240 Method: both panels share the same horizontal axis x, with the mean μ at 0 (so at σ = 1 one unit is one standard deviation). The shaded PDF area and the CDF height are the same number, computed with the standard-normal CDF approximation; the tangent line’s slope is the PDF value f(x). Reducing σ narrows the bell and raises its peak — past σ ≈ 0.4 the peak exceeds a height of 1. The landmarks line up in a satisfying way. At the mean, the PDF is at its peak, so the CDF is at its steepest — and passes through exactly 0.5. Out in the tails, the PDF flattens toward zero, so the CDF goes nearly flat, levelling off at 0 on the left and 1 on the right. And the probability of landing between two values is an area on the PDF and a vertical gap on the CDF — the same number either way: P ( a ≤ X ≤ b ) = ∫ b a f ( x ) d x = F ( b ) − F ( a ) The integrate/differentiate link is not special to the normal — it holds for every distribution. The Weibull is a tidy example because its CDF has a clean closed form: integrating the Weibull density gives F ( t ) = 1 − e −( t /η) β This is exactly the “probability of failure by time t ” that reliability software reports. Setting t = η (the scale) gives F = 1 − e −1 ≈ 0.632 — which is why η is called the characteristic life : by that time about 63.2% of units have failed. Differentiate this CDF and you get the Weibull density back. The same idea shows up with real data too: the cumulative relative frequency curve (an ogive ) is the empirical CDF, and differencing it recovers the density histogram — the discrete mirror of differentiation.

sections.heading: Interactive: the Central Limit Theorem, live
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Interactive: the Central Limit Theorem, live
sections.text: Don’t take the CLT on faith — watch it happen. Pick a population that is clearly not normal , choose how many measurements go into each average, and the simulator draws 2,000 sample means instantly — every slider move re-runs it. The histogram shows the averages; the dashed curve is the normal the CLT predicts. The Draw button re-rolls a fresh batch. Population (raw data shape) Sample size n (values per average): 1 Histogram of 2,000 simulated sample means Normal curve predicted by the CLT Loading the first simulation… With n = 1, each “average” is just one raw value, so the histogram shows the population’s true (skewed) shape. Slide n upward and watch the bell emerge. Population mean μ Population σ Predicted SE = σ/√n Observed SD of the 2,000 means Method: for each of 2,000 repetitions, the simulator draws n random values from the chosen population and records their average. The dashed overlay is a normal curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, scaled to the histogram’s area. Randomness means your histogram will look slightly different each run — that is the point. What to try: exponential population with n = 1 (very skewed), then n = 5 (skew fading), then n = 30 (a clean bell). Notice two things: the bell appears and it gets narrower — the √n in the standard error at work. Then try the bimodal population: even two separate peaks can’t resist averaging.

sections.heading: Interactive: when does a binomial become a bell?
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Interactive: when does a binomial become a bell?
sections.text: Counts of successes — defective units in a batch, positive responses in a survey — follow a binomial distribution. For large enough samples, a normal curve with μ = np and σ = √ np(1−p) is an excellent stand-in. The classic rule of thumb: the approximation is safe when np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10 . Test it yourself. Number of trials n: 40 Probability of success p: 0.50 Exact binomial probabilities Normal approximation (μ = np, σ = √np(1−p)) Approximation OK np n(1−p) μ = np σ = √np(1−p) Method: bars show exact binomial probabilities P(X = k) computed with log-factorials; the dashed curve is the normal density with μ = np and σ = √np(1−p). When either np or n(1−p) drops below 10, the binomial is pushed against 0 or n, becomes skewed, and the symmetric normal curve stops fitting — watch the badge.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: choosing the right distribution
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Identify the data type. Continuous measurement, time-to-event, count of events, or count of successes out of n trials? This alone eliminates most wrong choices. Plot the data. Histogram plus, ideally, a probability plot. Note symmetry versus skew, boundaries (can it be negative? is it capped?), and the number of peaks. Match the physical story. Sum of many small effects → normal. Product of many small effects → lognormal. Time until a random event → exponential. Time until wear-out → Weibull with β > 1. Successes in n trials → binomial. Rare-event counts → Poisson. Check whether you’re analysing raw values or averages. If your question is about a mean and n is reasonably large, the CLT usually lets you use normal methods regardless of step 3 (with SE = σ/√n; use Student’s t when σ is estimated from a small sample). Fit and verify. Estimate parameters in software, then check the fit with a probability plot or goodness-of-fit statistic (e.g. Anderson–Darling: lower is better, and its p-value should not be small). Apply the model. Compute the probabilities, percentiles, or reliability figures the question asks for — using continuity correction if a normal is standing in for a discrete distribution. Document. Record the chosen distribution, fitted parameters, sample size, fit evidence, and any transformations (especially logs), so the analysis can be audited and repeated.

sections.heading: Worked example: skewed data, normal answer
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Worked example: skewed data, normal answer
sections.text: The problem: a support centre’s individual call-handling times are strongly right-skewed (a lognormal-ish shape): most calls are quick, a few drag on. Management asks: “On a day when we handle 36 calls, what is the chance the day’s average handling time exceeds 10 minutes?” The data: long-run records show the population of individual call times has mean μ = 8 minutes and standard deviation σ = 6 minutes. Calls can be treated as independent. The method: the question is about an average of n = 36 values. Even though raw call times are skewed, the CLT says the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n. So: compute the standard error, standardise, and read off the tail. The formula: z = x̄ − μ σ / √ n Substitute the values: z = 10 − 8 6 / √ 36 Intermediate calculations: √36 = 6 , so the standard error is SE = 6 ÷ 6 = 1 minute . (Individual calls wobble by 6 minutes; a 36-call average wobbles by only 1.) The numerator is 10 − 8 = 2 minutes . z = 2 ÷ 1 = 2.0 . Final answer: a 10-minute daily average sits 2 standard errors above the expected average. From the 68–95–99.7 rule (or software), the probability beyond +2 is about 2.3% . Practical interpretation: only about 1 day in 44 should see an average above 10 minutes by chance alone. If it happens repeatedly, something about the process has genuinely changed — staffing, call mix, or system issues — and it’s worth investigating rather than blaming luck. Limitations: the CLT approximation is good here because n = 36 is respectable, but with heavily skewed data and small n (say, 5 calls) it would be unsafe. We also used the long-run σ as if known; if σ were estimated from a small sample, Student’s t (df = n − 1) would be the honest choice.

sections.heading: Interpretation guide
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: When you see this, it means this When you see… It means… Raw data skewed, but histogram of daily averages looks bell-shaped The CLT at work — normal methods are fine for the averages, not for individual values. A fitted Weibull with β < 1 Failure rate is decreasing : early-life (infant-mortality) failures dominate. Suspect manufacturing or installation defects; burn-in testing may help. A fitted Weibull with β ≈ 1 Roughly constant failure rate — effectively exponential; failures are random and age-independent. Preventive replacement won’t help much. A fitted Weibull with β > 1 (say 2–5) Failure rate increases with age: wear-out. Scheduled maintenance or replacement makes sense. Right-skewed positive data whose histogram of ln(x) looks normal Lognormal behaviour — analyse on the log scale, then transform conclusions back. A t-distribution curve noticeably wider than the normal Small sample: extra uncertainty from estimating σ. Expect wider confidence intervals. np or n(1−p) below about 10 The binomial is skewed — don’t substitute a normal curve; use exact binomial calculations. An Anderson–Darling p-value below 0.05 on a normality test Evidence the data is not normal — consider a relative (lognormal, Weibull) or a transformation.

sections.heading: 1. Applying the CLT to a single value Interpretation error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
1. Applying the CLT to a single value Interpretation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: the CLT normalises averages , not raw observations. One call, one part, one invoice still follows the skewed population distribution. How to recognise it: a “probability” for an individual value computed with σ/√n. How to avoid it: ask first: is the question about one value (use σ) or an average (use σ/√n)?

sections.heading: 2. Forgetting the √n in the standard error Calculation error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
2. Forgetting the √n in the standard error Calculation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: using σ/n makes averages look far too precise; using plain σ makes them look far too noisy. How to recognise it: z-scores that are wildly large or suspiciously tiny for a mean. How to avoid it: memorise the sanity check — quadrupling n should halve the SE, not quarter it.

sections.heading: 3. Swapping Weibull shape and scale Software-output error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
3. Swapping Weibull shape and scale Software-output error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: β (shape) and η (scale) play completely different roles; Excel’s WEIBULL.DIST(x, alpha, beta, ...) uses alpha for shape and beta for scale — the Greek letters don’t match the common engineering notation, and it trips people constantly. How to recognise it: a fitted “shape” of 5,000 hours, or a characteristic life of 2.3. How to avoid it: the shape parameter is dimensionless and usually between 0.3 and 6; the scale carries the time units.

sections.heading: 4. Exponentiating a log-scale mean and calling it “the mean” Interpretation error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
4. Exponentiating a log-scale mean and calling it “the mean” Interpretation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: for lognormal data, e mean of ln(x) is the median of x, not the mean — the true mean is higher (e μ+σ²/2 ). How to recognise it: a “mean repair time” that sits suspiciously below most textbook summaries of the same data. How to avoid it: decide up front whether the median (typical case) or mean (total-workload planning) answers the business question — for skewed data they genuinely differ.

5. Using the normal approximation with small np Assumption error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: when np < 10 (or n(1−p) < 10) the binomial is skewed and pressed against a boundary, so symmetric-normal tail probabilities can be badly wrong. How to recognise it: approximate answers that differ wildly from exact BINOM.DIST results, or negative “possible” counts. How to avoid it: check np and n(1−p) before approximating — the interactive checker above shows exactly why.

sections.heading: 6. Skipping the continuity correction Exam trap

6. Skipping the continuity correction Exam trap
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: a smooth curve is standing in for whole-number bars, so P(X ≥ 20) corresponds to the area beyond 19.5, not 20. How to recognise it: your answer differs from the marking scheme by a consistent small margin. How to avoid it: when approximating binomial or Poisson counts with a normal, widen the region by 0.5 in the direction that includes the boundary value.

sections.heading: 7. Reaching for t only when data “looks weird” Assumption error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
7. Reaching for t only when data “looks weird” Assumption error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: Student’s t is not a fix for non-normal data — it corrects for estimating σ from a small sample of (roughly) normal data. How to recognise it: a t-test quoted on 8 wildly skewed observations as if the t fixed the skew. How to avoid it: small n + estimated σ → t; skewed data → transformation, a better-fitting distribution, or a nonparametric method.

sections.heading: Minitab
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Where to find it: Graph › Probability Distribution Plot draws and shades any of these distributions. To identify which relative fits your data best, use Stat › Quality Tools › Individual Distribution Identification — it fits normal, lognormal, Weibull, exponential and more, side by side. Output that matters: for each candidate distribution, look at the probability plot (points near the line = good fit) and the Anderson–Darling (AD) statistic — smaller is better, and a p-value above 0.05 means no evidence against that distribution. For reliability work, Stat › Reliability/Survival › Distribution Analysis reports the Weibull shape and scale with confidence intervals. Common Minitab mistake: picking the distribution with the prettiest curve instead of comparing AD statistics, and ignoring that several distributions may fit almost equally well — when they do, prefer the one with the stronger physical justification.

sections.heading: Practice activity: the maintenance manager’s week
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Practice activity: the maintenance manager’s week
sections.text: Scenario: you’re reviewing two datasets for a plant maintenance manager. Pump bearings: a Weibull analysis of time-to-failure data returns shape β = 0.7 and scale η = 18,000 hours. The manager plans to introduce scheduled replacement of old bearings at 12,000 hours. Is that plan well-aimed? Repair times: individual repair jobs are right-skewed with population mean μ = 5 hours and standard deviation σ = 4 hours . Next month the team will complete n = 64 jobs. Estimate the probability that the month’s average repair time exceeds 6 hours . Work through both (the interpretation guide and the SE formula are all you need), then check yourself. 1. The plan is aimed at the wrong problem. A shape parameter of β = 0.7 is below 1 , which means a decreasing failure rate: bearings that survive their early life become more reliable, not less. Failures are concentrated in infancy — likely installation or manufacturing defects. Replacing old (surviving) bearings at 12,000 hours would discard the most reliable units and install new ones that carry fresh infant-mortality risk. Better actions: improve installation practices, incoming inspection, or burn-in — and investigate the early failures. Scheduled age-based replacement only makes sense for wear-out behaviour (β > 1). 2. About 2.3%. The question concerns an average of n = 64 jobs, so the CLT applies despite the skew: SE = σ / √n = 4 / √64 = 4 / 8 = 0.5 hours . z = (x̄ − μ) / SE = (6 − 5) / 0.5 = +2.0 . The area beyond +2 on a normal curve is about 2.3% (from the 68–95–99.7 rule: (100% − 95%) ÷ 2). The reasoning pattern: question about an average → standard error with √n → z-score → empirical rule. Note the contrast with part 1: there, the question was about individual lifetimes , so the CLT was irrelevant and the Weibull shape parameter carried the answer.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: The normal distribution is the hub of a family: some distributions converge to it, some are transformations of it, and some can imitate it. The Central Limit Theorem makes averages approximately normal regardless of the raw data’s shape — with spread SE = σ/√n. Precision grows with √n: four times the data buys twice the precision of the mean. Weibull’s shape parameter tells the failure story: β < 1 infant mortality, β = 1 random (exponential), β > 1 wear-out, β ≈ 3.6 near-normal. Lognormal data is a normal in disguise: take logs, use the bell-curve toolkit, and remember e μ is the median . Student’s t is the normal’s small-sample stand-in — heavier tails that fade as df grows; it corrects for estimating σ, not for skew. Approximate a binomial with a normal only when np and n(1−p) are both at least about 10, and use a continuity correction. Choose distributions by data type, shape, boundaries, and the physical story — then verify with a probability plot or Anderson–Darling test.

sections.heading: Decision rule
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Question about an average with decent n → CLT: use the normal with SE = σ/√n (or t if σ is estimated from a small sample). Question about individual values → model the raw data: symmetric → normal; positive and right-skewed → lognormal or Weibull; time-to-failure → Weibull (read β); success counts → binomial (approximate with a normal only if np and n(1−p) ≥ 10). Remember this: the CLT rescues averages, not individuals — and √n is doing the heavy lifting. Suggested next lesson: revisit The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve if any foundations felt shaky, or continue to Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing Basics , where the standard error and Student’s t from this lesson become your everyday tools.

sections.heading: Exact Minitab workflow: polynomial regression with validated selection
breadcrumb: Finding the Best Predictive Regression Model in Minitab
Exact Minitab workflow: polynomial regression with validated selection
sections.text: The sequence below is designed for a continuous response and a mix of continuous and categorical predictors. 1 Define the model purpose and data boundary Prediction target, operating range, grouping unit, and holdout logic ⌄ State what the model will predict, for which population, and within what process range. Decide whether the validation target is a new row, a new heat, a new coil, a future campaign, or a later time period. Exclude post-outcome variables and data created after the prediction decision. Flag impossible values, missingness, duplicate records, and data-quality rules before fitting. Reserve a true future or external test set when the decision is high consequence. 2 Open Fit Regression Model Assign the response and predictor types correctly ⌄ Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model Enter the continuous outcome in Response . Enter numeric process inputs in Continuous predictors . Enter grade, mill, product family, shift, operator, or other factors in Categorical predictors . Verify the categorical reference level under Coding so coefficients compare against a meaningful baseline. 3 Create the candidate term pool Main effects, squares, and two-way interactions ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Model Select the continuous predictors you want to expand. Choose Terms through order . Enter 2 . Click Add . Review the term list and remove combinations that are physically impossible, redundant, or unsupported. Terms through order 2 adds individual squares for continuous predictors and all interactions through order 2 among the selected predictors. 4 Center continuous predictors Reduce nonessential collinearity from powers and interactions ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Coding → Standardize continuous predictors → Subtract the mean Centering changes each predictor from X to X − X̄. This reduces the artificial correlation between X, X², and interaction terms and makes lower-order coefficients meaningful near the center of the observed operating region. X centered = X − X̄ Do not confuse centering with dividing by the standard deviation. Scaling can be useful for coefficient comparison, but it changes the unit interpretation. 5 Configure forward selection with validation Let validation choose the model size ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Stepwise Method: Forward selection with validation Validation: K-fold cross-validation for smaller data; test-set validation for larger data Folds: 5 or 10 are practical starting points; Minitab’s regression default is 10 Group-aware folds: Assign rows by a prepared fold-ID column Display: Include model-selection details Graph: Display R² versus model-selection step How it works: within each fold, Minitab performs forward selection. It then evaluates the sequence across folds and identifies the step with the best K-fold stepwise R². Finally, it runs forward selection on the full dataset and stops at that selected step. 6 Enforce hierarchy Keep higher-order terms statistically coherent ⌄ Stepwise → Hierarchy Hierarchical model: Require a hierarchical model at each step Require hierarchy for: All terms Terms entering: Extra terms can enter to maintain hierarchy For X₁X₂, retain X₁ and X₂. For X₁³, retain X₁ and X₁². For X₁²X₂, retain the applicable lower-order components required by the hierarchy rule. 7 Request diagnostics and stored statistics Do not stop at the selected equation ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Graphs / Results / Storage Display the four-in-one residual plots. Display VIF values and unusual observations. Store fits, residuals, standardized residuals, leverage, Cook’s distance, and DFITS when deeper investigation is needed. Plot residuals against production order or timestamp when the process is time-dependent. 8 Interpret the validation curve—not only the peak Prefer a stable plateau over a fragile maximum ⌄ If the highest validation R² occurs at step 12 but steps 7–10 are nearly identical, prefer the simpler model unless the additional terms provide a material, repeatable improvement. Compare training R² with validation R². Look for a widening training–validation gap. Check whether selected terms are stable under alternate fold assignments. Confirm coefficient directions and interactions make engineering sense. Stepwise selection is exploratory. It cannot incorporate every practical consideration, can choose one of several correlated predictors arbitrarily, and can produce different “best” models under different criteria. Treat selected-term p-values cautiously and validate with new data whenever possible. Step 4

sections.heading: A defensible model-selection rule
breadcrumb: Finding the Best Predictive Regression Model in Minitab
sections.text: Do not allow a single metric to decide. Use sequential gates so that a model cannot “win” on accuracy while failing interpretability, stability, or process logic. Gate 1: Valid design No leakage, correct grouping, correct prediction horizon, and no post-outcome predictors. Gate 2: Competitive error Validation error meets the practical tolerance and is close to the best challenger. Gate 3: Adequate diagnostics No unresolved structural residual pattern, severe instability, or dominant data defect. Gate 4: Engineering utility Interpretation, measurement burden, deployment feasibility, and safe operating range are acceptable. Recommended final decision statement: “MARS was selected because its grouped five-fold validation RMSE was within 3% of the best model, while providing substantially greater interpretability and stable predictor effects. The model passed residual, influence, and operating-range checks. TreeNet was retained as a benchmark but not selected for deployment.”

sections.heading: 5. Variable-selection methods in the Stepwise dialog
breadcrumb: 5. Variable-selection methods in the Stepwise dialog
sections.text: The methods in Minitab’s Stepwise dialog differ in three fundamental ways: where the search starts, whether terms can enter or leave, and what rule controls the next move. The examples below use six candidate predictors—A, B, C, D, E, and F—so you can see exactly how each method proceeds. Method Starts with Can enter? Can leave? Main selection rule Typical use None User-defined model No No No automatic selection Predefined engineering model Stepwise Usually intercept or initial terms Yes Yes Entry and removal p-values Flexible screening Forward Selection Small model Yes No Smallest qualifying p-value Simple sequential selection Backward Elimination Full model No Yes Largest nonqualifying p-value removed Reduce a plausible full model Forward Information Criteria Small model Yes Typically no AIC/AICc-type improvement Fit-complexity balance Forward Selection with Validation Small model Yes No along forward path Stepwise rule builds path; validation selects step Prediction-focused model-size selection Common setup for the examples: assume the candidate predictors are A, B, C, D, E, and F. For p-value-based methods, suppose the alpha-to-enter and alpha-to-remove thresholds are both 0.15 unless stated otherwise. 5.1 None — fit exactly the model you specify With None , Minitab performs no variable-selection search. You decide the model before fitting it. If you place A, B, C, and the interaction A×B in the model, Minitab fits exactly that equation: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃C + β₄(A×B) Minitab does not ask whether D, E, or F should enter, and it does not remove A, B, C, or A×B automatically.

sections.heading: 7.9 The hierarchy principle
sections.text: Best Subsets treats an interaction column as an ordinary numeric predictor. It does not automatically understand that A_B represents A×B or that A and B should accompany it. This means Best Subsets can return a mathematically possible but structurally undesirable model such as: Y = β₀ + β₁(A×B) In most engineering and statistical applications, prefer the hierarchical form: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃(A×B) This is called the principle of hierarchy . When an interaction is retained, the associated lower-order main effects should ordinarily remain in the model.

sections.heading: Why hierarchy matters
sections.text: The interaction describes how the effect of A changes with B. Without A and B, the coefficient of A×B becomes difficult to interpret. Dropping the main effects can make the result depend strongly on how the variables are centered or coded. Hierarchical models are usually easier to communicate and defend scientifically.

sections.text: For the hierarchical model: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃(A×B) The effect of A is not just β₁. It depends on B: Effect of A = β₁ + β₃B Similarly, the effect of B depends on A: Effect of B = β₂ + β₃A Because the main effects are conditional when an interaction is present, interpret them at meaningful reference values. Centering continuous predictors before creating interaction columns often makes the coefficients easier to interpret.

sections.heading: 7.11 Recommended Best Subsets workflow with interactions
breadcrumb: 7.11 Recommended Best Subsets workflow with interactions
sections.text: Use engineering knowledge, prior studies, process maps, or DOE principles to identify plausible interactions and curved terms. Create those interaction and polynomial columns using Calc → Calculator . Run Best Subsets using the main effects and the manually created derived terms. Review the strongest candidate models, but reject nonhierarchical combinations unless there is a compelling technical reason. Rebuild the chosen candidate in Fit Regression Model . Check hierarchy, VIF, residual plots, influential observations, predicted R², and engineering plausibility. Validate the final model on new or held-out data before using it for decisions or prediction. Best practice: use Best Subsets to generate candidate models, then finalize the model in Fit Regression Model, where you can explicitly control main effects, interactions, polynomial terms, hierarchy, diagnostics, and interpretation.

sections.heading: 7.12 Best method when your model contains interaction terms

sections.heading: Why Best Subsets becomes awkward with many interactions
breadcrumb: 7.12 Best method when your model contains interaction terms
Why Best Subsets becomes awkward with many interactions
sections.text: Suppose your candidate terms are: A , B , C , A_B , A_C , and B_C . Best Subsets treats all six worksheet columns as unrelated numeric predictors. It does not inherently understand that A_B represents A×B. Therefore, it can select: Y = β₀ + β₁₂(A×B) without selecting A or B. That model is mathematically estimable, but it is normally undesirable because it violates hierarchy and makes the interaction difficult to interpret.

sections.heading: Recommended approach: Fit Regression Model
breadcrumb: 7.12 Best method when your model contains interaction terms
sections.text: Minitab path: Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model Place the response variable in Response . For example, use Tensile_Strength_MPa . Place the continuous predictors in Continuous predictors . For example, use Carbon, Rolling Temperature, Cooling Rate, and Thickness. Place categorical predictors, such as grade, rolling practice, production line, or furnace, in the appropriate categorical or factor field. Do not manually multiply text-coded categories to create interaction columns. Click Model... . Highlight the predictors that should participate in the interaction structure. Choose Interactions through order 2 to generate all two-way interactions among the selected predictors. Click Add . Minitab adds the requested main effects and interaction terms to the model specification. Return to the main dialog and click Stepwise... if automatic term selection is required. Choose Stepwise, Forward Selection, Backward Elimination, Forward Information Criteria, or Forward Selection with Validation, depending on your modeling purpose. Use the hierarchy controls so lower-order terms remain whenever a higher-order interaction or polynomial term is retained.

sections.heading: Recommended engineering workflow
breadcrumb: 7.12 Best method when your model contains interaction terms
sections.text: Use process knowledge to identify plausible main effects, interactions, and curved terms. Open Fit Regression Model and define the response, continuous predictors, and categorical factors. Use the Model dialog to generate the required interaction and polynomial terms. Apply hierarchy so interactions retain their component main effects and squared terms retain their linear terms. If screening is necessary, use Stepwise, Forward Selection, Forward Information Criteria, or Forward Selection with Validation within the structured model. Refit and review the selected model using coefficient tables, VIF, residual plots, influential-observation diagnostics, adjusted R², predicted R², and validation performance. Confirm that the selected interactions make physical and process sense before using the model for optimization or prediction. Practical rule: Best Subsets is excellent for comparing prepared subsets. Fit Regression Model is usually better for building and selecting models that contain many interactions, categorical factors, or polynomial terms.

Which variables may be useful? Stepwise, Forward, or Backward Provides automatic screening. Which combinations are strongest? Best Subsets Compares alternative subsets across model sizes. Which model size predicts new data best? Forward Selection with Validation Uses validation to choose among models along the forward path. Is a curved polynomial relationship adequate? Fitted Line Plot or Fit Regression Model Polynomial regression is still linear in coefficients. What are the parameters in a known nonlinear equation? Nonlinear Regression Uses iterative estimation for nonlinear parameters. Is the response yes/no? Binary Logistic Regression Models probability rather than an unbounded continuous response. Is the response an ordered category? Ordinal Logistic Regression Respects the order of categories. Is the response an unordered category? Nominal Logistic Regression Handles multiple unordered outcomes. Is the response a count? Poisson Regression Models count outcomes and rate structures.

sections.heading: 10. How to interpret model-selection statistics
sections.text: R² Variation explained in the training data Adjusted R² R² penalized for unnecessary predictors Predicted R² Estimated performance on new observations S Typical residual size in response units
sections.excerpt: R² Variation explained in the training data Adjusted R² R² penalized for unnecessary predictors Predicted R² Estimated performance on new observations S Typical residual size in response units

sections.heading: 10.1 R²
sections.text: R² measures the percentage of observed response variation explained by the fitted model. It never decreases when predictors are added, so it can reward unnecessary complexity.
sections.excerpt: R² measures the percentage of observed response variation explained by the fitted model. It never decreases when predictors are added, so it can reward unnecessary complexity.

sections.heading: 10.2 Adjusted R²
sections.text: Adjusted R² penalizes the addition of terms that do not improve the model enough. It is more useful than R² for comparing models with different numbers of predictors.
sections.excerpt: Adjusted R² penalizes the addition of terms that do not improve the model enough. It is more useful than R² for comparing models with different numbers of predictors.

sections.heading: 10.3 Predicted R²
sections.text: Predicted R² estimates how well the model predicts observations that were not used to estimate the coefficients. A large gap between adjusted R² and predicted R² can indicate overfitting, influential observations, or instability.
sections.excerpt: Predicted R² estimates how well the model predicts observations that were not used to estimate the coefficients. A large gap between adjusted R² and predicted R² can indicate overfitting, influential observations, or instability.

sections.heading: 10.4 Mallows’ Cp
sections.text: A desirable candidate often has a relatively small C p that is close to the number of model parameters, including the intercept. C p should be interpreted alongside predicted R², S, residual plots, and subject-matter logic.
sections.excerpt: A desirable candidate often has a relatively small C p that is close to the number of model parameters, including the intercept. C p should be interpreted alongside predicted R², S, residual plots, and subject-matter logic.

sections.heading: 10.5 S
sections.text: S is the residual standard deviation. It represents the typical distance between observed responses and fitted values, in the original units of the response.
sections.excerpt: S is the residual standard deviation. It represents the typical distance between observed responses and fitted values, in the original units of the response.

sections.heading: 10.6 P-values
sections.text: A coefficient p-value tests whether the data provide evidence that the adjusted coefficient differs from zero, given the other terms in the current model. It does not establish causality, practical importance, or predictive value by itself.
sections.excerpt: A coefficient p-value tests whether the data provide evidence that the adjusted coefficient differs from zero, given the other terms in the current model. It does not establish causality, practical importance, or predictive value by itself.

sections.heading: 10.7 VIF
sections.text: Variance Inflation Factors diagnose multicollinearity. Large VIF values mean that a coefficient is being estimated with greater uncertainty because predictors overlap in the information they provide.
sections.excerpt: Variance Inflation Factors diagnose multicollinearity. Large VIF values mean that a coefficient is being estimated with greater uncertainty because predictors overlap in the information they provide.

sections.heading: 11. Recommended practical workflow
sections.text: Define the response and purpose. Is the goal explanation, prediction, optimization, or screening? Confirm the response type. Continuous, binary, ordinal, nominal, or count? Plot the data. Use scatterplots, matrix plots, time plots, and fitted line plots. Use engineering knowledge. Identify required terms, likely interactions, physical bounds, and confounders. Fit a reasonable full model. Review coefficient signs, p-values, VIF, residual plots, leverage, and influential points. Use selection methods as screening tools. Compare Forward, Stepwise, Backward, and Best Subsets rather than blindly trusting one method. Validate. Use validation data, predicted R², PRESS-type results, or cross-validation where available. Choose the simplest defensible model. Prefer a model that is stable, interpretable, and nearly as predictive as larger alternatives. Confirm assumptions. Linearity, constant variance, residual normality where relevant, independence, and absence of severe influence. Document the final equation and its limits. State the data range, intended use, uncertainty, and conditions under which predictions are valid.

sections.text: Download the practice dataset below and work through the exercises in Minitab. It is a fictitious steel-coil dataset with 50 rows and 10 columns : an identifier, one response (Tensile Strength), and eight candidate predictors. It was built on purpose to contain useful predictors, one mostly irrelevant predictor, mild collinearity, a Carbon × Cooling Rate interaction, Rolling Temperature curvature, and random noise — so every selection method has something to reveal. ⇩ Download the practice dataset (Excel .xlsx) Column Role What it does in the data Coil ID Identifier Row label only — not a predictor. Rolling Temperature (°C) Predictor Curved (quadratic) effect; strength peaks mid-range. Cooling Rate (°C/s) Predictor Useful; interacts with Carbon. Thickness (mm) Predictor Useful; more thickness lowers strength. Furnace Time (min) Predictor Weak-to-moderate; mildly collinear with Rolling Temperature. Line Speed (m/min) Predictor Very weak effect. Ambient Humidity (%) Predictor Mostly irrelevant noise — a good test for selection methods. Before you start. The workbook has two tabs: Practice Data (load this into Minitab) and Data Dictionary (documents every column and the structure built into the data). When you choose predictors, ignore Coil ID — it is only a row label.

sections.heading: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
breadcrumb: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
sections.text: Mistake 1: Treating variable selection as proof Automatic selection is exploratory. It does not prove that selected terms are causal or that omitted variables are unimportant. Mistake 2: Believing forward selection searches every model Forward selection follows one path. Best Subsets is the more exhaustive procedure for moderate predictor counts. Mistake 3: Believing validation chooses the next variable in Minitab’s forward-validation method The forward stepwise rule determines the sequence. Validation chooses the preferred model size along that sequence. Mistake 4: Choosing the largest R² R² always favors larger models. Compare adjusted R², predicted R², S, C p , validation error, and practical simplicity. Mistake 5: Calling every curve “nonlinear regression” A polynomial curve is still linear regression if the unknown coefficients enter linearly. Mistake 6: Ignoring hierarchy If an interaction or squared term is included, retain the associated lower-order terms unless there is a strong, defensible reason not to. Mistake 7: Ignoring residual diagnostics A selected model can still violate assumptions, contain influential points, or show unmodeled curvature. Mistake 8: Extrapolating beyond the data Regression predictions outside the observed predictor range can be physically unrealistic and highly uncertain.

sections.heading: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Once you have chosen a model, a common next step is to predict the response at particular predictor values — for example, “what tensile strength should I expect at these settings?” You could substitute the values into the fitted equation by hand, but the reliable approach is to let Minitab predict from the stored model , because it also reports the uncertainty around the prediction. This section shows the official workflow, a worked example, and how to read the output.

sections.heading: 15.1 First make sure the model is stored
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
15.1 First make sure the model is stored
sections.text: Best Subsets Regression only identifies candidate models — it does not leave behind a fitted model that Minitab can predict from. So if you are working from Best Subsets, refit your chosen subset with Fit Regression Model first. Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model In the Best Subsets output, identify the model you selected using the X marks in its row. Enter your response (Y). Enter the selected predictors as continuous or categorical terms. Under Model , add the exact interaction and polynomial terms that the chosen subset includes. Check the residual plots and model assumptions, then click OK . This creates a stored regression model . Everything in the Predict step below uses that stored equation, so the model must exist before you can predict from it.

breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Suppose your fitted equation is: ŷ = 10 + 2A − 1.5B + 0.4(A × B) and you want the predicted response at A = 3 and B = 4 . Minitab computes: ŷ = 10 + 2(3) − 1.5(4) + 0.4(3 × 4) = 10 + 6 − 6 + 4.8 = 14.8 So the predicted response is ŷ = 14.8 . Entering interaction terms correctly. If A×B was added through the Model dialog, enter only A = 3 and B = 4 — Minitab computes the interaction for you. If instead you built an A_B worksheet column manually before running Best Subsets, Minitab will ask for that column too, and you must enter its value yourself: Predictor Value to enter A 3 B 4 A_B 3 × 4 = 12

sections.heading: 15.4 Understanding the prediction output
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Output What it means Fit The best point estimate of the response at those settings. SE Fit The uncertainty in that estimated mean response. 95% CI A range for the average response at those settings. 95% PI A range for a single individual future result at those settings. For our example the output might read: Fit 95% CI 95% PI 14.8 13.9 – 15.7 11.2 – 18.4 Read that as: The estimated average response at these settings is 14.8 . That average is likely between 13.9 and 15.7 (the 95% confidence interval). One new result could reasonably fall between 11.2 and 18.4 (the 95% prediction interval). Confidence interval vs. prediction interval. When you care about a single future coil, heat, slab, or test result, the prediction interval is the one that matters. It is wider than the confidence interval because an individual outcome carries more variation than an estimated average.
