sections.heading: 15.5 A caution on extrapolation
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Avoid predicting far outside the predictor ranges used to build the model. Minitab may flag such settings as unusual (an X in the output), and extrapolated predictions can be unreliable because the fitted relationship was never verified in that region. Exam tip (CSSBB/CQE). sections.heading: Why straighten a curved scatter plot?
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Why straighten a curved scatter plot?
sections.text: Ordinary least-squares regression assumes four things about the model \( y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon \): the mean of \(y\) is a straight-line function of \(x\), the errors \(\varepsilon\) have constant variance, they are independent, and for intervals and tests they are roughly normal. A curved scatter plot breaks the first assumption. A plot that fans out breaks the second. A transformation re-expresses one or both variables so that both assumptions hold on the new scale. Straightening pays off in three ways. The model fits the data, so residuals carry no leftover pattern. The slope becomes a single, interpretable number such as a growth rate or an exponent. And confidence and prediction intervals have the right width everywhere, not too narrow at one end and too wide at the other. Two different problems, one family of fixes. Curvature is a problem with the mean . Uneven spread is a problem with the variance . Transforming y changes both. Transforming x changes only the mean. Keeping that distinction in mind is most of the skill. You do not always need to linearize. If you only need predictions and have plenty of data, a nonlinear model or a flexible method may serve you better. If physics hands you a nonlinear law with parameters you care about, fit that law directly with nonlinear regression. Part 13 covers these exits. Part 2

sections.heading: The ladder of powers
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: John Tukey arranged the useful re-expressions in order of strength, as powers \(x^{p}\). Moving down the ladder (smaller \(p\)) pulls in large values and spreads out small ones. Moving up (larger \(p\)) does the opposite. The further you move from \(p = 1\), the stronger the bend you remove. Tukey's ladder of powers (applies to x or y) Power \(p\) Re-expression Effect on large values Typical use 3 \(x^{3}\) Stretches strongly Rare; strong left-bulging curves 2 \(x^{2}\) Stretches Curves that steepen at the high end of x 1 \(x\) No change The starting point 0.5 \(\sqrt{x}\) Compresses mildly Counts; variance proportional to the mean 0 \(\ln x\) Compresses Multiplicative effects; growth; spread proportional to the mean −0.5 \(-1/\sqrt{x}\) Compresses strongly Hall–Petch grain-size effect −1 \(-1/x\) Compresses very strongly Rates and times; Arrhenius temperature terms −2 \(-1/x^{2}\) Most compression Rare; extreme right skew

sections.heading: Why the log sits at power 0
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Why the log sits at power 0
sections.text: The raw power \(x^{0}\) is just 1, which is useless. The Box–Cox form fixes this by scaling each power so the ladder is continuous: \[ x^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda}, & \lambda \ne 0 \\[6pt] \ln x, & \lambda = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\text{because}\qquad \lim_{\lambda \to 0} \frac{x^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda} = \ln x . \] where \(x > 0\) and \(\lambda\) is the power. The limit follows from \(x^{\lambda} = e^{\lambda \ln x} \approx 1 + \lambda \ln x\) for small \(\lambda\). Dividing by \(\lambda\) also keeps the order of the points for negative powers. That is why the lab and the table write \(-1/x\) rather than \(1/x\): the minus sign stops the plot from flipping left to right, so the direction of the trend stays easy to read. Range matters. Power transformations only bend data that span a wide ratio. If the largest value is less than about twice the smallest, every rung looks almost the same. Look for an offset to subtract first, or use a polynomial term. The Recovery time dataset in the lab shows this. Part 3

sections.heading: How the two checks work
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: The curvature check is a partial F-test. It refits the transformed data with squared and cubed terms added and asks whether they explain significantly more than the straight line: \[ F = \frac{(\text{SSE}_{1} - \text{SSE}_{3})/2}{\text{SSE}_{3}/(n-4)} \] where \(\text{SSE}_{1}\) is the error sum of squares of the straight line, \(\text{SSE}_{3}\) that of the cubic, and \(n\) the number of points. A p-value below 0.05 means a curve remains. The cubic term matters: a symmetric S-curve has no quadratic signal, so a quadratic-only test would miss it. The spread check correlates the absolute residuals \(|e_i|\) with the fitted values \(\hat{y}_i\) and tests that correlation with \(t = r\sqrt{n-2}/\sqrt{1-r^{2}}\). A p-value below 0.05 means the spread trends with the level: a funnel. Both checks are screening tools. With large samples they flag tiny departures, and with small ones they miss real ones, so always look at the residual plot too. Watch the two \(R^{2}\) values. The transformed-scale \(R^{2}\) describes the line you fitted, but it is measured in different units for every choice of y. The original-scale \(R^{2}\) back-transforms the predictions and scores them against the raw y, so it is comparable across choices. Part 5

Match the curve to a known model
sections.text: Before you reach for the ladder, ask whether the process already has a law. If it does, the law tells you the exact transformation and gives the slope a physical meaning. Many engineering relationships are one of a handful of forms. sections.heading: Which axis to transform: curvature or spread?
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Which axis to transform: curvature or spread?
sections.text: The bulge rule says you may move x or y. The residual spread decides which. Look at the residuals from a straight-line fit on raw data: Spread is even, only the trend curves. Transform x . It straightens the mean and leaves the well-behaved errors alone. Spread grows with the level (a funnel). Transform y . The error is multiplicative, and the right y transform usually removes the curve as well. Both problems, and fixing y over-corrects the curve. Fix the spread with y first, then straighten what is left with x.

sections.heading: Choosing the y transform from the mean–variance relationship
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Which axis to transform: curvature or spread?
Choosing the y transform from the mean–variance relationship
sections.text: The delta method gives the variance of a transformed variable \(g(Y)\) with mean \(\mu\): \[ \operatorname{Var}\!\left[g(Y)\right] \approx \left[g'(\mu)\right]^{2} \operatorname{Var}(Y). \] If the standard deviation grows as a power of the mean, \(\sigma_Y \propto \mu^{k}\), then choosing \(g(y) = y^{1-k}\) gives \(g'(\mu) \propto \mu^{-k}\), and the variance of \(g(Y)\) becomes constant. So the variance-stabilizing power is \(\lambda = 1 - k\). \[ \begin{aligned} \sigma_Y \propto \mu^{k} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 1 - k \\ k = 0.5\ \text{(counts)} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 0.5,\ \sqrt{y} \\ k = 1\ \text{(constant CV)} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 0,\ \ln y \\ k = 2 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = -1,\ 1/y \end{aligned} \] where \(k\) is estimated as the slope of \(\ln(\text{SD})\) against \(\ln(\text{mean})\) across groups or bins of x. Variance-stabilizing transformations Data behaviour Variance pattern Transform y Better model, if available Counts (defects, inclusions) \(\sigma^{2} \propto \mu\) \(\sqrt{y}\) or \(\sqrt{y + 3/8}\) with small counts Poisson regression Percentage errors, growth, concentrations \(\sigma \propto \mu\) \(\ln y\) Gamma or lognormal model with a log link Times to complete, rates of very skewed processes \(\sigma \propto \mu^{2}\) \(1/y\) Gamma model with an inverse link Proportions from n trials \(\sigma^{2} = p(1-p)/n\) \(\arcsin\sqrt{p}\) or \(\operatorname{logit}(p)\) Binary or binomial logistic regression Correlation coefficients depends on \(\rho\) Fisher's \(z = \operatorname{artanh}(r)\) – Transforming y moves the errors with it. If y has constant spread and you take its log, you create a reverse funnel: small y values spread out and large ones get squeezed. Load Yield strength vs grain size in the lab and set y to \(\ln y\) to see that the spread check gets worse, not better. Part 7

sections.heading: Let the data choose y: the Box–Cox method
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Let the data choose y: the Box–Cox method
sections.text: Box and Cox (1964) proposed estimating the power for y by maximum likelihood. To compare SSE across powers, the transformed response must be on a common scale, so it is divided by a power of the geometric mean \(\dot{y}\): \[ z^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda\,\dot{y}^{\,\lambda - 1}}, & \lambda \ne 0 \\[6pt] \dot{y}\,\ln y, & \lambda = 0 \end{cases} \qquad \dot{y} = \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln y_i\right) \] where \(y_i > 0\). For each \(\lambda\), regress \(z^{(\lambda)}\) on the predictors and record the error sum of squares \(\text{SSE}(\lambda)\). The profile log-likelihood is \[ \ell(\lambda) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln\!\left(\frac{\text{SSE}(\lambda)}{n}\right), \qquad \text{95\% CI: } \left\{\lambda : \ell(\lambda) \ge \ell(\hat{\lambda}) - \tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{1,\,0.95}\right\} \] where \(\hat{\lambda}\) maximises \(\ell\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{1,\,0.95} = 1.92\). In practice you then round to the simplest rung inside the interval (1, 0.5, 0, −0.5, −1). A rounded power is easier to explain, and the fit is almost as good. Uses the dataset and x transform currently set in the lab. Best \(\lambda\), \(\hat{\lambda}\) – 95% interval – Simplest rung in interval – The Box–Cox menu trap. Minitab's Stat > Control Charts > Box-Cox Transformation , Python's scipy.stats.boxcox and most "normalize this column" tools look at y alone . They choose \(\lambda\) to make the distribution of y look normal. That is the right question for a capability study, but the wrong one for regression. In regression the residuals must be normal and even, and y itself can have any shape because x moves it around. Use the Box–Cox option inside the regression dialog, which profiles the SSE of the model as above. Box–Cox has limits. It needs every y to be positive. It optimises normality and constant variance together with linearity, so when those goals conflict the estimate is a compromise. A single outlier can drag \(\hat{\lambda}\) a long way, so check the profile after removing any point with a large residual. Part 8

sections.heading: Let the data choose x: the Box–Tidwell method
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Let the data choose x: the Box–Tidwell method
sections.text: When the spread is already even, you want to transform x, not y. Box and Tidwell (1962) estimate the power \(\alpha\) in \(E(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^{\alpha}\) with a short iteration based on a Taylor expansion around the current guess \(\alpha_0\): \[ \begin{aligned} x^{\alpha} &\approx x^{\alpha_0} + (\alpha - \alpha_0)\,x^{\alpha_0}\ln x \\ &= z + \frac{\alpha - \alpha_0}{\alpha_0}\, z \ln z, \qquad z = x^{\alpha_0} \end{aligned} \] So the iteration is: Fit \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z\) and keep \(\hat{\beta}_1\). Fit \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z + \gamma\, z \ln z\) and keep \(\hat{\gamma}\). Update \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_0\left(1 + \hat{\gamma}/\hat{\beta}_1\right)\) and repeat until it settles. where \(z\) is x raised to the current power and \(\gamma\) is the coefficient on the correction term. Starting at \(\alpha_0 = 1\), one step is often close enough. A t-test on \(\hat{\gamma}\) in the first step is also a test of whether any power transformation of x is needed. Uses the dataset, offset and y transform currently set in the lab. Iteration history Step \(\alpha\) in \(\hat{\beta}_1\) \(\hat{\gamma}\) \(\alpha\) out Load the lab to run the iteration. Estimated \(\alpha\) – Nearest rung – Minitab has no Box–Tidwell command, but you can run the one-step version by hand: create \(x\ln x\) with Calc > Calculator , add it to the regression, and compute \(1 + \hat{\gamma}/\hat{\beta}_1\). R users have car::boxTidwell() . Like Box–Cox, it needs positive x, and it can diverge when the curve is not a power of x at all. Divergence is information: it tells you to look for a different model, an offset, or a curve that changes direction. Part 9

sections.heading: Zeros
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: \(\ln 0\) and \(1/0\) do not exist. The usual patch is \(\ln(y + c)\), but the answer depends on \(c\). Adding 1 to counts in the hundreds changes almost nothing; adding 1 to counts near 0 changes the shape completely. If you must shift, choose \(c\) for a reason (half the detection limit, or the smallest non-zero value divided by two), report it, and check that the conclusions survive a different \(c\). Often the better answer is \(\sqrt{y}\), which handles zeros, or a Poisson or Tweedie model with a log link, which models \(\ln E(y)\) without ever logging a zero.

sections.heading: Negative values
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: The power ladder needs positive data. For variables that cross zero (deviations, residuals, temperature in °C), use the Yeo–Johnson transformation, which applies Box–Cox to \(y + 1\) for \(y \ge 0\) and a mirrored version for \(y < 0\): \[ \psi(\lambda, y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{(y + 1)^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda}, & y \ge 0,\ \lambda \ne 0 \\[6pt] \ln(y + 1), & y \ge 0,\ \lambda = 0 \\[6pt] -\dfrac{(1 - y)^{2 - \lambda} - 1}{2 - \lambda}, & y < 0,\ \lambda \ne 2 \\[6pt] -\ln(1 - y), & y < 0,\ \lambda = 2 \end{cases} \] Better still, ask whether the variable has a natural zero. Temperature converted to kelvin is positive, and Arrhenius needs kelvin anyway.

sections.text: A transformation is a hypothesis about the data. Test it the same way you test any regression model: Residuals vs fitted. A horizontal band with no curve and no funnel. This is the single most important plot. Residuals vs each predictor. Catches curvature in one x that the fitted-value plot hides in a multiple regression. Normal probability plot of residuals. Roughly straight. Heavy tails after transforming may mean outliers rather than the wrong power. Residuals in time order. Transformations do nothing for autocorrelation or drift. Lack-of-fit test. sections.heading: Comparing models fairly
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: \(R^{2}\) measures the share of variance explained in the response you fitted . If one model predicts \(y\) and another predicts \(\ln y\), their \(R^{2}\) values describe different quantities and cannot be ranked. Three fair comparisons: Back-transform each model's predictions to the original scale and compute \(R^{2}_{\text{orig}} = 1 - \sum(y_i - \tilde{y}_i)^{2} / \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^{2}\), where \(\tilde{y}_i\) is the back-transformed prediction. The lab reports this. Compare the Box–Cox log-likelihood \(\ell(\lambda)\) at each candidate power. The geometric-mean scaling makes them comparable. Compare out-of-sample prediction error on the original scale with cross-validation. Comparing models with different x transforms but the same y is simpler: the \(R^{2}\) values and \(S\) are directly comparable. Part 11

sections.heading: Worked example: defect growth after a roll change
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
Worked example: defect growth after a roll change
sections.text: A finishing mill records surface defects per 100 pipes at six points after a roll change. Tonnage x is in thousands of tonnes. Defects per 100 pipes by tonnage since roll change (fictitious) \(x\) (kt) \(y\) (defects / 100 pipes) \(\ln y\) Residual, linear fit on \(y\) 1 0.82 −0.1985 +0.364 2 1.15 0.1398 −0.029 3 1.60 0.4700 −0.302 4 2.31 0.8372 −0.315 5 3.18 1.1569 −0.168 6 4.52 1.5085 +0.450 Step 1: the raw fit looks good and is wrong. A straight line on raw y gives \(R^{2} = 0.943\). The residuals run plus, minus, minus, minus, minus, plus: a U-shape. The curve bulges down and right, and the jumps between points grow with y, which suggests a multiplicative process. Move y down. Step 2: fit \(\ln y\) on x. \[ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\ln y} &= -0.5430 + 0.3415\,x \\ R^{2} &= 0.9998 \end{aligned} \] The residuals on the log scale are all within \(\pm 0.015\) with no pattern. Strictly, \(0.9998\) cannot be compared with \(0.943\) because the responses differ; the evidence is the residual pattern. Step 3: interpret the slope. Each extra thousand tonnes multiplies the defect rate by \(e^{0.3415}\): \[ \begin{aligned} e^{0.3415} &= 1.407 \;\Rightarrow\; +40.7\% \text{ per kt} \\ \text{Doubling distance} &= \frac{\ln 2}{0.3415} = 2.03\ \text{kt} \end{aligned} \] Step 4: back-transform a prediction. At 7 kt the model gives \(\widehat{\ln y} = -0.5430 + 0.3415 \times 7 = 1.8478\), so the predicted median rate is \(e^{1.8478} = 6.35\) defects per 100 pipes. The smearing correction here is \(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum e^{e_i} = 1.00003\) because the residuals are tiny, so the mean and median agree. With noisier data they would not; Part 12 shows how far apart they can drift. Step 5: act. The rate doubles about every 2 kt. Seven kilotonnes is outside the observed range, so treat the 7 kt figure as a warning for planning the next roll change, not a forecast to bank on. Part 12

sections.heading: Retransformation bias
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: Transforming back with the inverse function gives the right answer for quantiles , because monotone functions preserve order. So \(e^{\widehat{\ln y}}\) is a good estimate of the median of y. It is not the mean. If the log-scale errors are normal with variance \(\sigma^{2}\), the mean on the original scale is larger: \[ E(y \mid x) = \exp\!\left(\mu_x + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\right) \] where \(\mu_x\) is the log-scale prediction. Duan's smearing estimator makes no normality assumption. It multiplies the naive back-transform by the average of the exponentiated residuals \(e_i\): \[ \hat{E}(y \mid x) = e^{\hat{\mu}_x} \cdot \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e^{e_i} \] Use the median when you are describing a typical part. Use the mean when you are summing across parts, such as total scrap cost or total defects per shift. Interval endpoints back-transform directly: exponentiate the lower and upper limits of a prediction interval on the log scale and you get a valid, asymmetric interval on the original scale. Log-scale standard deviation \(\sigma\): 0.60 200 simulated parts, true median 20.0 Estimates of the mean of y Estimate Value Error vs true mean Part 13

sections.text: Assume x in A2:A41 and y in B2:B41 . Power law (log–log). In C2 enter =LN(A2) , in D2 enter =LN(B2) , and fill down. The exponent is =SLOPE(D2:D41,C2:C41) and the coefficient is =EXP(INTERCEPT(D2:D41,C2:C41)) . Exponential in one step. =INDEX(LOGEST(B2:B41,A2:A41),1) returns \(m\); the growth per unit of x is =INDEX(LOGEST(B2:B41,A2:A41),1)-1 . =LN(INDEX(LOGEST(B2:B41,A2:A41),1)) equals the slope of \(\ln y\) on x. Box–Cox profile. Put a trial \(\lambda\) in H1 . In E2 enter =IF($H$1=0,GEOMEAN($B$2:$B$41)*LN(B2),(B2^$H$1-1)/($H$1*GEOMEAN($B$2:$B$41)^($H$1-1))) and fill down. Then SSE is =DEVSQ(E2:E41)*(1-RSQ(E2:E41,A2:A41)) . Use Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table over \(\lambda\) from −2 to 2, pick the smallest SSE, and keep every \(\lambda\) whose SSE is below =MIN(SSE range)*EXP(CHISQ.INV(0.95,1)/40) as the 95% interval. Fair \(R^{2}\) on the original scale. After fitting \(\ln y\), put =EXP(TREND($D$2:$D$41,$A$2:$A$41,A2)) in F2 and fill down. Then =1-SUMXMY2(B2:B41,F2:F41)/DEVSQ(B2:B41) . Smearing correction. With log-scale residuals in G2:G41 , the factor is =AVERAGE(EXP(G2:G41)) in Excel 365 (enter as an array formula in older versions). Multiply each back-transformed prediction by it. Chart trendline caution. Excel's Exponential and Power trendlines fit on the log scale, and the \(R^{2}\) they display is the log-scale value. Do not set it beside a Linear trendline's \(R^{2}\) and pick the bigger number.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: Memorise the Box–Cox map: \(\lambda = 2\) square, 1 none, 0.5 square root, 0 natural log, −0.5 reciprocal square root, −1 reciprocal. Box–Cox needs strictly positive data. ASQ CSSBB and CQE questions often pair data types with transforms: counts → square root, proportions → arcsine square root, multiplicative or right-skewed data → log. For capability on transformed data, both the data and the specification limits are transformed with the same \(\lambda\). Johnson transformation is the alternative when Box–Cox fails. On a log–log plot the slope is an exponent; on a semi-log plot (\(\log y\)) the slope is a growth rate. Expect a question that asks which plot makes an exponential straight. Higher \(R^{2}\) after transforming y is not evidence that the model is better. Answer choices that rely on it are usually the distractor. In practice, record the transformation, the reason, and the back-transform method in the analysis report so the next engineer can reproduce it. Part 17

breadcrumb: Choosing a Transformation to Linearize Data
sections.text: The same workflow in code: profile Box–Cox on the regression, run one Box–Tidwell step, and back-transform with smearing. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import stats def boxcox_profile(x, y, lambdas=np.arange(-2, 3.01, 0.01)): """Regression-aware Box-Cox: profile SSE of z(lambda) on x.""" gm = np.exp(np.mean(np.log(y))) X = sm.add_constant(x) ll = [] for lam in lambdas: z = gm * np.log(y) if abs(lam) < 1e-9 else (y**lam - 1) / (lam * gm**(lam - 1)) sse = sm.OLS(z, X).fit().ssr ll.append(-len(y) / 2 * np.log(sse / len(y))) ll = np.array(ll) best = lambdas[ll.argmax()] ci = lambdas[ll >= ll.max() - stats.chi2.ppf(0.95, 1) / 2] return best, (ci.min(), ci.max()) def box_tidwell_step(x, y, alpha=1.0): """One Box-Tidwell update for the power on x (x > 0).""" z = x**alpha b1 = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().params[1] gamma = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(np.column_stack([z, z * np.log(z)]))).fit().params[2] return alpha * (1 + gamma / b1) # Fit ln(y) on x, then back-transform with Duan's smearing estimator fit = sm.OLS(np.log(y), sm.add_constant(x)).fit() smear = np.mean(np.exp(fit.resid)) mean_pred = np.exp(fit.fittedvalues) * smear # mean of y median_pred = np.exp(fit.fittedvalues) # median of y # Counts: model the mean directly instead of transforming poisson = sm.GLM(counts, sm.add_constant(length), family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() library(MASS) # boxcox() library(car) # boxTidwell() fit <- lm(y ~ x) boxcox(fit, lambda = seq(-2, 2, 0.05)) # regression-aware profile with 95% CI boxTidwell(y ~ x) # estimated power on x with a score test scipy.stats.boxcox(y) and scipy.stats.yeojohnson(y) are univariate, like Minitab's control-chart Box–Cox. They are right for normalizing a single variable and wrong for picking a regression transform.

sections.heading: Three charts, three different questions
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
sections.text: A process specialist is investigating wall-thickness differences between two pipe lines. Before fitting a model, they want to understand the distribution of measurements, the consistency of each operating group, and whether the shift effect changes between lines. These charts help answer those questions visually. What each Minitab quality chart is for Chart Question it answers Inputs Typical use case Symmetry plot Is a distribution balanced around its median? One numeric variable, such as thickness or downtime. Explore skewness before choosing summaries or an analysis approach. Variability chart Which factor combinations have different averages and different within-group spread? A numeric response and grouping factors, with repeated observations per cell. Find the line/shift/position combinations that are least consistent. Multi-vari chart How do factor-level means differ, and does one factor's effect depend on another? A numeric response and two or more meaningful factor levels. Look for position effects and Line × Shift interactions before ANOVA or regression. One important distinction: these are exploratory quality tools. They do not have control limits and do not establish time-ordered process stability. A symmetry plot does not establish normality. A visible factor pattern does not establish statistical significance or causation.

sections.heading: Symmetry plot: are the two tails balanced?
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Symmetry plot: are the two tails balanced?
sections.text: A symmetry plot compares observations above and below the median . Imagine folding a distribution at its median: values at corresponding distances on the two sides should line up if the distribution is symmetric. A few long stoppages can stretch the right tail even when most stoppages are short. Use it for: exploring wall-thickness distributions, cycle times, waiting times, repair durations, or other numeric measurements. It helps you see skewness that a single mean can hide. Examine a histogram as well to see features such as multiple peaks.

sections.heading: How the plot is constructed
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Symmetry plot: are the two tails balanced?
sections.text: Sort the observations and find the median. Pair the closest observation below the median with the closest above it. Continue outward through the tails. Plot the upper observation's distance above the median on the horizontal axis , and the lower observation's distance below the median on the vertical axis . Compare the plotted points with the diagonal equality line. d above = x upper − m d below = m − x lower Here, m is the sample median. The diagonal represents equal distances on the two sides. Read the axes before judging skewness Point pattern Meaning Why Near the diagonal Approximately symmetric. Above-median and below-median distances are similar. Diverges below the diagonal Right-skewed. The upper tail extends farther: horizontal distance is larger. Diverges above the diagonal Left-skewed. The lower tail extends farther: vertical distance is larger. Worked example: the wall median is 9.530 mm. The extreme pair is 9.340 and 9.720 mm, so both distances are 0.190 mm and the point lies on the diagonal. The downtime median is 11.5 min. Its extreme pair is 3 and 190 min: the horizontal distance is 178.5 min and the vertical distance is 8.5 min. That point lies far below the diagonal, showing a long right tail.

sections.heading: Variability chart: compare averages and spread
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Variability chart: compare averages and spread
sections.text: A variability chart groups individual measurements by factor levels so you can compare their means and their within-cell variation . Two groups can have the same average and very different consistency. Conversely, their averages can differ while their spreads remain similar. Use it for: comparing machines, lines, operators, shifts, suppliers, batches, or positions. In this example, the question is: “Which Line / Shift / Position combinations produce the greatest variation in wall thickness?”

sections.heading: Read the parts of the chart
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Variability chart: compare averages and spread
Read the parts of the chart
sections.text: Individual points show the actual wall readings. Cell mean shows the average for one complete factor combination. Range bar joins that cell's observed minimum and maximum. A longer bar indicates more spread. It is not a confidence interval or a control limit. Connecting lines of cell means make changes in average response easier to follow. Overall mean is an optional horizontal reference line. It does not represent a specification or target. Standard deviation chart is an optional second graph comparing sample SDs within the cells. Five pipes per cell make SD estimation possible here. R = x max − x min s = ∑ i = 1 n ( x i − x ¯ ) 2 n − 1 Calculate the range and sample SD separately for each cell. A mean uses the five measurements in that cell. Why include Position? Leading, Middle, and Trailing means intentionally differ. If you group only by Line and Shift, the spread of the 15 readings mixes those position differences with the scatter of pipes measured at the same position. Including Position isolates the five-pipe comparison within each location.

sections.heading: B / Night has a higher mean and greater spread
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Variability chart: compare averages and spread
B / Night has a higher mean and greater spread
sections.text: Actual Minitab average-response chart. Select the image to open a full-size view. The standard-deviation output and its explanation follow below. Read the grouping. Leading, Middle, and Trailing appear within Day and Night, grouped under Lines A and B. Find the overall mean. The horizontal reference is 9.5875 mm across all 60 readings. It is a sample mean, not a target or limit. Compare cell ranges. A / Day and A / Night ranges are 0.040 mm. B / Day ranges are 0.080 mm. B / Night ranges are 0.160 mm at each position. Compare averages. The 15-reading Line / Shift means are 9.530, 9.540, 9.560, and 9.720 mm respectively. B / Night stands out in both location and spread. Compare with the SD output below. Its values are approximately 0.01581 mm for each A cell, 0.03162 mm for each B / Day cell, and 0.06325 mm for each B / Night cell. These are within-position SDs, not SDs of all 15 readings pooled across positions. Recommend an investigation. “Prioritize B / Night because it has both a higher average thickness and greater within-position variation. Review setup, measurement-system performance, and relevant operating conditions.” The chart alone does not identify a cause or show out-of-specification product.

sections.heading: Standard deviation: compare consistency within each cell
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
Variability chart: compare averages and spread
Standard deviation: compare consistency within each cell
sections.text: Original supplied Minitab standard-deviation output, embedded unchanged. Select the image for a full-size view. What this output adds: the first graph shows cell averages and individual readings. This second graph isolates the spread of the five measurements within each Line / Shift / Position cell. A higher point means greater within-cell variation. Read the horizontal grouping. Start at Line A, compare Day and Night, and within each shift read Leading, Middle and Trailing. Repeat for Line B. There are twelve points, one for each cell, with five different pipes behind each point. Read the vertical scale. Although the axis label is Wall_mm , the chart title identifies the plotted statistic as standard deviation in millimetres . A point at 0.06325 is an SD, not an average wall thickness of 0.06325 mm. Compare the three plateaus. All six A cells have SD approximately 0.01581 mm. The three B / Day cells have SD approximately 0.03162 mm. The three B / Night cells have SD approximately 0.06325 mm. B / Night's SD is twice B / Day's and four times A's. These comparisons concern SD, not variance. Understand the horizontal line. At approximately 0.03162 mm, it is the arithmetic mean of the twelve cell SDs: (6 × 0.01581 + 3 × 0.03162 + 3 × 0.06325) ÷ 12, using rounded values. It is a comparison reference, not a control limit, specification limit, or the SD of all sixty readings pooled together. Separate position from consistency. Each Line / Shift group is flat across its three positions, so the constructed data have equal within-cell SDs across positions. The earlier mean chart still rises from Leading to Trailing. Means can change while the spread stays the same. The connecting line joins factor cells; it is not a time trend. Write the conclusion. “B / Night has the greatest within-cell variation at every measured position. Its SD is about 0.06325 mm, compared with 0.03162 mm on B / Day and 0.01581 mm on A. Investigate B / Night operating conditions and measurement consistency.” Five observations per cell give a limited estimate; this graph alone does not establish statistical significance, a cause, or process stability. Check it yourself: in the original workbook, =STDEV.S(Factor_Data!E47:E51) gives 0.06324555 mm for B / Night / Leading. Compare that value with the first point on the highest plateau. Use the five readings from one cell, not all sixty readings. 5 · Factor effects and interactions

sections.text: An interaction occurs when the effect of one factor depends on the level of another. Here, changing Day to Night increases average wall thickness by 0.010 mm on Line A and 0.160 mm on Line B . The unequal changes suggest a Line × Shift interaction. Lines do not have to cross for an interaction to exist. Δ A = 9.540 − 9.530 = 0.010 mm Δ B = 9.720 − 9.560 = 0.160 mm Δ B − Δ A = 0.150 mm Position effect: Trailing-position means exceed Leading-position means by 0.080 mm in all four Line / Shift groups. That position effect is consistent across those groups in this deliberately constructed example.

sections.text: Calculate the B / Night / Leading range from its five measurements: 9.600, 9.640, 9.680, 9.720, and 9.760 mm. Range (mm) Enter your result, then select Check my calculation. Explain the two symmetry plots. Which sample is symmetric and which has a long right tail? Check the explanation Wall_mm is symmetric around 9.530 mm because matching tail distances lie on the diagonal. Downtime_min is right-skewed: above-median distances exceed below-median distances, moving the points below the diagonal. Separate the mean problem from the consistency problem. Why should B / Night receive attention? Check the explanation Its overall Line / Shift mean is 9.720 mm, and each position cell has a range of 0.160 mm and sample SD about 0.06325 mm. Both the average and the within-position spread stand out. Specifications are not included, so this alone does not show whether the product fails a specification. Explain the interaction. Why would a single Day-to-Night average change be incomplete? Check the explanation The change is only 0.010 mm on A and 0.160 mm on B. The equally weighted pooled shift change is 0.085 mm, which hides these two different responses. Keep Line × Shift in the investigation. Investigate the sampling structure. How would the analysis change if Leading, Middle, and Trailing readings came from the same pipe? Check the explanation Measurements on the same pipe would be related. Record a shared Pipe_ID and use an appropriate repeated-measures or mixed-effects design when doing inference. Do not count those related readings as independent pipes. The graphs can still be useful descriptively. Write a short recommendation. Name the group, quote mean and spread evidence, identify checks, and state the next analysis. Read a worked recommendation “Prioritize Line B during Night. Its mean wall thickness is 9.720 mm and its within-position range is 0.160 mm, compared with 9.560 mm and 0.080 mm on B during Day. Check measurement-system performance, setup records, and operating conditions. Collect independent replicated data and use a model that includes Line × Shift, with assumption checks, to assess the pattern.”

sections.text: The Excel checks use the exact column layout of the downloaded workbook. The multi-criteria functions use equal-sized ranges. Functions with FILTER or SORT require a version with dynamic arrays, such as Microsoft 365. Functions for the chart calculations Function Syntax Purpose When to use MEDIAN =MEDIAN(number1,[number2],…) Find the middle of a sorted sample. Center the symmetry plot. SORT =SORT(array,[sort_index],[sort_order],[by_col]) Return an ordered array. Arrange the measurements for median-tail pairing. INDEX =INDEX(array,row_num,[column_num]) Retrieve a value at a given position. Take the corresponding lower and upper values from a sorted sample. AVERAGE / AVERAGEIFS =AVERAGE(number1,[number2],…) =AVERAGEIFS(average_range,criteria_range1,criteria1,…) Calculate an overall or selected-group mean. Verify cell, Line / Shift, and overall means. MIN / MAX =MIN(number1,[number2],…) =MAX(number1,[number2],…) Find the lowest and highest values. Calculate a cell range as MAX minus MIN. MINIFS / MAXIFS =MINIFS(min_range,criteria_range1,criteria1,…) =MAXIFS(max_range,criteria_range1,criteria1,…) Find extremes meeting several criteria. Verify the range of a chosen factor combination. STDEV.S =STDEV.S(number1,[number2],…) Estimate sample standard deviation with the n − 1 denominator. Match Minitab's within-cell sample SD. COUNT / COUNTIFS =COUNT(value1,[value2],…) =COUNTIFS(criteria_range1,criteria1,…) Count numeric measurements or rows matching criteria. Verify 30/60 measurements and five observations per cell. FILTER =FILTER(array,include,[if_empty]) Return rows that meet conditions. Pass one cell's measurements to STDEV.S.

sections.heading: Excel Use Cases
breadcrumb: Introduction to Symmetry Plot, Variability Chart and Multi-Vari Chart in Minitab
sections.text: Enter these formulas in unused cells in Excel. Do not overwrite the raw data columns. All results below refer to the original practice dataset. Verify the symmetry center. =MEDIAN(Symmetry_Data!B2:B31) gives 9.530 mm. =MEDIAN(Symmetry_Data!C2:C31) gives 11.5 min. =COUNT(Symmetry_Data!B2:B31) gives 30. Build the extreme wall pair. =INDEX(SORT(Symmetry_Data!B2:B31),1) gives 9.340; use row number 30 for 9.720. Subtract the median from the upper value for horizontal distance, and subtract the lower value from the median for vertical distance. Both distances equal 0.190 mm. Verify B / Night / Leading's mean. =AVERAGEIFS(Factor_Data!E2:E61,Factor_Data!B2:B61,"B",Factor_Data!C2:C61,"Night",Factor_Data!D2:D61,"Leading") gives 9.680 mm. Drop the Position criterion to obtain the B / Night mean, 9.720 mm. Verify the cell's replication. =COUNTIFS(Factor_Data!B2:B61,"B",Factor_Data!C2:C61,"Night",Factor_Data!D2:D61,"Leading") gives 5. Verify its range. =MAX(Factor_Data!E47:E51)-MIN(Factor_Data!E47:E51) gives 0.160 mm. Those rows are the five B / Night / Leading pipes in the original sheet. If you sort or reorder the data, select the cell with criteria instead: use MAXIFS and MINIFS with Line = B, Shift = Night, and Position = Leading. Verify its sample SD. =STDEV.S(Factor_Data!E47:E51) gives approximately 0.06324555 mm. A sort-safe Microsoft 365 formula is =STDEV.S(FILTER(Factor_Data!E2:E61,(Factor_Data!B2:B61="B")*(Factor_Data!C2:C61="Night")*(Factor_Data!D2:D61="Leading"))) . Multiplication means all three conditions must be true. Verify the interaction. Use AVERAGEIFS to obtain each Line / Shift mean. Calculate Night minus Day within each line, then subtract A's change from B's. The difference is 0.150 mm. The overall mean =AVERAGE(Factor_Data!E2:E61) is 9.5875 mm. Version alternative: if FILTER or SORT is unavailable, copy the selected measurements into an unused range and sort/filter them with Excel's data commands before calculating. For selected-cell SD, use the five actual measurements; do not use SUBTOTAL or a whole-range STDEV.S that still includes other groups.

sections.heading: Control charts in plain English
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: A control chart is a time-ordered process graph with statistically calculated limits. It answers: “Is the process behaving like one stable system, or is something unusual changing it?”
sections.excerpt: A control chart is a time-ordered process graph with statistically calculated limits. It answers: “Is the process behaving like one stable system, or is something unusual changing it?”

sections.heading: What a control chart tells you

What a control chart tells you
sections.text: Whether variation appears consistent over time. Whether an unusual point, shift, trend, cycle, or mixture pattern may require investigation. Whether process changes produced a sustained change.

breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Term Plain-language meaning Practical interpretation Common-cause variation Routine background variation built into the current system. Improve the system; do not chase individual points. Special-cause variation An unusual source that is not consistently present. Investigate the specific time, material, setup, equipment, operator, or environment. Center line The expected process level or rate. Usually estimated from baseline data unless a validated historical parameter is entered. Control limits Expected boundaries for a stable process. Usually based on approximately ±3 standard deviations, with chart-specific distributions. Specification limits Engineering or customer acceptance requirements. They evaluate conformance, not stability. They should not replace control limits. Rational subgroup Observations collected under nearly identical short-term conditions. Within-subgroup variation represents short-term noise; between-subgroup differences reveal process changes. Defective A unit classified once as pass/fail. Use P, NP, or Laney P′ charts. Defect An individual nonconformity; one unit may have several. Use C, U, or Laney U′ charts. Phase I Establish and clean a historical baseline. Investigate special causes and estimate defensible limits. Phase II Monitor future production against established limits. Use frozen historical limits unless the process is intentionally changed.

sections.text: Test Pattern What it can suggest 1 One point more than 3σ from the center line A large isolated special cause. 2 Nine points in a row on the same side A sustained process shift. 3 Six points in a row increasing or decreasing A trend or drift. 4 Fourteen points alternating up and down Systematic over-adjustment or alternating sources. 5 Two of three points more than 2σ from the center line on the same side A moderate shift. 6 Four of five points more than 1σ from the center line on the same side A small sustained shift. 7 Fifteen points in a row within 1σ of the center line Stratification or control limits that are too wide. 8 Eight points in a row more than 1σ from the center line on either side A mixture pattern or limits that are too narrow for the data structure. Availability varies by chart. Minitab provides Tests 1–8 for most variables charts; R, S, MR, and attribute charts support fewer tests; EWMA and Moving Average support only Test 1; CUSUM, Zone, and multivariate charts use their own signaling logic.

sections.heading: Interpretation guide: when you see this, it means this
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
Interpretation guide: when you see this, it means this
sections.text: When you see this What it may mean What to do next Variation chart out of control The short-term variation estimate is unstable. Investigate variation signals first; delay conclusions from the mean chart. One point beyond a control limit A large special cause may have occurred. Trace the exact time to material, equipment, setup, measurement, and operating records. Nine points on one side The process level may have shifted. Identify a change point, verify whether it was intentional, and consider staged limits. Six points steadily increasing A drift may be occurring. Check wear, thermal buildup, tool condition, calibration drift, or progressive material change. P or U limits change each subgroup Sample size or opportunity varies. Do not force constant limits; verify the subgroup-size column is correct. Many P/U signals with huge samples Overdispersion, underdispersion, or mixed process structure may exist. Investigate the structure, then assess Laney P′ or U′ if appropriate. G/T point becomes very low Rare adverse events are occurring closer together. Escalate the investigation even though low values may look visually “better” on ordinary charts. T² signal with stable univariate charts The joint combination of variables is unusual. Examine contributions, correlations, and process context rather than dismissing the signal. All points inside limits but process misses specs The process may be stable but incapable. Perform capability analysis after confirming stability.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and software traps
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Selection error: using P for defects. A P chart counts defective units, not multiple defects. Use C/U/Laney U′ for defects. Subgroup error: grouping unrelated observations. A subgroup should represent short-term common conditions, not a convenient set of five rows. Interpretation error: reading Xbar before R or S. Unstable variation compromises the location-chart limits. Software error: entering sample size as the number defective. For P and U charts, verify the response and opportunity columns are assigned to the correct boxes. Limit error: drawing specification limits as control limits. Specifications come from design or customer requirements; control limits come from process behavior. Chronology error: sorting values from low to high. Control charts require production order. Sorting by magnitude destroys the time pattern. Phase I error: deleting every red point. Exclude a point only after identifying and documenting a credible special cause. Mixed-product error: placing unlike products on one I-MR chart. Use separate charts, stages, or a Z-MR short-run approach with validated product targets. False-alarm error: turning on every test automatically. Additional tests increase sensitivity and the chance of false signals. Follow a documented monitoring plan. Capability error: calculating Cpk on an unstable process. Capability estimates are unreliable when the process distribution changes over time.

Choose the correct chart for a surface-inspection process
sections.text: Each shift, an inspector records the number of visible surface defects found on coils. The inspected surface area changes from shift to shift because coil lengths and widths vary. One coil may contain several defects. Your task: select the chart, state the required worksheet columns, provide the full Minitab navigation path, and explain why a C chart would be inappropriate. Correct chart: U chart. Why: the response is a count of defects, multiple defects can occur on one coil, and inspection opportunity varies. The U chart standardizes the count as defects per unit of opportunity. Worksheet: one column for defect count and one column for inspected surface area or another defensible opportunity measure. Stat > Control Charts > Attributes Charts > U A C chart is inappropriate because it assumes constant inspection opportunity. Laney U′ should be considered only after assessing whether overdispersion or underdispersion makes the conventional U chart misleading.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Choose the chart from the data-generating process, not from preference. Continuous subgroup data use Xbar-R, Xbar-S, or I-MR-R/S. Continuous individual data usually use I-MR; mixed short runs may require Z-MR. Defectives use P/NP/Laney P′; defects use C/U/Laney U′. EWMA and CUSUM improve sensitivity to small sustained shifts. T², Generalized Variance, and MEWMA monitor correlated variables jointly. G and T charts monitor spacing between rare events. Stability must be established before capability is interpreted.

sections.heading: What CUBE functions are and why they matter
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
What CUBE functions are and why they matter
sections.text: A normal Excel formula such as SUMIFS reads cells on a worksheet. A CUBE function reads a model instead: either the Data Model built into your workbook with Power Pivot, or an external OLAP cube such as SQL Server Analysis Services. The model already knows your tables, relationships and calculations (called measures ). A CUBE function simply names which slice of the model you want and returns the answer. Think of a PivotTable. Every value cell in a PivotTable is the intersection of a measure (for example Total Rejects) with the row and column items (for example Grade X70 and Mill A). CUBE functions let you place each of those intersections in any cell you like, mixed with normal formulas, text and formatting. You keep the power of the model and lose the rigid PivotTable grid.

sections.heading: Set up the Data Model with the practice data
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
Set up the Data Model with the practice data
sections.text: The practice workbook holds one fictitious table named Tests with 96 rows: six months (January to June 2026), two mills, two shifts and four line-pipe grades. Each row records the pipe joints inspected ( Pieces ), the joints rejected ( Rejects ) and the batch average Charpy energy in joules ( CharpyJ ). A Data Dictionary tab documents every column. Download the practice dataset (Excel .xlsx) Download the same data (CSV) Requirements: Excel for Windows (Microsoft 365 recommended) is needed to build a Data Model and DAX measures. Every value quoted in this lesson comes from this workbook, so you can check your formulas against the text.

sections.heading: Step by step
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
Set up the Data Model with the practice data
sections.text: Open the workbook. The data on the Tests sheet is already an Excel table named Tests (check under Table Design → Table Name ). Name your tables before loading them: the table name becomes part of every member expression. Add the table to the Data Model. Click inside the table, then choose Insert → PivotTable → From Table/Range and tick Add this data to the Data Model . If you have the Power Pivot tab, Power Pivot → Add to Data Model does the same job. Create four explicit measures. In the PivotTable Fields pane, right-click the Tests table and choose Add Measure (or use Power Pivot → Measures → New Measure ). Create the DAX measures below. Confirm the connection name. A workbook Data Model is always reached through the connection named ThisWorkbookDataModel . You will type it as the first argument of every CUBE function in this lesson. Total Pieces := SUM ( Tests[Pieces] ) Total Rejects := SUM ( Tests[Rejects] ) Reject Rate := DIVIDE ( [Total Rejects], [Total Pieces] ) Avg Charpy J := AVERAGE ( Tests[CharpyJ] ) Why explicit measures? If you drag Pieces into a Data Model PivotTable, Excel creates an implicit measure called Sum of Pieces . CUBE functions can use it ( [Measures].[Sum of Pieces] ), but it disappears if you remove the field and you cannot reuse it inside other measures. Explicit measures are stable names you control, so every formula in this lesson uses them. No Power Pivot tab? Turn it on under File → Options → Add-ins → Manage: COM Add-ins → Go , then tick Microsoft Power Pivot for Excel . You can still complete most of this lesson with the PivotTable Fields pane alone. Part 1 · Beginner

sections.heading: Member expressions: the language inside the quotes
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
Member expressions: the language inside the quotes
sections.text: Every CUBE function takes text arguments that name things in the model. These strings use MDX (Multidimensional Expressions) naming, the query language of OLAP cubes. You only need a small part of MDX to be productive. [Tests] table (dimension) .[Grade] column (hierarchy) .&[X70] member, by key The patterns you will use most Pattern Example Meaning A measure [Measures].[Total Rejects] Every measure lives in the special [Measures] dimension. Member by key [Tests].[Grade].&[X70] The & means "match the key value". This is the form Excel itself generates. Use it by default. Member by name [Tests].[Grade].[X70] Matches the member caption. Works for text columns, but numbers and dates can have a caption that differs from the key. The All member [Tests].[Grade].[All] The grand total of that column, the same as not filtering it at all. All children (a set) [Tests].[Grade].[All].Children Every grade. This is a set , so it belongs in CUBESET , not CUBEMEMBER . Tuple (a combination) ([Tests].[Grade].&[X70],[Tests].[Mill].&[Mill A]) One member from each of several columns, in parentheses, separated by commas. Set literal {[Tests].[Grade].&[X65],[Tests].[Grade].&[X70]} A hand-picked list of members from one column, in braces.

sections.heading: Rules that prevent most errors
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
Member expressions: the language inside the quotes
sections.text: Every name sits in square brackets , especially names with spaces: [Mill A] , [Total Rejects] . The whole expression is a text string , so it is wrapped in double quotes in the formula: "[Tests].[Mill].&[Mill A]" . Names come from the model, not the worksheet. [Tests] is the table name in the Data Model, not the sheet name. Let Excel help. When you type =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[ Excel offers a list of tables, measures and members. Press Tab to accept a suggestion. Dates and numbers have keys that look different. A date member in the Data Model has a key such as &[2026-03-01T00:00:00] . That is why the practice data stores the month as text ( 2026-03 ). If you are unsure of a key, build a PivotTable and use Convert to Formulas (Part 6) to see the exact text Excel generates.

breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
sections.text: =CUBEVALUE(connection, [member_expression1], [member_expression2], ...) CUBEVALUE evaluates the model at the intersection of every member you pass. Each member_expression can be a text expression, a cell that contains CUBEMEMBER , a cell that contains CUBESET , or the name of a slicer. Columns you do not mention are not filtered (they stay at their All member). If you name no measure, the model's default measure is used, so always name one.

sections.heading: Shortcut: let Excel write the formulas (Convert to Formulas)
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
Shortcut: let Excel write the formulas (Convert to Formulas)
sections.text: You never have to memorise exact member keys. Excel can turn a Data Model PivotTable into CUBE formulas for you: Build a PivotTable from the Data Model with Grade on Rows, Mill on Columns and Total Rejects in Values. Select any cell in it and choose PivotTable Analyze → OLAP Tools → Convert to Formulas . (In older versions the tab is called Analyze or Options .) If the PivotTable has report filters, Excel asks whether to convert them too. Choose to convert them if you want every cell as a formula. Inspect the result: headers become CUBEMEMBER , values become CUBEVALUE , with the exact member text Excel uses. Workflow tip: prototype with a PivotTable, convert, then delete, move and restyle cells freely. The converted cells are ordinary formulas, so you can copy them to other sheets or rewrite them with cell references. Convert to Formulas is only available for PivotTables based on the Data Model or an OLAP source. A PivotTable built from a plain range has no model behind it, so the option is greyed out. sections.text: =CUBESET(connection, set_expression, [caption], [sort_order], [sort_by]) CUBESET arguments Argument Required? What to pass connection Yes "ThisWorkbookDataModel" or your OLAP connection name. set_expression Yes Text that returns a set, such as "[Tests].[Grade].[All].Children" , or a cell reference to a CUBEMEMBER that returns members. caption No Text shown in the cell. A set has no single caption of its own, so always supply one. sort_order No A number from 0 to 6 (table below). Default 0. sort_by Only for sort_order 1 or 2 The measure to sort by, for example "[Measures].[Total Rejects]" . sort_order values Value Name Sorts by Needs sort_by? 0 SortNone Leaves the set in its existing order No 1 SortAscending The sort_by value, smallest first Yes 2 SortDescending The sort_by value, largest first Yes 3 SortAlphaAscending Caption, A to Z No 4 Sort_Alpha_Descending Caption, Z to A No 5 Sort_Natural_Ascending The model's natural (hierarchy) order No 6 Sort_Natural_Descending The model's natural order, reversed No A CUBESET cell shows only its caption. Its value is the set itself, which you pass to CUBESETCOUNT , CUBERANKEDMEMBER or CUBEVALUE .

sections.text: All grades, largest reject count first =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Tests].[Grade].[All].Children","Grades by rejects",2,"[Measures].[Total Rejects]") A hand-picked list (set literal) =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","{[Tests].[Grade].&[X65],[Tests].[Grade].&[X70]}","High grades") A range of members (first quarter) =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Tests].[Month].&[2026-01]:[Tests].[Month].&[2026-03]","Q1 2026") Everything except one member =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","Except([Tests].[Grade].[All].Children,{[Tests].[Grade].&[X52]})","All but X52") The top 2 grades by rejects (MDX TopCount) =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","TopCount([Tests].[Grade].[All].Children,2,[Measures].[Total Rejects])","Top 2 grades") Only grades above a 2.5% reject rate (MDX Filter) =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","Filter([Tests].[Grade].[All].Children,[Measures].[Reject Rate]>0.025)","Over 2.5%") In the practice data, the TopCount set holds X70 (327 rejects) and X65 (241 rejects), and the Filter set holds X70 alone (3.07% reject rate). The practice workbook does not. Data Model users: the workbook Data Model (Power Pivot) does not have member properties, so this function has nothing to return there. Add the attribute as a column in your table instead and slice by it with CUBEMEMBER and CUBEVALUE , or put it in a lookup table and use XLOOKUP on the member caption. Part 3 · Advanced

CUBEKPIMEMBER: value, goal, status and trend of a KPI
sections.text: =CUBEKPIMEMBER(connection, kpi_name, kpi_property, [caption]) A KPI (key performance indicator) is a measure plus a target and status thresholds, defined in the model. In the Data Model you create one with Power Pivot → KPIs → New KPI : choose the base measure (for example Reject Rate ), an absolute target such as 0.02, and status thresholds. CUBEKPIMEMBER returns the KPI component you ask for as a member, and CUBEVALUE turns it into a number. kpi_property values Value Constant Returns 1 KPIValue The actual value of the KPI measure 2 KPIGoal The target 3 KPIStatus The status at that moment, typically a number from -1 to 1 4 KPITrend The trend value, if the model defines one 5 KPIWeight The relative importance assigned to the KPI 6 KPICurrentTimeMember A temporal context for the KPI B1 =CUBEKPIMEMBER("ThisWorkbookDataModel","Reject Rate",2,"Goal") B2 =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel",$B$1,$A2) goal for the grade in A2 C2 =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel",CUBEKPIMEMBER("ThisWorkbookDataModel","Reject Rate",3),$A2) status Pair the status with conditional-formatting icon sets (and a text label such as "Above target") so the meaning never depends on colour alone. Not every model defines trend, weight or a current time member; when a component is missing, there is nothing for CUBEVALUE to return. Part 3 · Advanced

breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
sections.text: A single member expression longer than 255 characters makes the function return #VALUE! . Long sets (many hand-picked members) hit this quickly. Split the work: build the set once in its own CUBESET cell, or build members in CUBEMEMBER cells, and pass the cell references. References also make formulas easier to read and audit.

sections.heading: 5. Refresh and performance
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
sections.text: CUBE functions calculate asynchronously. Cells show #GETTING_DATA briefly while the model answers; this is normal. Data → Refresh All reloads the model from its source and then recalculates the CUBE formulas. Reuse header cells. A sheet with 2,000 CUBEVALUE cells that reference shared CUBEMEMBER headers is faster and easier to audit than 2,000 formulas that each repeat long text expressions. Put the logic in DAX measures, not in Excel arithmetic on top of CUBEVALUE . A ratio measure such as Reject Rate stays correct at every level of aggregation; dividing two CUBEVALUE cells works only if you remember to do it at each level. CUBE functions return one value per cell. They do not spill like dynamic-array formulas, so lay out one formula per cell.

sections.heading: Errors and troubleshooting
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
sections.text: What each result usually means You see Usual cause Fix #NAME? The connection name is wrong or the model/server is not available. Use "ThisWorkbookDataModel" exactly; check the OLAP connection under Data → Queries & Connections . #N/A The member does not exist, a name is misspelled, brackets are missing, or two members in a set come from different columns. Re-type with autocomplete, or copy the expression from Convert to Formulas. #VALUE! An element of the tuple is invalid, or an expression exceeds 255 characters. Split long expressions into CUBEMEMBER / CUBESET cells. Empty cell No data at that intersection (for example a grade never made on that mill). Expected. Wrap in N() before arithmetic. #GETTING_DATA The model is still calculating. Wait; if it persists, refresh the model. Wrong total Using an implicit measure or averaging percentages in Excel. Use explicit DAX measures (ratios as DIVIDE ). Date member not found Using the caption ( 3/1/2026 ) instead of the key. Use the key form shown by Convert to Formulas, for example &[2026-03-01T00:00:00] . Reference

sections.heading: Practice exercises
breadcrumb: Excel CUBE Functions: Beginner to Advanced
sections.text: Use the practice workbook. Try each exercise before opening the answer, then check your number against it. Exercise 1 (beginner): total pieces for Mill B =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Measures].[Total Pieces]","[Tests].[Mill].&[Mill B]") Answer: 20,843 pieces. Exercise 2 (beginner): rejects for Mill B =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Measures].[Total Rejects]","[Tests].[Mill].&[Mill B]") Answer: 479 rejects. Mill A has 414. Exercise 3 (beginner): overall reject rate =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Measures].[Reject Rate]") Answer: 0.0212, or 2.12% when formatted as a percentage (893 rejects out of 42,130 pieces). Exercise 4 (intermediate): a grade-by-mill grid Build headers with CUBEMEMBER for the four grades (A2:A5) and two mills (B1:C1), the measure in A1, then one formula in B2 copied to B2:C5: =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel",$A$1,$A2,B$1) Check: the X70 row should add up to 327 rejects across the two mills. Exercise 5 (intermediate): March rejects for grades X65 and X70 combined H1 =CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","{[Tests].[Grade].&[X65],[Tests].[Grade].&[X70]}","X65 + X70") H2 =CUBEVALUE("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Measures].[Total Rejects]",H1,"[Tests].[Month].&[2026-03]") Answer: 92 rejects (X65 had 41 and X70 had 51 in March). You can confirm each part in Live builder 2. Exercise 6 (intermediate): a Top 2 grades list by rejects Use the Top N pattern with N = 2. Answer: X70 (327) then X65 (241). Exercise 7 (advanced): which month had the fewest rejects? =CUBERANKEDMEMBER("ThisWorkbookDataModel", CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","[Tests].[Month].[All].Children","Months",1,"[Measures].[Total Rejects]"),1) Answer: 2026-06 with 137 rejects (sort_order 1 puts the smallest first). Exercise 8 (advanced): count grades above a 2.0% reject rate =CUBESETCOUNT(CUBESET("ThisWorkbookDataModel","Filter([Tests].[Grade].[All].Children,[Measures].[Reject Rate]>0.02)")) Answer: 2 (X65 at 2.29% and X70 at 3.07%).

lessons.title: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
lessons.description: Learn Cp and Cpk with a live capability explorer: specs, spread, centering, the 1.33 benchmark, and Excel & Minitab how-tos.
keywords: process capability cp cpk capability index specification limits usl lsl voice of customer voice of process six sigma capability analysis 1.33 ppk pp minitab excel lean six sigma beginner interactive

sections.heading: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Lean Six Sigma Your customer sets the goalposts. Your process kicks the ball. Process capability measures — with two simple numbers, C p and C pk — whether your process can reliably land inside those goalposts. Why this matters at work: capability indices are the standard language between suppliers and customers. A contract that says “maintain C pk ≥ 1.33” is a precise, testable promise about defect rates — and knowing how to compute and read these numbers is a core skill for quality roles and a guaranteed topic on the ASQ CSSBB and CQE exams.

sections.heading: Before you start
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: This lesson builds directly on The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve . You should be comfortable with the mean μ, the standard deviation σ, and the idea that almost all values of a normal process fall within ±3σ of the mean. That “±3σ” span — 6σ wide in total — is the star of this lesson. Before estimating capability, assess measurement error with a Gage R&R study , then use control charts to assess process stability.

sections.heading: Voice of the process — the natural spread
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
Two voices: the customer and the process
Voice of the process — the natural spread
sections.text: The process doesn’t care what the drawing says. It produces values with its own mean μ and standard deviation σ. For a stable, roughly normal process, essentially all output (99.73%) lands within μ ± 3σ — a natural spread that is 6σ wide . Capability is the comparison of the two widths. If the goalposts (spec width) are much wider than the ball’s scatter (6σ), nearly everything lands in-spec. If the scatter is as wide as the goalposts — or the aim is off-centre — defects follow. One sentence to remember: C p asks “is the spread small enough?” and C pk asks “is the spread small enough where the process is actually aimed ?”

sections.heading: The formulas: Cp and Cpk
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: \[ C_{p} = \frac{\mathrm{USL} - \mathrm{LSL}}{6\sigma} \] Here \(\mathrm{LSL}\) and \(\mathrm{USL}\) are the specification limits, \(\mu\) is the process mean, and \(\sigma\) represents within-process variation. For sample estimates, use the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) and a justified within-process standard deviation estimate. Under the Minitab reporting convention used below, substituting the overall sample standard deviation \(s\) gives \(P_{p}\) and \(P_{pk}\), rather than the within-process indices. C p is a simple ratio of the two widths: specification width on top, natural process spread underneath. C p = 1 means the goalposts and the scatter are exactly the same width — the process barely fits, with zero room for error. C p = 2 means the goalposts are twice as wide as the scatter. But C p has a blind spot: it completely ignores where the process is centred. A process aimed way off-target can still have a beautiful C p . \[ C_{pk} = \min\left( \frac{\mathrm{USL} - \mu}{3\sigma}, \frac{\mu - \mathrm{LSL}}{3\sigma} \right) \] C pk fixes the blind spot. It measures the distance from the process mean to the nearest spec limit, in units of 3σ, and reports the worse side. If the process is perfectly centred, C pk = C p . The further the mean drifts toward a limit, the lower C pk falls — even while C p stays put. That gap between the two numbers is itself a diagnosis: C p high but C pk low? The spread is fine — the process is simply off-centre. Re-aim it (usually the cheap fix). Both low? The spread itself is too wide — you have a variation-reduction project on your hands (the expensive fix).

sections.heading: How to run a capability study, step by step
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
How to run a capability study, step by step
sections.text: Confirm the process is stable first. Run a control chart (see Control Charts Explained ). Capability numbers from an unstable process are fiction — the spread you measure today won’t be the spread you get tomorrow. Check the data are roughly normal. A histogram or normal probability plot is enough at this level. Strongly skewed data need a transformation or a different method before the formulas apply. Collect enough data. Aim for at least 30 measurements — 50 to 125 is better — taken across a representative stretch of production, not one lucky hour. Estimate the mean and identify the variation basis. Use \(\bar{x}\) for the mean. For \(C_{p}\) and \(C_{pk}\), estimate within-process variation from rational subgroups or an appropriate individuals-chart method. The standard deviation \(s\) of all observations over the study period is the overall estimate used for \(P_{p}\) and \(P_{pk}\). Apply the formulas. C p from the two widths; C pk from the nearest-limit distance. Interpret and act. Compare against the agreed benchmark, then diagnose: centring problem, spread problem, or both.

sections.heading: Worked example: the coffee bag line
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
Worked example: the coffee bag line
sections.text: A packing line fills \(500\,\mathrm{g}\) coffee bags with a spec of \(500 \pm 6\,\mathrm{g}\) (\(\mathrm{LSL} = 494\,\mathrm{g}\), \(\mathrm{USL} = 506\,\mathrm{g}\)). For this example, sixty bags from a stable run give a sample mean of \(\bar{x} = 501.2\,\mathrm{g}\) and a within-process standard deviation estimate of \(\hat{\sigma}_{\mathrm{within}} = 1.5\,\mathrm{g}\) . Specification width: 506 − 494 = 12 g . Natural spread: 6σ = 6 × 1.5 = 9 g . C p = 12 / 9 = 1.33 . Potential looks healthy: the goalposts are a third wider than the scatter. Upper side: (506 − 501.2) / (3 × 1.5) = 4.8 / 4.5 = 1.07 . Lower side: (501.2 − 494) / 4.5 = 7.2 / 4.5 = 1.60 . C pk = min(1.07, 1.60) = 1.07 . The story the two numbers tell: the spread is fine (C p = 1.33), but the line is overfilling by 1.2 g on average, pushing output toward the upper limit and dragging C pk down to 1.07 — below the 1.33 benchmark. The fix isn’t a costly variation-reduction project; it’s re-targeting the filler back to 500 g. Centre it, and C pk rises to meet C p at 1.33 — and the overfill give-away stops too.

sections.heading: Reading the numbers
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Common \(C_{pk}\) benchmarks: centred, stable normal model, two-sided specs, no mean shift \(C_{pk} = C_{p}\) Modelled out-of-spec ppm Typical reading \(< 1.00\) More than approximately \(2700\,\mathrm{ppm}\) Not capable — the process cannot reliably hold the spec \(1.00\) \(\approx 2700\,\mathrm{ppm}\) Barely fits — any drift increases the defect rate \(\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\) \(\approx 63.3\,\mathrm{ppm}\) The classic minimum most customers require \(\frac{5}{3} \approx 1.67\) \(\approx 0.573\,\mathrm{ppm}\) Strong — typical target for safety-critical characteristics \(2.00\) \(\approx 0.002\,\mathrm{ppm}\) “Six Sigma” capability with the mean on target Why \(1.33\)? The rounded benchmark \(\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\) puts the nearest spec limit \(4\sigma\) from the mean — an extra \(\sigma\) of margin beyond the \(3\sigma\) benchmark. This is a margin, not a guarantee against defects or future drift. The ppm values assume the mean is centred between the limits and use the same normal-model standard deviation as the indices, with no \(1.5\sigma\) shift. The fractional indices in the table are exact; their decimal labels are rounded. An off-centre \(C_{pk}\) alone does not determine the total out-of-spec rate. Calculate both tails: \[ \begin{aligned} z_{\mathrm{L}} &= \frac{\mathrm{LSL} - \mu}{\sigma}, \\ z_{\mathrm{U}} &= \frac{\mathrm{USL} - \mu}{\sigma}, \\ \mathrm{PPM} &= 10^{6}\left[\Phi(z_{\mathrm{L}}) + 1 - \Phi(z_{\mathrm{U}})\right]. \end{aligned} \] Here \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, \(z_{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{U}}\) are the standardised specification limits, and \(\mathrm{PPM}\) is the modelled number outside the limits per million units. Predictions based on within-process variation need not equal overall observed performance. One more distinction you’ll meet immediately in software: \(C_{pk}\) vs \(P_{pk}\) . Minitab uses a within-process estimate for \(C_{pk}\) and the overall standard deviation of all observations for \(P_{pk}\). Overall variation includes any differences between subgroups in the study period, so \(P_{pk}\) may be lower; it is not guaranteed to be lower. A sample standard deviation can estimate a common process \(\sigma\) for a justified stable, homogeneous sample. State that sampling assumption and estimation method explicitly rather than treating the function name alone as the definition of the index.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Computing capability on an unstable process. If the control chart shows special causes, the σ you measured is a moving target and the index is meaningless. Stability first, capability second — always. Quoting C p when the process is off-centre. C p is blind to centring. Reporting “C p = 1.6, we’re fine” while C pk is 0.7 hides a real defect stream. Report both; act on C pk . Forcing the formulas onto non-normal data. The ppm predictions in the table assume a normal shape. Cycle-time and flatness data, for example, are often skewed — transform first or use a non-normal capability method. Confusing 6σ in the denominator with “Six Sigma” the programme. The 6σ in C p is simply the width of the natural spread. “Six Sigma quality” refers to specs sitting six standard deviations from the mean — C p = 2.0 territory.

sections.heading: Exam tips (ASQ CSSBB / CQE)
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Memorise both formulas cold. Exam questions hand you μ, σ, LSL, USL and expect C p and C pk in under a minute. Practice until the coffee-bag example takes you 30 seconds. Know the signature patterns: C p = C pk ⇒ perfectly centred; C p > C pk ⇒ off-centre; C pk can never exceed C p . A negative C pk means the mean is outside a spec limit. One-sided specs: with only a USL, C pk = (USL − μ)/3σ and C p is undefined — a favourite exam trap. Short-term vs long-term: C p /C pk pair with within-subgroup (short-term) σ; P p /P pk with overall (long-term) σ. Questions about “which index uses which sigma” appear on both exams. Benchmarks: for a centred normal model with no mean shift, \(C_{pk} = 1\) gives approximately \(2700\,\mathrm{ppm}\), \(C_{pk} = \frac{4}{3}\) gives approximately \(63.3\,\mathrm{ppm}\), and \(C_{pk} = \frac{5}{3}\) gives approximately \(0.573\,\mathrm{ppm}\). Knowing \(\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\) means \(4\sigma\) to the nearest limit lets you re-derive the rest. Prerequisites are testable: “What must be true before a capability study?” — stability (in control) and approximate normality. Stability always comes first.

breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: A machining line cuts shafts to a diameter spec of 10.0 ± 0.5 mm (LSL = 9.5, USL = 10.5). A stable run gives μ = 10.1 mm and σ = 0.12 mm . Compute both indices to two decimal places. Your C p : Your C pk : Spec width = 10.5 − 9.5 = 1.0 mm; natural spread = 6 × 0.12 = 0.72 mm. C p = 1.0 / 0.72 = 1.39 . Upper side: (10.5 − 10.1) / 0.36 = 1.11; lower side: (10.1 − 9.5) / 0.36 = 1.67. C pk = min(1.11, 1.67) = 1.11 — the spread is fine, the aim is 0.1 mm high.

sections.heading: Final summary
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Capability compares the voice of the customer (spec width) with the voice of the process (6σ spread). C p = (USL − LSL) / 6σ measures potential; it ignores centring. C pk = min[(USL − μ)/3σ, (μ − LSL)/3σ] measures reality; it reports the worse side. A gap between them is a diagnosis: re-aim if only C pk is low, reduce variation if both are. Benchmarks: 1.00 barely fits, 1.33 the classic requirement, 1.67 safety-critical territory. Stability first, capability second — and check normality before trusting the ppm predictions. If you remember one thing: C p asks whether the process could fit the spec; C pk tells you whether it actually does . Report both — the gap between them tells you what to fix.

Conventions shown Population versus sample statistics, within versus overall sigma, and distribution parameter definitions. Excluded duplication Published statistical tables and chart-constant tables are referenced rather than reproduced as thousands of individual values. “Every formula” is interpreted as every distinct governing equation or calculation family relevant to the supplied handbook content. Repeated substitutions, software output calculations and individual values in statistical lookup tables are not treated as separate formulas. Where an equation depends on a study design, the required assumptions are stated.

sections.heading: Bernoulli and binomial distributions
sections.text: A04 Analyze Discrete Distributions CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} P(X=x)_{\text{Bernoulli}} &=p^x(1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x\in\{0,1\} \\[3pt] P(X=x)_{\text{Binomial}} &={n\choose x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x} \\[3pt] E(X)&=np \\[3pt] Var(X)&=np(1-p) \end{aligned} Use: Model independent trials with a constant probability and two possible outcomes. Exam trap: A changing probability, dependent trials or more than two outcomes violates the standard binomial assumptions. CSSBB and CQE probability distributions.

sections.text: A05 Analyze Discrete Distributions CQE \begin{aligned} P(X=x)_{\text{Geometric}} &=(1-p)^{x-1}p, \quad x=1,2,\ldots \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{1}{p}, \qquad Var(X)=\frac{1-p}{p^2} \\[5pt] P(X=x)_{\text{NegBin}} &={x-1\choose r-1}p^r(1-p)^{x-r}, \quad x=r,r+1,\ldots \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{r}{p}, \qquad Var(X)=\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2} \end{aligned} Use: Model the number of trials required to obtain the first or r-th success. sections.text: A06 Analyze Discrete Distributions CSSBB CQE \begin{aligned} P(X=x)_{\text{Hypergeom}} &=\frac{{K\choose x}{N-K\choose n-x}} {{N\choose n}} \\[3pt] E(X)&=n\frac{K}{N} \\[3pt] Var(X) &=n\frac{K}{N} \left(1-\frac{K}{N}\right) \frac{N-n}{N-1} \\[5pt] P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_k=x_k) &=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_k!} \prod_{j=1}^{k}p_j^{x_j} \end{aligned} Use: Hypergeometric for sampling without replacement; multinomial for more than two categories.
