sections.heading: Reading the sums-of-squares formulas
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Worked example: dot notation in two-factor ANOVA
sections.text: For this balanced, replicated, fixed-effects two-factor model, define the correction factor \(C=y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}^{2}/(abn)=104^2/8=1352\). The raw sum of squared observations is \(8^2+10^2+12^2+14^2+10^2+12^2+18^2+20^2=1472\). \[SS_T=\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}^{2}-C=1472-1352=120\] \[SS_A=\frac{1}{bn}\sum_{i=1}^{a}y_{i\cdot\cdot}^{2}-C=\frac{44^2+60^2}{4}-1352=32\] \[SS_B=\frac{1}{an}\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{\cdot j\cdot}^{2}-C=\frac{40^2+64^2}{4}-1352=72\] \[SS_{AB}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{ij\cdot}^{2}-C-SS_A-SS_B\] \[SS_{AB}=\frac{18^2+26^2+22^2+38^2}{2}-1352-32-72=8\] \[SS_E=SS_T-SS_A-SS_B-SS_{AB}=120-32-72-8=8\] Here T means total corrected variation , A and B are the main effects, AB is their interaction, and E is within-cell error. Check the result directly: every observation is one unit from its cell mean, so eight squared deviations of 1 give \(SS_E=8\). The correction factor removes the overall mean contribution; it is not an error correction or a chi-square continuity correction. ANOVA calculation check Source SS Degrees of freedom MS = SS / df F = effect MS / error MS A 32 a − 1 = 1 32 16 B 72 b − 1 = 1 72 36 A × B 8 (a − 1)(b − 1) = 1 8 4 Error 8 ab(n − 1) = 4 2 — Total 120 abn − 1 = 7 — — ANOVA compares variation between factor-level means with residual variation. The observed B2–B1 difference is 4 at A1 and 8 at A2: this difference of differences explains the nonzero interaction SS. Statistical significance requires the appropriate F distribution and degrees of freedom, not just comparing raw SS values. Model conditions: inference assumes independent errors, approximately normal errors, and common error variance. Replicates must be independent experimental units, not repeated readings treated as new runs. With n = 1 there is no within-cell error df for this full interaction model. Unequal cell sizes require a general linear model and an explicit choice of sums of squares. Model and decomposition reference: NIST: two-way ANOVA . The dataset and arithmetic here are original teaching examples.

sections.heading: Worked example: chi-square test of independence
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Worked example: chi-square test of independence
sections.text: Now the cells contain counts of items , not strength measurements. In this synthetic example, 100 independently sampled pipes are classified by production line and inspection result. Each pipe is counted once. Let \(O_{ij}\) be the observed count in row i and column j. Some books write \(n_{ij}\) instead. Observed inspection counts Line (i) Pass (j = 1) Fail (j = 2) Row total \(O_{i\cdot}\) Line 1 30 20 50 Line 2 45 5 50 Column total \(O_{\cdot j}\) 75 25 \(O_{\cdot\cdot}=100\) \[O_{i\cdot}=\sum_j O_{ij},\quad O_{\cdot j}=\sum_i O_{ij},\quad N=O_{\cdot\cdot}=\sum_i\sum_j O_{ij}\] The null hypothesis is that line and inspection result are independent. Under independence, each line would have the overall pass proportion, 75/100, and fail proportion, 25/100. Multiply the row size by these proportions to obtain expected counts: \[E_{ij}=\frac{O_{i\cdot}O_{\cdot j}}{O_{\cdot\cdot}}\] \[E_{11}=\frac{50(75)}{100}=37.5,\qquad E_{12}=\frac{50(25)}{100}=12.5\] Line 2 has the same row total, so its expected counts are also 37.5 and 12.5. Expected counts can be fractional. Their row totals, column totals, and grand total match those of the observed table. \[\chi^2=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}\] \[\chi^2=\frac{(30-37.5)^2}{37.5}+\frac{(20-12.5)^2}{12.5}+\frac{(45-37.5)^2}{37.5}+\frac{(5-12.5)^2}{12.5}\] \[\chi^2=1.5+4.5+1.5+4.5=12,\qquad df=(r-1)(c-1)=1\] The uncorrected Pearson test gives p ≈ 0.000532. At α = 0.05, reject independence: there is evidence of an association between line and inspection result. This does not establish that the line caused the difference. Two jobs in one test: the dots provide marginal totals for the expected counts; the summation signs add the four cell contributions to the test statistic. Do not include the margins themselves as extra cells in that sum. Use nonnegative frequency counts, mutually exclusive categories, independent observations, and adequately large expected counts. All four expected counts here exceed 5. For sparse tables, consider a suitable exact method rather than relying on the chi-square approximation. This example uses no Yates continuity correction. Question ANOVA Chi-square independence What is recorded? A numerical response for each experimental unit A count for each pair of categories What do dots summarize? Response totals or, with a bar, means Row counts, column counts, and sample size What does Σ combine? Squared totals or squared deviations, as the formula specifies Standardized squared observed–expected differences What is tested? Mean effects and interaction in the specified model Association between two categorical variables Method and implementation references: Microsoft: CHISQ.TEST and Minitab: table analyses .

sections.heading: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: Understand what is changing, how fast it changes, and how much accumulates. Calculus connects a process curve to decisions: how sensitive a response is to temperature, how defects accumulate during a shift, and how failure probabilities change with time. This lesson starts with the ideas, builds the rules, then applies them to engineering. Download formula cheat sheet (PDF) By the end, you can: interpret a slope and an integral; select product, quotient and chain rules; use substitution and integration by parts; calculate a definite integral; and connect failure density, reliability and hazard. Before you begin: be comfortable with fractions, powers, function notation and basic algebra. All engineering numbers here are teaching examples, not production predictions.

sections.text: An integral adds contributions across an interval. A defect-generation rate in defects per hour multiplied by a small duration in hours gives defects. The bounds a and b identify where accumulation starts and stops. C is an arbitrary constant. Fractions are stacked, powers are superscripts, and integral limits appear above and below the integral sign.

sections.text: There is no general integration quotient rule. For rational functions, algebra or partial fractions may help: 1 [ x ( x + 1 ) ] = 1 x − 1 x + 1 \displaystyle \frac{1}{[x(x + 1)]} = \frac{1}{x }- \frac{1}{x + 1} . Integrate the pieces to get ln|x| − ln|x + 1| + C. Trigonometric substitution can simplify roots: for a 2 − x 2 \displaystyle \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} , use x = a sin ⁡ θ \displaystyle x = a \sin \theta with a suitable angle interval, then d x = a cos ⁡ θ d θ \displaystyle dx = a \cos \theta d\theta . These are pattern-based methods; numerical integration handles many cases without simple antiderivatives.

sections.text: Split [a,b] into n intervals of width Δ x = ( b − a ) n \displaystyle \Delta x = \frac{(b - a)}{n} . A rectangle has height f ( x i ) \displaystyle f(x_i) and area f ( x i ) Δ x \displaystyle f(x_i)\Delta x . Adding the rectangles estimates the integral. For a continuous curve, the estimates converge as the largest interval width approaches zero. We use a limit; we do not literally calculate an infinite number of rectangles.

sections.text: For continuous f, define A ( x ) = ∫ a x f ( t ) d t \displaystyle A(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t) dt . Then A ′ ( x ) = f ( x ) \displaystyle A'(x) = f(x) : the rate at which accumulated area grows is the height of the original curve. Conversely, if G ′ = f \displaystyle G' = f , the definite integral is G(b) − G(a). OpenStax explains both parts. ∫ 0 3 x 2 d x = [ x 3 3 ] 0 3 = 27 3 − 0 = 9 \displaystyle \int_0^3x^2\,dx=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3=\frac{27}{3}-0=9 “Undoing” comes with a condition: ∫ f ′ d x \displaystyle \int f' dx gives f + C. To recover the exact original process level, you need a starting value. Integrating velocity gives displacement; distance travelled requires integrating speed, |velocity|.

sections.text: Suppose the expected defect rate is r ( t ) = 2 + 0.5 t \displaystyle r(t) = 2 + 0.5t defects per hour, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8 \displaystyle 0 \leq t \leq 8 hours. Expected defects = ∫ 0 8 ( 2 + 0.5 t ) d t = [ 2 t + 0.25 t 2 \displaystyle = \int_{0}^{8}(2 + 0.5t)dt = [2t + 0.25t^{2} ]₀⁸ = 32 \displaystyle = 32 defects. The average rate is 32 8 = 4 \displaystyle \frac{32}{8 }= 4 defects per hour. If instead you know a defect fraction q(t), multiply by throughput v(t): expected defective units = ∫ q ( t ) v ( t ) d t \displaystyle = \int q(t)v(t)dt .

sections.heading: 06 / Calculus in quality and reliability
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: In quality, area under a continuous measurement density between specification limits gives the conforming probability. In reliability, the variable is time to failure T. The same slope-and-area ideas connect four quantities: Quantity Meaning Units F ( t ) \displaystyle F(t) Probability of failure by t Dimensionless R ( t ) = 1 − F ( t ) \displaystyle R(t) = 1 - F(t) Probability of surviving beyond t Dimensionless f ( t ) = F ′ ( t ) = − R ′ ( t ) \displaystyle f(t)=F'(t)=-R'(t) Failure-time density; integrate it for probability inverse time h ( t ) = f ( t ) R ( t ) \displaystyle h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{R(t)} Instantaneous failure rate among survivors inverse time For continuous lifetimes, P( T = t ) \displaystyle T = t) is zero; f ( t ) \displaystyle f(t) is a density, not a point probability. Hazard is also not a probability. Over a short Δ t , h ( t ) Δ t \displaystyle \Delta t, h(t)\Delta t approximates the conditional probability of failure, given survival to t.

sections.heading: Live lab: exponential reliability
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: The exponential model assumes constant hazard λ, as described in the NIST handbook . Its survival curve is R ( t ) = e − λ t \displaystyle R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} , with time in hours and λ per hour. Raise λ and watch survival drop faster. The shaded area under the density from 0 to t is F ( t ) \displaystyle F(t) . Hazard λ (per hour) Time t (hours) At λ = 0.002 h \displaystyle \lambda = \frac{0.002}{h} and t = 100 h \displaystyle t = 100 h , reliability is 81.87% and failure probability is 18.13%. The mean time to failure is 500 h. At 500 h, reliability is 36.79%, not 50%: a mean is not a median.

sections.heading: Derive the relationships yourself
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: Differentiate R ( t ) = e − λ t \displaystyle R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} using the chain rule: R ′ ( t ) = − λ e − λ t \displaystyle R'(t) = -\lambda e^{-\lambda t} . Therefore f ( t ) = − R ′ ( t ) = λ e − λ t \displaystyle f(t) = -R'(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t} . Divide f ( t ) \displaystyle f(t) by R ( t ) \displaystyle R(t) to recover h ( t ) = λ \displaystyle h(t) = \lambda . Integrating f from 0 to t gives 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle 1 - e^{-\lambda t} . Integrating R from 0 to infinity gives M T T F = 1 λ \displaystyle MTTF = \frac{1}{\lambda } . For a changing hazard, use H ( t ) = ∫ 0 t h \displaystyle H(t) = \int_{0}^{t} h (s)ds and R ( t ) = exp ⁡ [ − H ( t ) ] \displaystyle R(t) = \exp [-H(t)] , assuming R ( 0 ) = 1 \displaystyle R(0) = 1 . Do not force a constant-hazard model onto wear-out or early-life failure patterns. MTTF describes a lifetime model; it is not automatically the MTBF of a repaired system.

sections.heading: A. Differentiate the CDF to obtain the PDF
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
Worked example: differentiation and integration go both ways
A. Differentiate the CDF to obtain the PDF
sections.text: Step 1 — Write the relationship and substitute the CDF. The density is the derivative of cumulative probability. f ( t ) = d F ( t ) d t = d d t ( 1 − e − λ t ) \displaystyle f(t)=\frac{dF(t)}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right) Step 2 — Differentiate each term. The derivative of the constant one is zero. Keep the subtraction sign in front of the exponential. f ( t ) = d d t ( 1 ) − d d t ( e − λ t ) = 0 − d d t ( e − λ t ) \displaystyle f(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(1)-\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right)=0-\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right) Step 3 — Identify the inner function. The outer function is the exponential. The exponent is the inner function; its derivative is the negative constant hazard. g ( t ) = − λ t , g ′ ( t ) = − λ \displaystyle g(t)=-\lambda t,\qquad g^{\prime}(t)=-\lambda d d t e g ( t ) = e g ( t ) g ′ ( t ) \displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}e^{g(t)}=e^{g(t)}g^{\prime}(t) d d t e − λ t = e − λ t ( − λ ) = − λ e − λ t \displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}e^{-\lambda t}=e^{-\lambda t}(-\lambda)=-\lambda e^{-\lambda t} Step 4 — Substitute and simplify both minus signs. One minus comes from the CDF’s subtraction; the other comes from differentiating the exponent. f ( t ) = 0 − ( − λ e − λ t ) = 0 + λ e − λ t = λ e − λ t \displaystyle f(t)=0-\left(-\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\right)=0+\lambda e^{-\lambda t}=\boxed{\lambda e^{-\lambda t}} Interpretation. The slope of the CDF at a selected time is the height of the density at that time. The density is nonnegative, so the CDF never decreases.

sections.heading: B. Integrate the PDF to recover the CDF
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
Worked example: differentiation and integration go both ways
B. Integrate the PDF to recover the CDF
sections.text: Step 1 — Set up the accumulated probability. Use u \displaystyle u as the integration variable so that t \displaystyle t remains the fixed upper endpoint. The lower bound is zero because this model has no negative failure times and no probability mass at zero. F ( t ) = ∫ 0 t f ( u ) d u = ∫ 0 t λ e − λ u d u \displaystyle F(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du=\int_0^t\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du Step 2 — Find an antiderivative by substitution. Replace the exponent with a simpler variable. Solve explicitly for the differential. w = − λ u \displaystyle w=-\lambda u d w d u = − λ , d w = − λ d u , d u = − 1 λ d w \displaystyle \frac{dw}{du}=-\lambda,\qquad dw=-\lambda\,du,\qquad du=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\,dw Step 3 — Substitute both the exponential and the differential. The constant hazard cancels its reciprocal. The minus sign remains. ∫ λ e − λ u d u = ∫ λ e w ( − 1 λ ) d w \displaystyle \int\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=\int\lambda e^w\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)\,dw = − ∫ e w d w = − e w + C \displaystyle = -\int e^w\,dw=-e^w+C Step 4 — Return to the original integration variable. ∫ λ e − λ u d u = − e − λ u + C \displaystyle \int\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=-e^{-\lambda u}+C Step 5 — Evaluate upper endpoint minus lower endpoint. Use the antiderivative at each bound. The same constant cancels. F ( t ) = [ − e − λ u ] 0 t \displaystyle F(t)=\left[-e^{-\lambda u}\right]_0^t = ( − e − λ t + C ) − ( − e − λ ⋅ 0 + C ) \displaystyle =\left(-e^{-\lambda t}+C\right)-\left(-e^{-\lambda\cdot0}+C\right) = − e − λ t + e 0 = − e − λ t + 1 = 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle =-e^{-\lambda t}+e^0=-e^{-\lambda t}+1=\boxed{1-e^{-\lambda t}} Alternative: change the bounds during substitution. If you keep the new variable throughout, transform both limits. This gives the same result without substituting back. u = 0 ⇒ w = 0 , u = t ⇒ w = − λ t \displaystyle u=0\Rightarrow w=0,\qquad u=t\Rightarrow w=-\lambda t F ( t ) = − ∫ 0 − λ t e w d w = − [ e w ] 0 − λ t = − ( e − λ t − 1 ) = 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle F(t)=-\int_0^{-\lambda t}e^w\,dw=-\left[e^w\right]_0^{-\lambda t}=-(e^{-\lambda t}-1)=1-e^{-\lambda t}

sections.text: ∫ 0 t λ e − λ u d u = 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle \int_0^t\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=1-e^{-\lambda t} Area under the density becomes failure probability. The indefinite integral alone gives − e − λ t + C \displaystyle -e^{-\lambda t}+C . To recover a CDF, use the starting condition: F ( 0 ) = 0 ⇒ − e 0 + C = 0 ⇒ − 1 + C = 0 ⇒ C = 1 \displaystyle F(0)=0\Rightarrow -e^0+C=0\Rightarrow -1+C=0\Rightarrow C=1 The definite integral already builds in that starting condition. More generally, integrating a derivative from zero to a time gives the original function’s change over that interval: ∫ 0 t F ′ ( u ) d u = F ( t ) − F ( 0 ) \displaystyle \int_0^t F^{\prime}(u)\,du=F(t)-F(0) Choose the direction carefully. To go from a CDF to a PDF, differentiate. Integrating the CDF produces a different quantity; it does not produce the density. First calculate the dimensionless exponent. λ t = ( 0.002 h − 1 ) ( 100 h ) = 0.2 \displaystyle \lambda t=(0.002\,\mathrm{h}^{-1})(100\,\mathrm{h})=0.2 e − λ t = e − 0.2 ≈ 0.818730753 \displaystyle e^{-\lambda t}=e^{-0.2}\approx0.818730753 Density from differentiation: f ( 100 ) = 0.002 e − 0.2 ≈ 0.001637462 h − 1 \displaystyle f(100)=0.002e^{-0.2}\approx0.001637462\,\mathrm{h}^{-1} Cumulative probability from integration: F ( 100 ) = ∫ 0 100 0.002 e − 0.002 u d u = 1 − e − 0.2 ≈ 0.181269247 \displaystyle F(100)=\int_0^{100}0.002e^{-0.002u}\,du=1-e^{-0.2}\approx0.181269247 The probability of failure by 100 hours is approximately 18.13% . sections.heading: 07 / Mistakes to catch before using the answer
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
07 / Mistakes to catch before using the answer
sections.text: Missing the inner derivative: ( e − λ t ) ′ \displaystyle (e^{-\lambda t})' is − λ e − λ t \displaystyle -\lambda e^{-\lambda t} , not just e − λ t \displaystyle e^{-\lambda t} . Using the power integral for 1 x \displaystyle \frac{1}{x} : use ln|x| + C. Omitting C: include it for indefinite integrals; endpoint subtraction cancels it in definite integrals. Confusing products: ( u v ) ′ ≠ u ′ v ′ \displaystyle (uv)' \ne u'v' and ∫ u v d x ≠ ( ∫ u d x ) ( ∫ v d x ) \displaystyle \int uv dx \ne (\int u dx)(\int v dx) . Misreading area: below-axis contributions are negative; probability densities must be nonnegative and integrate to 1. Ignoring units: integrating hazard gives cumulative hazard, not failure probability. Convert with F = 1 − e − H \displaystyle F = 1 - e^{-H} . Over-trusting a model: confirm its domain, data quality and assumptions before making engineering decisions.

sections.heading: What Is Reliability? What Is Maintainability?
breadcrumb: What Is Reliability? What Is Maintainability?
sections.text: Start here — plain-language definitions, no formulas yet. Everything later in this lesson is just these two ideas made precise.
sections.excerpt: Start here — plain-language definitions, no formulas yet. Everything later in this lesson is just these two ideas made precise.

sections.heading: Reliability
breadcrumb: What Is Reliability? What Is Maintainability?
sections.text: Reliability is the probability that something keeps working, without failing, for a stated length of time, under stated conditions. Say a batch of light bulbs is rated "90% reliable at 1,000 hours." That means if you ran a lot of them for 1,000 hours, about 90% would still be working and 10% would have burned out. Reliability always comes with a time attached — a bulb that's 90% reliable at 1,000 hours will be less reliable at 2,000 hours, because more time means more chances to fail. Reliability answers: "What's the chance this still works after time t?"

sections.heading: Maintainability
breadcrumb: What Is Reliability? What Is Maintainability?
sections.text: Maintainability is the probability that something broken gets fixed and working again within a stated length of time, once repair begins. Say a machine is "80% maintainable within 4 hours." That means if it breaks down, there's an 80% chance the repair crew has it running again within 4 hours of starting the fix. The other 20% of the time, the repair drags on longer — parts aren't on hand, the fault is hard to find, and so on. Maintainability answers: "What's the chance it's fixed within time t?" Notice these two ideas are mirror images of each other. Reliability is about staying up ; maintainability is about getting back up . Put them together and you get availability — the fraction of time something is actually usable, which depends on both how rarely it breaks and how quickly it gets fixed. A machine that almost never breaks but takes a month to repair when it does can end up less available than one that breaks often but is fixed in ten minutes. This lesson builds up to that idea at the end. Why calculus shows up at all: "probability of still working by time t" is a curve that changes as t grows — it starts near 100% and drifts down toward 0% as more things get a chance to fail. Calculus is just the tool for describing curves and the rates at which they change. You don't need to be a mathematician to follow this — every formula below is introduced with the plain-language idea first, and the interactive charts let you watch the curves move instead of only reading the equations.

sections.heading: The vocabulary, defined before it's used
breadcrumb: What Is Reliability? What Is Maintainability?
The vocabulary, defined before it's used
sections.text: These five terms appear constantly in reliability work. Skim them now — they'll be defined again, more precisely, as each one comes up later in the lesson. Term Plain-language meaning TTF Time To Failure — how long a single item ran before it broke. Only makes sense for something that gets scrapped, not repaired. MTTF Mean Time To Failure — the average TTF across many identical items. "On average, how long do these last?" MTBF Mean Time Between Failures — for something that gets repaired and put back in service, the average time from one failure to the next. MTTR Mean Time To Repair — the average time it takes to fix something once repair starts. Hazard rate How likely something is to fail right now , given that it has survived up to this point. Not the same as "how likely to fail overall" — it's a conditional, moment-by-moment risk. One more distinction worth having in mind from the very start, because it decides which of these terms applies:

sections.heading: Repairable vs. Non-Repairable Systems
sections.text: Before any formulas, the single most important fork in reliability engineering: does this item get thrown away when it fails, or fixed and put back into service? The answer changes which index you track for the rest of this lesson.
sections.excerpt: Before any formulas, the single most important fork in reliability engineering: does this item get thrown away when it fails, or fixed and put back into service? The answer changes which index you track for the rest of this lesson.

sections.heading: Non-repairable
sections.text: Once it fails, it is discarded or replaced — never restored to service. There is exactly one Time-to-Failure (TTF) per unit, so a population of units gives you a distribution of TTFs. This is precisely the f(x)/F(x)/R(x)/h(x) machinery above. Examples: a light bulb, a weld coupon, a fuse, a single bearing (if scrapped rather than reworked), a tensile test specimen. Governing index: MTTF — Mean Time To Failure, \(E[T]=\int_0^\infty R(t)\,dt\).
sections.excerpt: Once it fails, it is discarded or replaced — never restored to service. There is exactly one Time-to-Failure (TTF) per unit, so a population of units gives you a distribution of TTFs. This is precisely the f(x)/F(x)/R(x)/h(x) machinery above. Examples: a…

sections.heading: Repairable
sections.text: Once it fails, it is restored to an operating state (repaired, refurbished) and returned to service. A single unit now generates a sequence of up-times and down-times over its life — a point process of failures, not one number. Examples: a rolling mill stand, a reheat furnace, a pump, a CNC line — almost all production equipment. Governing indices: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures), MTTR (Mean Time To Repair), and Availability . Life of a repairable asset: alternating Up and Down states. Each up interval is one Time Between Failures (TBF); each down interval includes active repair (MTTR) plus any logistics/admin delay. A non-repairable item would only ever show the first green segment, ending permanently at the first red mark. The down interval is rarely just "repair" — it usually splits into MTTD (Mean Time To Diagnose: find the fault) and MTTR (Mean Time To Repair: fix it once found), sitting between First Failure and End Repair. MTBF spans the whole cycle — diagnose + repair + the following correct-behavior interval — from one failure to the next. Driving MTTD down (better instrumentation, clearer alarms, condition data) is often cheaper than driving MTTR down, and both shrink the down interval that Availability above is built from. Because repair resets the clock, reliability engineers distinguish "as good as new" repair (full renewal — the classic renewal-process assumption, appropriate for a full bearing/roll change) from "as good as old" minimal repair (fix the immediate fault only, wear state otherwise unchanged — often the realistic case for a quick swap of a sensor or seal on an otherwise worn machine). This distinction is exactly why repairable systems eventually need a different rate function than h(x) (see ROCOF later in this lesson) — but first, the next two sections build the core calculus (f, F, R, h) that describes a single non-repairable item's life. That math is the foundation everything else in this lesson builds on, so it's worth working through carefully before moving on to repairable systems. ↑ Back to contents Now the math With reliability, maintainability, and the repairable/non-repairable split defined above, here's the calculus that makes "probability of still working" precise for a single non-repairable item — drag the sliders and watch it move. What's actually being plotted: the charts below use the Weibull distribution , the standard model for time-to-failure in reliability engineering, because two knobs let it produce all three bathtub-curve phases (decreasing, flat, or increasing risk over time): \[ f(x) = \frac{\beta}{\eta}\left(\frac{x}{\eta}\right)^{\beta-1} e^{-(x/\eta)^{\beta}} \] η (eta) — the scale parameter: roughly, the "typical" lifetime. Bigger η stretches everything further out in time; it doesn't change the shape of the risk, just how far along the time axis it happens. β (beta) — the shape parameter: controls whether risk falls, stays flat, or rises with age — this is the exact same β that defines the three zones of the bathtub curve later in this lesson. You don't need to memorize this formula or plug numbers into it by hand — treat β and η as knobs, move the sliders, and watch how the four curves respond. The formula is here so the curves aren't a black box.

sections.heading: How the PDF and CDF are connected
breadcrumb: How the PDF and CDF are connected
sections.text: The probability density function (f(x)) and cumulative distribution function (F(x)) are two views of the same continuous probability model. The PDF shows where values are concentrated; the CDF keeps a running total of probability from the far left up to x. \[ F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)\,du \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)=\frac{dF(x)}{dx} \]

sections.heading: What each graph means
sections.text: The bell-shaped curve is the PDF, (f(x)) . Its height describes the concentration or density of possible values around x. The S-shaped curve is the CDF, (F(x)) . Its height is the total probability accumulated up to x. The slope of the CDF at any point equals the height of the PDF at the same point. Therefore, when (f(x)) is small, (F(x)) is nearly flat. As (f(x)) increases, (F(x)) becomes steeper. Where (f(x)) reaches its peak, (F(x)) has its steepest slope. As (f(x)) falls, (F(x)) continues increasing, but more slowly. The PDF eventually approaches zero while the CDF approaches 1.

An area under the CDF would represent (int F(x)\,dx), which is not (P(x_1<X\le x_2)). sections.heading: Reliability interpretation
sections.text: When (T) is time to failure, (F(t)=P(T\le t)) is the probability that the unit has failed by time t, while (R(t)=1-F(t)=P(T>t)) is the probability that it is still operating. The failure density connects both curves: \[ f(t)=\frac{dF(t)}{dt}=-\frac{dR(t)}{dt} \] Bottom line: (F(x_2)) is the accumulated probability up to x₂, (f(x_2)) is the CDF's slope at x₂, and (F(x_2)-F(x_1)) is the probability between the two draggable bounds. The same calculus relationship applies to the Weibull failure-time model used elsewhere in this lesson.

sections.heading: CDF → PDF via differentiation
sections.text: \[ f(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F(x) \] The PDF is the instantaneous rate of change of the CDF — it tells you how fast probability is accumulating at any point x.
sections.excerpt: \[ f(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F(x) \] The PDF is the instantaneous rate of change of the CDF — it tells you how fast probability is accumulating at any point x.

sections.heading: PDF → CDF via integration
sections.text: \[ F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt \] The CDF is the accumulated area under the PDF up to point x — i.e., \(F(x) = P(X \le x)\). So differentiation and integration are inverse operations linking the two: F(x) is the "running total," f(x) is the "instantaneous slope" of that running total.

sections.heading: Extending to Reliability
sections.text: Reliability function R(x) — probability a unit survives past time x: \[ R(x) = 1 - F(x) = \int_x^{\infty} f(t)\,dt \] It's just the complement/mirror of the CDF — the unaccumulated area (survivors), rather than the accumulated area (failures). Since R(x) = 1 − F(x): \[ f(x) = -\frac{d}{dx}R(x) \] The PDF is also the negative derivative of the reliability function — the instantaneous rate of failure (in absolute terms, unconditioned on survival).

sections.heading: Hazard Rate — the conditional rate
sections.text: This is the piece that ties it all together. The hazard rate h(x) is the instantaneous failure rate given the unit has survived to time x — a conditional density, not an unconditional one: \[ h(x) = \frac{f(x)}{R(x)} = \frac{f(x)}{1-F(x)} \] Why divide by R(x)? f(x) tells you the rate of failure across the whole original population . But by time x, some units have already failed and left the population — only R(x) fraction remain "at risk." Dividing by R(x) rescales the rate to apply only to survivors — same logic as conditional probability. Key identity (since \(f(x) = -R'(x)\)): \[ h(x) = \frac{-R'(x)}{R(x)} = -\frac{d}{dx}\ln R(x) \] This means the hazard rate is the negative logarithmic derivative of the reliability function — a very clean link back to differentiation.

sections.heading: Tying it back together (integrate to recover R)
breadcrumb: Tying it back together (integrate to recover R)
sections.text: Integrating h(x) recovers the cumulative hazard function H(x): \[ H(x) = \int_0^x h(t)\,dt = -\ln R(x) \] \[ R(x) = e^{-H(x)} = \exp\left(-\int_0^x h(t)\,dt\right) \]
sections.excerpt: Integrating h(x) recovers the cumulative hazard function H(x): \[ H(x) = \int_0^x h(t)\,dt = -\ln R(x) \] \[ R(x) = e^{-H(x)} = \exp\left(-\int_0^x h(t)\,dt\right) \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take β = 2, η = 100 (a fairly typical wear-related shape) and evaluate everything at x = 50 — halfway to the scale parameter. This matches the default sliders in the interactive panel above, so you can set the marker to x = 50 and check these numbers against the live readout. \[ \begin{aligned} f(50) &= \frac{2}{100}\left(\frac{50}{100}\right)^{1} e^{-(50/100)^2} \approx 0.0078 \\ F(50) &= 1 - e^{-(50/100)^2} \approx 0.2212 \\ R(50) &= e^{-(50/100)^2} \approx 0.7788 \\ h(50) &= f(50)/R(50) \approx 0.0100 \\ H(50) &= (50/100)^2 = 0.25 \end{aligned} \] Sanity checks worth doing by hand once: F(50) + R(50) should equal 1 (0.2212 + 0.7788 = 1.0 ✓); \(e^{-H(50)}\) should equal R(50) (\(e^{-0.25}\approx 0.7788\) ✓). Those two identities are the whole point of this section — if they don't hold, one of the numbers is wrong. ↑ Back to contents

sections.heading: The Bathtub Curve
sections.text: The classic qualitative shape of h(x) over a product's life — three failure mechanisms, three slopes. Same h(x) axis as the interactive panel above — this is the qualitative composite curve traced out if a single Weibull-like β shifts from <1 to ≈1 to >1 across a unit's life. Real equipment is often a mixture of failure modes rather than one clean Weibull, which is why the observed bathtub is usually smoother and asymmetric. For your rolling-mill/pipe context: infant mortality shows up as early-life weld or roll-surface defects caught in the first production runs after a change; useful life is the steady, largely random failure regime maintenance strategies are built around (this is where MTBF-based planning is valid); wear-out is where condition monitoring (vibration, wall-thickness loss, hardness drift) earns its keep — the goal is to catch the upturn in h(x) and intervene before it, via planned replacement, not run-to-failure. ↑ Back to contents

sections.heading: Hazard rate h(x)
sections.text: Defined for a non-repairable item (or population of identical non-repairable items). It is a property of a probability distribution: \(h(x)=f(x)/R(x)\). It describes the instantaneous failure risk of one unit that has never failed before , conditioned on having survived to x.

sections.heading: ROCOF ρ(t)
sections.text: Rate of Occurrence Of Failures — defined for a repairable system's failure/repair history. It is the intensity function of a counting process: the expected number of failures per unit time at system age t, regardless of how many times it has already failed and been repaired . \[ \rho(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{E[N(t+\Delta t) - N(t)]}{\Delta t} \] where N(t) counts cumulative failures of the repairable system up to age t. If repairs are minimal ("as good as old"), the process is often modeled as a Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process (NHPP) — plainly, a statistical model for random events occurring over time, where the rate is allowed to drift up or down — with a Power-Law intensity — ρ(t) increasing means the system is deteriorating (aging faster than repairs can offset, a signal to move from repair to overhaul/replace); ρ(t) roughly constant means failures are occurring at a stable rate, and the classic constant-λ / exponential MTBF math is a reasonable approximation; ρ(t) decreasing means reliability growth (common right after commissioning, as early bugs are fixed out — a repairable-system echo of infant mortality). Rule of thumb: if you're tracking a fleet of identical, discard-on-failure parts (bearings pulled and scrapped, test coupons), use h(x)/MTTF language. If you're tracking one asset's failure history over its operating life (a specific mill stand's trip log), use ROCOF/MTBF language — and check whether ρ(t) is trending before assuming a constant MTBF is valid. ↑ Back to contents

sections.heading: Maintainability
sections.text: The mirror image of reliability: instead of "how long until it breaks," maintainability asks "how long until it's fixed." Maintainability M(t) is defined exactly like a CDF, but over repair time T repair instead of time-to-failure: it is the probability that an active repair, once started, is completed within time t. \[ M(t) = P(T_{repair} \le t) \] Repair-time data is typically right-skewed — most repairs are quick, but a long tail of difficult ones (parts not on hand, hidden damage found once the unit is opened up) pulls the mean well above the median. The lognormal distribution is the standard model for this reason (a sum of many small multiplicative delays tends to lognormal, by the same logic the CLT gives you a normal for additive delays): \[ M(t) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln t - \mu}{\sigma}\right), \qquad \text{median repair time} = e^{\mu} \] MTTR is the mean of this distribution, \(MTTR = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\) — because of the skew, MTTR is always somewhat larger than the median repair time, and a handful of very long repairs can move MTTR a lot without moving the median much at all. This is the same relationship as f(x) and F(x) above, just applied to repair duration instead of failure time.

sections.heading: Availability
sections.text: Where reliability (MTBF) and maintainability (MTTR) combine into the number operations actually cares about. Inherent Availability is the steady-state fraction of time a repairable system is up, considering only active repair time (not logistics delays, not planned/preventive maintenance): \[ A_i = \frac{MTBF}{MTBF + MTTR} \] Availability type Formula What it adds over A i Inherent, A i MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) baseline — active repair time only Achieved, A a MTBM / (MTBM + M̄) + preventive maintenance time (MTBM = mean time between all maintenance, M̄ = mean maintenance time, corrective + preventive) Operational, A o MTBM / (MTBM + MDT) + logistics & administrative delay — MDT (Mean Down Time) ≥ MTTR; this is what the plant floor actually experiences

sections.heading: Excel Functions
sections.text: Function Syntax Purpose When to use it WEIBULL.DIST =WEIBULL.DIST(t,beta,eta,TRUE) Returns the Weibull cumulative failure probability F(t). Use when failure time follows a Weibull model. In Excel, the argument named alpha is the lesson's shape β and the argument named beta is the lesson's scale η. WEIBULL.DIST =WEIBULL.DIST(t,beta,eta,FALSE) Returns the Weibull probability density f(t). Use to compare how densely failures are expected around a selected time. Weibull reliability =1-WEIBULL.DIST(t,beta,eta,TRUE) Returns R(t)=1−F(t). Use for the probability that a non-repairable item survives beyond time t. EXPON.DIST =EXPON.DIST(t,1/mean_time,TRUE) Returns an exponential CDF using rate λ=1/mean time. Use only when a constant-rate model is defensible, such as a simple exponential repair-time approximation. EXPON.DIST =EXPON.DIST(t,1/mean_time,FALSE) Returns the exponential probability density. Use to inspect density under the same constant-rate assumption. LOGNORM.DIST =LOGNORM.DIST(t,LN(median),sigma,TRUE) Returns the cumulative lognormal probability. Use for right-skewed repair times when ln(repair time) is approximately normal, matching the maintainability visual in this lesson. LOGNORM.DIST =LOGNORM.DIST(t,LN(median),sigma,FALSE) Returns the lognormal probability density. Use to see where repair durations are most concentrated. GAMMA =eta*GAMMA(1+1/beta) Calculates Weibull MTTF from scale η and shape β. Use after a defensible two-parameter Weibull model has been fitted.

sections.heading: Minitab Navigation
sections.text: Choose a lifetime distribution: use Stat → Reliability/Survival → Distribution Analysis (Right Censoring) → Distribution ID Plot when the data contain exact failure times plus units that have not yet failed. Compare candidate distributions before committing to Weibull. Estimate reliability: use Stat → Reliability/Survival → Distribution Analysis (Right Censoring) → Parametric Distribution Analysis , select Weibull only when the fit is defensible, enter the censoring column, and request survival probabilities or percentiles. Use the arbitrary-censoring version when observations are left- or interval-censored. If no parametric distribution fits adequately, use the corresponding nonparametric analysis. Analyze repairable equipment: use Stat → Reliability/Survival → Repairable System Analysis → Parametric Growth Curve to estimate the mean cumulative function and ROCOF with a power-law or homogeneous Poisson process. This is the repairable-system route; it is not the same as fitting a hazard function to one non-repairable lifetime.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
sections.text: For ASQ CSSBB and CQE preparation, connect each formula to the system type and the question being asked: Excel is useful for transparent hand calculations, while the Minitab routes above show how the same decisions are made with censored field data. In real work, document the distribution-fit evidence and operating assumptions instead of selecting a model from the formula alone. Write R(t)=1−F(t) first. It prevents the common error of reporting cumulative failures as survivors. Remember the Weibull shape rule: β<1 means decreasing hazard, β=1 means constant hazard, and β>1 means increasing hazard. Use MTTF for a non-repairable population; use MTBF, MTTR, ROCOF, and availability for repairable systems. Do not confuse hazard h(t), conditional on surviving to t, with ROCOF, which counts repeated failures from a repairable system. For the simple steady-state approximation, inherent availability is MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR) . State the assumptions before applying it to operational availability. In real analysis, retain right-censored units. Discarding units that have not failed wastes exposure information and can bias the fitted life model.

sections.heading: Index Summary
sections.text: Non-repairable vs. repairable — same underlying calculus, different vocabulary. Concept Non-repairable system Repairable system Core time metric TTF (Time To Failure) TBF (Time Between Failures) Central tendency MTTF = ∫R(t)dt MTBF Rate function h(x) — hazard rate ρ(t) — ROCOF "Survives to x" probability R(x) = 1 − F(x) not generally defined — use ρ(t) trend instead Repair-time metric n/a — item is scrapped MTTR, M(t) Combined figure of merit R(x) alone Availability A = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR) Typical distribution Weibull (β shape) Exponential (constant ρ) or NHPP power-law (trending ρ) Example in your world bearing sent to scrap, weld coupon, fuse mill stand, reheat furnace, pump, CNC line Bottom line: the same differentiation/integration relationship that links f, F, R, and h for a single non-repairable item reappears — in a modified, process-level form — once you move to repairable equipment: M(t) is a CDF over repair time, ρ(t) is a rate function like h(x) but for a renewal/counting process rather than a static distribution, and Availability is the ratio that finally lets you compare "how often it breaks" against "how fast it gets fixed" on one scale. That's the full lesson. ↑ Back to contents to revisit any section, or scroll back up to the interactive panels and try your own numbers.

sections.heading: Scope summary
sections.text: Search the formulas in The ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook by Hulting and McShane-Vaughn, including the numbered equations and the governing displays that have no equation number. They are grouped into the five scored CRE sections. Each card is an original study note, not a copy of the handbook text. I. Fundamentals Life, failure rate, repair, and availability. II. Risk management No displayed equation in Chapters 3 to 5. III. Probability Data, probability, regression, and life functions. IV. Planning and modeling Accelerated tests and reliability models. V. Lifecycle Demonstration, availability, and spare parts. Every numbered equation is one card, and so is each governing formula the handbook displays without a number. A worked numerical substitution is not a separate card. Risk management stays visible because it is a scored section, and Chapters 3 to 5 still have no equation. sections.heading: Reliability at time t
sections.text: CRE-2.1 Equation 2.1 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures R(t)=\Pr(X>t)=1-\Pr(X\le t) Use: Reliability at time t is the probability that life exceeds t. Exam trap: Do not report the probability of failure, Pr(X at or below t), as the reliability. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.1.

Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures R(t)=\frac{\text{units functioning at the end of the period}}{\text{units functioning at the start of the test}} Use: Use the count still functioning divided by the count that started the test. Exam trap: Do not put the failed units in the numerator. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.2.

sections.heading: Mean time to failure
sections.text: CRE-2.3 Equation 2.3 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \mathrm{MTTF}=\theta=\frac{\sum t_i}{n} Use: For complete failure times, the mean is the total of the times divided by the number of items. Exam trap: Do not divide by the number of survivors. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.3.

sections.heading: Mean time between failures
sections.text: CRE-2.4 Equation 2.4 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \mathrm{MTBF}=\frac{nm}{r} Use: n items each exposed for m hours, with r failures, give total time nm divided by r. Exam trap: Do not divide by the number of items when the question asks for time per failure. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.4.

sections.heading: Mean cycles between failures
sections.text: CRE-2.5 Equation 2.5 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \mathrm{MCBF}=\frac{nc}{r} Use: The same total-exposure idea, counted in cycles instead of hours. Exam trap: Do not leave the answer in hours when the exposure is in cycles. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.5.

sections.text: CRE-2.6 Equation 2.6 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \mathrm{MTBCF}=\frac{nc}{C} Use: The denominator is the count of critical failures, not every failure. Exam trap: Using all failures in the denominator gives MTBF, not the critical-failure measure. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.6.

sections.text: CRE-2.7 Equation 2.7 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \lambda=\frac{1}{\mathrm{MTBF}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{MTTF}} Use: Under a constant rate, the rate is the reciprocal of the mean life. Exam trap: Do not multiply the mean by the rate and call that \(\lambda\). ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.7.

sections.text: CRE-2.11 Equation 2.11 I. Reliability Fundamentals Availability \mathrm{MDT}=\frac{\text{total downtime}}{\text{number of downtime occurrences}} Use: Downtime includes more than active repair when the record says so. sections.text: CRE-2.12 Equation 2.12 I. Reliability Fundamentals Availability A=\frac{\text{time the unit is capable of use}}{\text{length of the interval}} Use: Compare capable time with the full interval named in the question. sections.text: CRE-2.13 Equation 2.13 I. Reliability Fundamentals Availability A=\frac{\text{average uptime}}{\text{average uptime}+\text{average downtime}} Use: Availability is uptime divided by uptime plus downtime. Exam trap: Leaving downtime out of the denominator produces 1. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.13.

sections.text: CRE-2.14 Equation 2.14 I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures R(t)=e^{-\lambda t} Use: A constant failure rate gives an exponential reliability. sections.text: CRE-2.15 Equation 2.15 I. Reliability Fundamentals Availability A=\frac{\mathrm{MTBF}}{\mathrm{MTBF}+\mathrm{MTTR}} Use: Use this when the only times given are the mean life and the mean repair. Exam trap: Do not put MTTR in the numerator. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 2.15.

Reliability Fundamentals Availability \mathrm{MTBMA}=\frac{1}{\lambda+\mu} Use: \(\lambda\) is the failure rate and \(\mu\) is the preventive maintenance rate. Both remove the item from service. sections.text: CRE-6.2 Equation 6.2 III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability Descriptive statistics and regression r=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{s_x s_y}=\frac{SS_{xy}}{\sqrt{SS_{xx}\,SS_{yy}}} Use: Scale the sample covariance by the two sample standard deviations. The same ratio is the corrected sum of products over the square root of the two corrected sums of squares. Exam trap: A correlation is not a slope. The slope still has the units of Y per unit of X. sections.heading: Two-sided test statistic for the slope
breadcrumb: III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability
sections.text: CRE-6.7 Equation 6.7 III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability Descriptive statistics and regression \begin{aligned} t^{*}&=\frac{b_1-\beta_1}{s_{b_1}}\\ s_{b_1}&=\frac{s_e}{\sqrt{SS_{xx}}}\\ s_e&=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^{2}}{n-2}}=\sqrt{\frac{SSE}{n-2}} \end{aligned} Use: Compare the estimated slope with the hypothesized slope. The standard error uses the residual standard deviation and SS sub xx. Reject the null when the absolute value of t-star exceeds the two-sided critical value with n minus 2 degrees of freedom. Exam trap: The usual null value of beta sub 1 is 0, but only when the question says the slope is zero. The critical value uses alpha over 2 because the handbook states a two-sided rule. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 6.7.

sections.heading: General addition rule
breadcrumb: III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability
sections.text: CRE-6.10 Equation 6.10 III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability Probability \Pr(A\cup B)=\Pr(A)+\Pr(B)-\Pr(A\cap B) Use: Add the two events, then subtract the overlap that was counted twice. The handbook's note after Equation 6.10 describes that overlap. Exam trap: The printed Equation 6.10 shows the union symbol on both sides. The sentence after it says the overlap was counted twice, so subtract the intersection, not the union. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Equation 6.10.

sections.heading: Power-law life model
breadcrumb: IV. Reliability Planning, Testing, and Modeling
sections.text: CRE-9.2 Equation 9.2 IV. sections.heading: Overall equipment effectiveness
sections.text: CRE-OEE OEE I. Reliability Fundamentals Life and failure measures \begin{aligned} \mathrm{OEE}&=\mathrm{Availability}\times\mathrm{Performance}\times\mathrm{Quality}\\ \mathrm{Availability}&=\frac{\text{actual operating time}}{\text{planned production time}}\\ \mathrm{Performance}&=\frac{\text{total pieces}/\text{actual operating time}}{\text{ideal pieces}/\text{time period}}\\ \mathrm{Quality}&=\frac{\text{good pieces}}{\text{total pieces}} \end{aligned} Use: OEE is the product of the three ratios. Planned production time is the shift less breaks. Actual operating time subtracts setup and maintenance downtime. Exam trap: Do not add the three ratios. A zero in any one of them makes OEE zero. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Chapter 1 display. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the handbook text.

sections.text: CRE-POI POI III. sections.text: CRE-WEI WEI III. Probability and Statistics for Reliability Probability \begin{aligned} f(t)&=\frac{\beta}{\eta}\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta-1}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right]\\ F(t)&=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right]\\ R(t)&=\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right]\\ E(X)&=\eta\,\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \\ \mathrm{SD}(X)&=\eta\sqrt{\Gamma\left(1+\frac{2}{\beta}\right)-\left[\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)\right]^{2}} \end{aligned} Use: Beta is the shape and eta is the scale. The mean multiplies the scale by a gamma value. The reference table also gives the standard deviation. It writes the gamma arguments as 2 over beta plus 1 and 1 over beta plus 1, which are the same values. sections.text: CRE-SSN SSN V. Lifecycle Reliability Design and demonstration \begin{aligned} \mu_D&=\mu_Y-\mu_X\\ \sigma_D&=\sqrt{\sigma_Y^{2}+\sigma_X^{2}}\\ \Pr(\mathrm{failure})&=\Pr\left(Z<\frac{0-\mu_D}{\sigma_D}\right) \end{aligned} Use: Y is strength and X is stress. Failure is the event that their difference is negative. The handbook treats the two as independent normals. Exam trap: The standard deviation of the difference adds the variances, not the standard deviations. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Chapter 11 display. sections.heading: Croston forecast for intermittent spares
sections.text: CRE-CRO CRO V. Lifecycle Reliability Maintainability and spares \begin{aligned} Z_{t+1}&=\alpha X_t+(1-\alpha)Z_t\\ P_{t+1}&=\beta G_t+(1-\beta)P_t\\ R_{t+1}&=\frac{Z_{t+1}}{P_{t+1}} \end{aligned} Use: When demand is positive, smooth the size Z and the gap P, then divide those updated values. If the latest demand is zero, the handbook leaves Z, P, and the forecast unchanged. Example 13.8 uses alpha 0.2 and beta 0.3. After a demand of 16 with a gap of 2, the next size is 21.60 and the next gap is 1.30, and 21.60 divided by 1.30 is 16.62. Exam trap: The printed forecast line writes Z sub t over P sub t. The example header and the week-4 result divide the values just updated. Equation 13.9 smooths every period. Croston waits for a nonzero demand. ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer Handbook, Chapter 13 display and Example 13.8. The forecast ratio uses the updated size and gap because that is the value the example reports. This note is original study guidance, not a copy of the handbook text.

sections.heading: Human performance reliability
sections.text: CRE-HUM HUM V. Lifecycle Reliability Maintainability and spares R_e(t)=\exp\left[-\int_{0}^{t}h_e(t)\,dt\right] Use: h sub e is the human error rate. Reliability follows the same identity as the cumulative hazard. Exam trap: The handbook display writes this exponential without the minus. Cumulative hazard earlier in the book is the integral of the hazard, and reliability is e to that integral with a minus. The printed plus sign would make reliability greater than 1. sections.heading: A Defensible Crossed Study—Step by Step
breadcrumb: A Defensible Crossed Study—Step by Step
sections.text: Define the decision. State the characteristic, units, specification, intended use, and required measurement performance. Select representative parts. Use at least about 10 parts spanning the normal low-to-high process range—not ten nearly identical parts. Select typical appraisers. A common starting point is three people representing normal shifts, skill levels, and methods. Plan repeats. Use two or three trials per appraiser-part cell. A 10 × 3 × 2 design gives 60 readings. Randomize and blind. Hide part identity where practical, randomize order for every trial, and keep earlier results hidden. Reset the measurement. Remove, reposition, and re-fixture the part between repeats. Re-reading the same display understates error. Use normal conditions. Keep the production method, fixture, environment, instrument, and rounding rule realistic. Record—not erase—events. Document unusual conditions. Investigate questionable readings rather than silently deleting them. Destructive-test warning: if appraisers do not measure the same physical parts, the ordinary crossed model is not present. Use a justified nested or expanded design; do not relabel different specimens as the “same part.” 05 · Live study

sections.text: Metric Question answered Common guideline Important caution %Study Variation How large is measurement spread relative to the spread in this study? <10% acceptable; 10–30% conditional; >30% generally unacceptable Depends strongly on whether study parts represent the intended process variation. %Tolerance How much of USL − LSL is consumed by 6σ of measurement error? Same common 10% and 30% bands Needs the correct full tolerance and the chosen study-variation multiplier. %Contribution What share of total variance comes from each source? <1% acceptable; 1–9% conditional; >9% generally unacceptable for Total Gage R&R Uses variance, so it is the squared counterpart of the study-variation proportion. ndc How many distinct part categories can the system separate? Common minimum ≥5; ≥10 is stronger A narrow part sample can reduce ndc even when repeatability is unchanged. These are guidelines, not universal laws. Customer rules, decision risk, product safety, cost, and intended use can require stricter criteria. State the governing criterion in the report.

sections.heading: Gage R&R worked example: pipe-wall micrometer study
breadcrumb: Gage R&R worked example: pipe-wall micrometer study
sections.text: A quality team studies a 0.500 mm-wide tolerance using 10 pipe rings, 3 inspectors, and 2 randomized trials. ANOVA estimates: Repeatability σ 0.018 mm within-appraiser scatter Appraiser σ 0.012 mm between-appraiser effect Part σ 0.110 mm real sampled part spread \(\sigma_{GRR}=\sqrt{0.018^2+0.012^2}=0.0216\text{ mm}\) \(\%StudyVar=100\times0.0216/\sqrt{0.0216^2+0.110^2}=19.3\%\) \(\%Tolerance=100\times6(0.0216)/0.500=26.0\%\) \(ndc=\lfloor1.41(0.110/0.0216)\rfloor=7\) Conclusion: the system is conditionally acceptable under common guidelines, not automatically “passed.” It can distinguish at least five categories, but measurement error consumes a meaningful share of both study variation and tolerance. Repeatability is the larger component, so first investigate measurement force, contact cleanliness, positioning, fixturing, and instrument condition. Confirm the applicable customer criterion before release. 08 · Software implementation

Sample standard deviation STDEV.S() Descriptive scatter Do not substitute one overall SD for a crossed variance-component model. Bias AVERAGE(Measurements)-Reference Average offset Formal inference needs repeated reference measurements. Linearity slope SLOPE(BiasRange,ReferenceRange) Bias change across range Use the formal study output for tests and confidence intervals. sections.text: A highly repeatable gage can still be biased or nonlinear. Practice case: Should this system be released? A study reports %Study Variation = 8%, %Tolerance = 7%, and ndc = 12. A separate reference study shows +0.080 mm bias on a ±0.100 mm specification. Answer: Do not release it based on Gage R&R alone. Precision is strong, but the systematic offset is large relative to the specification. Investigate and correct bias, then verify accuracy and repeatability again. Practice case: Is a 35% Gage R&R always a gage failure? Answer: It is generally unacceptable under common guidelines, but first check the study design. sections.text: Bias, linearity, and stability can make precise results consistently wrong. Define the measurement decision and choose the correct study. Use representative parts, normal appraisers, repeats, randomization, blinding, and repositioning. Inspect graphs before reducing the study to one number. Interpret %Study Variation, %Tolerance, %Contribution, and ndc as different views—not interchangeable labels. Match the dominant source to corrective action, then repeat the study under the improved method. Never claim accuracy, linearity, or stability from Gage R&R alone. Once the measurement system is suitable, use control charts to assess process stability before interpreting process capability .

lessons.description: Learn the Prevention-Appraisal-Failure model, calculate COPQ, and practice classifying quality costs with a dive-the-iceberg interactive.

sections.heading: Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ)
sections.text: Interactive CSSBB / CQE Juran PAF Model Learn the Prevention-Appraisal-Failure model that turns nonconformances into dollars leadership actually budgets against — then dive an interactive iceberg, classify real cost scenarios, and run your own numbers through a live COPQ calculator. Why this matters at work: Most organizations only track the visible slice of quality failure — scrap, warranty, obvious rework — and miss the larger hidden cost underneath. COPQ gives you the vocabulary and the math to make that hidden cost visible to the people who control the budget. Every scrap unit, warranty claim, and re-inspection has a dollar sign on it — most organizations just aren't looking. Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ) is the framework that puts a number on the price of not doing it right the first time, and it's one of the most commonly tested cost-of-quality concepts on both the CSSBB and CQE exams. The core problem COPQ solves is a communication gap. Quality engineers talk in defect rates, Cpk values, and nonconformance reports. Executives talk in dollars. COPQ translates one language into the other — it takes "we had 42 nonconformances last quarter" and turns it into "we lost $950,000 last quarter," which is a sentence that gets budget approved. That translation is exactly why ASQ treats COPQ as a core competency for both the CSSBB (strategic, financial framing) and the CQE (operational, root-cause framing) exams. The idea traces to Joseph Juran, who in the 1950s argued that quality costs behave like any other manageable cost category and organized them into the Prevention-Appraisal-Failure (PAF) model you'll work with in this lesson. Philip Crosby popularized the idea for a broader business audience in his 1979 book Quality Is Free , arguing that the cost of poor quality routinely dwarfs the cost of preventing it — a claim borne out by the benchmark data below. ASQ's Quality Costs Committee later formalized the PAF structure into the standard most CSSBB/CQE materials use today. Rule of thumb: COPQ commonly runs 10–20% of sales revenue in manufacturing organizations, and in immature quality programs, failure costs alone can consume 60–70% of total quality spend — while prevention gets only 5–10%. The goal of quality management isn't to spend less on quality overall; it's to shift the spend from failure toward prevention.

sections.heading: COPQ as a maturity signal
sections.text: Because prevention spending suppresses the other three categories, the ratio of COPQ to revenue is one of the more reliable proxies for how mature an organization's quality system actually is — more reliable, often, than self-reported certifications or audit scores. The table below is a rough guide used across Six Sigma and lean literature; treat the bands as directional, not exact thresholds. COPQ as % of revenue Maturity band What you'd typically see Below 5% Low COPQ / high maturity Six Sigma-mature or highly developed lean systems; heavy in-process control and poka-yoke; most defects eliminated at the source 5% – 20% Moderate COPQ / mid maturity Structured quality systems with defined inspection processes; internal failures measured and tracked; external failures declining as inspection improves Above 20% High COPQ / low maturity Reactive, inspection-dependent quality management; failure costs dominate the budget; prevention chronically underfunded

sections.heading: The Prevention-Appraisal-Failure (PAF) Model
sections.text: Joseph Juran's PAF model, still the backbone of ASQ's quality cost framework, sorts every quality-related dollar into one of four categories. Understanding which bucket a cost belongs in — and how the buckets relate to each other — is the foundation for everything else in this lesson. The categories aren't independent — they're causally linked, and that link is the entire point of the model. A dollar spent on prevention reduces the number of defects created, which reduces the appraisal effort needed to find them, which reduces internal failure costs (fewer defects to scrap or rework), which reduces external failure costs (fewer defective units escaping to the customer). Spend on the far-left category and the other three fall like dominoes; spend only on inspection (appraisal) and you can catch defects but you're doing nothing to stop them from being created in the first place.

sections.heading: External Failure Costs
sections.text: Costs from defects the customer finds — warranty claims, field returns, complaint handling, recalls, lost future business. Notice the asymmetry between the last two cards. Internal failure is expensive, but it's a cost you control and can usually estimate accurately from labor and material records. External failure is far more dangerous, because the visible line items — warranty checks, freight to return a unit — are usually the smallest part of it. The real cost is a lost customer who doesn't tell you why they left, which is why external failure is the category most often under-counted, and the one this lesson's iceberg exercise focuses on below.

sections.heading: How the categories add up
sections.text: Once you can sort a cost into one of the four PAF buckets, three higher-level rollups let you talk about quality spend the way a controller or CFO would: Term Formula What it represents Cost of Good Quality (COGQ) Prevention + Appraisal What you spend on purpose, to catch or avoid defects Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ) Internal Failure + External Failure What you lose because a defect happened Total Cost of Quality (COQ) COGQ + COPQ Everything quality-related, in and out of your control COGQ is discretionary — leadership chooses how much to spend on it, and can spend more or less depending on strategy. COPQ is not discretionary in the same sense; it's the bill that arrives after the fact for whatever COGQ failed to prevent. A mature quality organization deliberately increases COGQ, on the bet that it will reduce COPQ by more than the increase cost — and, as the curves in the next section show, that bet almost always pays off up to a point. Exam trap: Some materials define COPQ loosely as "all four categories." On the CSSBB/CQE body of knowledge, hold the narrow definition — COPQ = Internal Failure + External Failure — and treat Prevention and Appraisal as the "cost of good quality" that reduces it over time.

sections.heading: Classical vs. Modern View of Optimal Quality Cost
breadcrumb: Classical vs. Modern View of Optimal Quality Cost
sections.text: Two competing models show up on CSSBB/CQE exams. The classical model says there's an interior "sweet spot," roughly mid-range on the conformance axis, where total cost of quality is minimized — pushing conformance higher than that point costs more than it saves, and the curve rises sharply on either side. The modern (zero-defects) view, which dominates current Six Sigma and lean thinking, doesn't argue the optimum disappears — it argues cheaper, more effective prevention technology pushes that optimum much further to the right and flattens the curve dramatically, so the penalty for chasing near-100% conformance becomes small instead of severe. Both panels plot Total COQ as the literal sum of the Failure Cost and Prevention & Appraisal curves at every point — the shapes above aren't just illustrative sketches, they're internally consistent with the formula COQ = Failure + (Prevention + Appraisal). Both models still have a lowest-cost point — the modern view doesn't erase the optimum, it moves it. When prevention is cheap and effective (automated poka-yoke, in-line sensors, statistical process control built into the equipment itself), the Prevention & Appraisal curve stays low for much longer, which drags the whole Total COQ curve flatter and pushes its minimum much further right — well into the 60–80% conformance range instead of the classical model's mid-range optimum — and the penalty for overshooting it is far smaller than the classical model predicts. Exam tip: If a question describes cheap, highly effective prevention technology (e.g. automated poka-yoke, in-line sensors), favor an answer that pushes conformance well above the classical "mid-range" optimum — the modern view still has a best point, it's just much closer to 100%. If the question describes a traditional, inspection-heavy environment with expensive prevention, the classical mid-range interior optimum is likely the intended answer.

You'll get instant feedback — this is the exact skill CSSBB/CQE exam questions test when they describe a cost and ask you to categorize it. Two questions do most of the sorting work for you. First: has the customer received this yet? If yes, it's external failure, full stop — it doesn't matter how small the cost was. If no, ask the second question: is this money spent to find a defect, or to fix/scrap one that was already found? Finding = appraisal. Fixing/scrapping = internal failure. Anything spent before a defect could even occur — training, design reviews, supplier vetting — is prevention.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Reading the Numbers
sections.text: Before you touch the calculator, it helps to walk through one real-shaped example by hand. Consider a medical device team that ships 10,000 units in a quarter against $5,000,000 in quarterly revenue. Their scrap and rework on rejected assemblies — caught before shipment — totals $150,000 in internal failure cost. A field corrective action plus ordinary warranty claims add up to $800,000 in external failure cost, once you include the labor to process each return, not just the parts. That's the trap: the $800,000 figure only shows up if someone deliberately tracks staff time and logistics against the warranty account instead of letting it get buried in "general operations." Step Calculation Result Cost of Poor Quality $150,000 + $800,000 $950,000 COPQ as % of revenue $950,000 ÷ $5,000,000 19.0% Maturity band 19.0% falls in the moderate band 5–20% — structured but reactive At 19%, this team is spending almost a fifth of every revenue dollar cleaning up after defects — and because external failure ($800,000) outweighs internal failure ($150,000) more than 5 to 1, most of that spend is happening after the product already reached the customer, which is the most expensive place for a defect to be found. That single ratio — external-to-internal failure cost — is often a faster diagnostic than the overall COPQ percentage: a team that's mostly internal failure has a controllable, in-house problem; a team that's mostly external failure has a detection problem, meaning appraisal isn't catching what it should before shipment.

sections.heading: Why COPQ Is Chronically Under-Reported
sections.text: Ask a plant manager for their scrap cost and they can usually answer within a minute. Ask for their true COPQ and most can't — not because the costs aren't real, but because they're scattered across ten different general-ledger accounts instead of one. Rework labor gets buried in direct labor. Warranty reserves sit in a finance account nobody in quality ever opens. Expedited freight to fix a shipment gets coded as ordinary freight. Engineering time spent firefighting a field issue gets coded as ordinary engineering hours. None of these are hidden on purpose — they're just never aggregated, so nobody sees the total. Practitioners with decades running DMAIC projects report seeing COPQ hide 15–40% of revenue in plants that believed their quality costs were well understood, purely because of this fragmentation. The practical fix is unglamorous: someone has to go account-by-account and deliberately tag quality-related transactions, rather than trusting that "quality costs" already live in a single line somewhere.

sections.heading: Reducing COPQ: Where the Leverage Is
breadcrumb: Reducing COPQ: Where the Leverage Is
sections.text: Because prevention spending suppresses appraisal, internal failure, and external failure costs all at once, it's the highest-leverage dollar in the model. That said, leverage isn't the same as an unlimited budget — the classical-view curve earlier in this lesson exists precisely because prevention and appraisal spending can itself become wasteful past a certain point. The sequence below is a DMAIC-aligned way to find that leverage without overspending on the wrong things. Measure — pull actual dollars from accounting, not estimates. Costs are typically scattered across ten different accounts, so under-reporting is the default failure mode. Build a simple cost-of-quality worksheet with one row per PAF category and populate it from source documents (scrap tickets, warranty claim logs, rework labor time cards, complaint tracking system exports) rather than trusting a single GL rollup. Analyze — Pareto the failure costs by category and by root cause; a small number of failure modes usually drive most of the dollars. Cross-reference against the external-to-internal failure ratio from the worked example above — a high ratio points you toward appraisal gaps, a low ratio points you toward process capability issues. Improve — shift budget toward prevention tools (FMEA, control plans, poka-yoke, supplier development) targeted at the top failure modes identified in Analyze, not spread evenly across every category. A common mistake is funding prevention broadly instead of aiming it at the Pareto-vital few failure modes. Control — track COPQ as % of revenue over time as a leading indicator of quality system maturity, not just a lagging financial metric. Report it alongside — not instead of — traditional quality metrics like defect rate and Cpk, since COPQ is what makes those metrics legible to a non-technical audience.

Example: conformance in a pipe mill
sections.text: Suppose a pipe must have wall thickness of 10.0 ± 0.5 mm, yield strength of at least 450 MPa, and length of 12.0 ± 0.1 m. Under Crosby’s definition, quality means meeting all applicable requirements. A premium finish cannot compensate for a failed strength requirement. Important nuance: Zero Defects is a performance standard, not a claim that people are physically incapable of error. It means management should not define a known level of defects as acceptable performance and then stop improving.

sections.heading: PDSA: a cycle for prediction and learning
breadcrumb: Quality Gurus: Crosby, Juran, and Deming
Improve the whole system and learn from variation
PDSA: a cycle for prediction and learning
sections.text: Plan Define the problem, build a theory, state what you predict, and decide what data will test the prediction. Do Run the change on a small scale, document what happened, and collect the planned data. Study Compare results with the prediction. Analyze the difference and identify what was learned. Act Adopt, adapt, or abandon the change, then begin the next learning cycle. PDSA versus PDCA: “Study” emphasizes analysis, comparison with a prediction, and learning. It is more than checking whether a task was completed. Deming’s 14 Points for Management The short descriptions below preserve the major exam-level themes. They are shown in Deming’s numbered order. Create constancy of purpose for improving products and services. Adopt the new philosophy rather than accepting chronic waste and poor quality. Cease dependence on mass inspection ; build quality into the process. End purchasing on price alone ; consider quality and total cost through long-term supplier relationships. Improve constantly and forever every process for planning, production, and service. Institute training on the job so people can perform and learn effectively. Institute leadership that helps people and systems perform better. Drive out fear so people can report problems and contribute honestly. Break down barriers between departments and work across the system. Eliminate slogans and exhortations that demand results without improving methods or systems. Eliminate arbitrary quotas and numerical targets that ignore how work is actually produced. Remove barriers to pride of workmanship , including poor systems and conflicting measures. Institute education and self-improvement for everyone. Put everyone to work on the transformation , led by management. A common exam contrast: Crosby is associated with Zero Defects as a performance standard. Deming opposed slogans and zero-defect exhortations aimed at workers when management did not improve the system or provide a method. The distinction is management approach, not whether defects matter. Integrated application

sections.heading: Signal phrases and common traps
breadcrumb: Quality Gurus: Crosby, Juran, and Deming
sections.text: Use the wording in the question. Identify the distinctive phrase before choosing an answer. If you see this phrase Think Why Conformance to requirements, prevention, Zero Defects, price of nonconformance Crosby These are the four absolutes. Fitness for use, Trilogy, breakthrough, vital few Juran These phrases connect customer use, managerial processes, and prioritization. 14 Points, drive out fear, system, variation, PDSA, tampering Deming These clues point to management-led system improvement and learning. Trap: Zero Defects = 3.4 defects per million opportunities. Correction: Zero Defects is Crosby’s performance standard; 3.4 DPMO is associated with Six Sigma performance under its conventional assumptions. Trap: inspection is prevention. Correction: inspection detects nonconformance after or during creation; prevention changes the system so the defect is less likely to occur. Trap: Juran’s control and improvement mean the same thing. Correction: control maintains the current intended level; improvement reaches a new level. Trap: “Study” in PDSA means verify that the task was completed. Correction: Study compares results with a prediction and extracts learning. Trap: a stable process needs operator adjustment after every fluctuation. Correction: adjusting common-cause variation without evidence can be tampering. Trap: the gurus place quality only on the quality department. Correction: all three make quality a management and organizational responsibility, even though their frameworks differ. Crosby = ZERO · Juran = TRILOGY · Deming = SYSTEM Final review

sections.heading: Advanced end-to-end roadmap
sections.text: This is not a mandatory fixed sequence. It is a dependency map showing which questions normally need answers before more advanced methods are credible. VOC / Charter → SIPOC / Flowchart → Check Sheet → MSA → Stratification → Pareto / Histogram → Fishbone / 5 Why → Hypothesis Test / Regression / ANOVA → DOE → Affinity / Tree / Prioritization → Matrix / PDPC / Network → SPC / Control Plan Why advanced tools come later: regression, ANOVA, and DOE can quantify or optimize relationships, but they cannot rescue a vague problem statement, poor traceability, mixed populations, or an unreliable measurement system.

sections.heading: Cost variance
sections.text: PMP-CV CV Process Earned value CV=EV-AC Use: Subtract actual cost from earned value. Exam trap: A negative result means the work completed cost more than its budget. Reversing the subtraction flips the meaning. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Schedule variance
sections.text: PMP-SV SV Process Earned value SV=EV-PV Use: Subtract planned value from earned value. Exam trap: This variance is in the budget units of work, not in days. A negative result means less work is done than was planned by the data date. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Cost performance index
sections.text: PMP-CPI CPI Process Earned value CPI=\frac{EV}{AC} Use: Divide earned value by actual cost. Exam trap: A result below 1 means the completed work cost more than its budget. Actual cost does not belong in the numerator. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Schedule performance index
sections.text: PMP-SPI SPI Process Earned value SPI=\frac{EV}{PV} Use: Divide earned value by planned value. Exam trap: A result below 1 means the project is behind the planned work. Planned value is the denominator, not actual cost. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Variance at completion
sections.text: PMP-VAC VAC Process Earned value VAC=BAC-EAC Use: Subtract the estimate at completion from the budget at completion. Exam trap: A negative result means the forecast finishes over budget. Do not subtract the budget from the forecast. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.
