sections.heading: Estimate at completion, current cost efficiency
sections.text: PMP-EAC-CPI EAC Process Forecasting EAC=\frac{BAC}{CPI} Use: Use this when the cost efficiency so far is expected to continue through the rest of the work. Exam trap: Do not add actual cost again. Dividing the budget by CPI already estimates the whole project. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Estimate at completion, budgeted rate for remaining work
sections.text: PMP-EAC-BUDGET EAC Process Forecasting EAC=AC+BAC-EV Use: Use this when the remaining work is expected to proceed at the original budgeted rate. Exam trap: This is not the budget divided by CPI. That other form assumes the current cost efficiency continues. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.text: PMP-EAC-BOTTOM EAC Process Forecasting EAC=AC+\text{bottom-up ETC} Use: Use this when the original plan is no longer valid and the remaining work is estimated again from the bottom up. Exam trap: Bottom-up ETC is a new estimate of what is left. It is not EAC minus AC taken from an older forecast, and a reestimate is not its own equation. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. This note is original study guidance for that display, not a copy of the guide.

sections.text: PMP-EAC-BOTH EAC Process Forecasting EAC=AC+\frac{BAC-EV}{CPI\times SPI} Use: Use this when both the cost efficiency and the schedule efficiency are expected to affect the remaining work. Exam trap: The denominator multiplies CPI by SPI. Adding the two indexes is a different number. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and 8th edition Table 5-1. sections.text: PMP-TCPI-BAC TCPI Process Forecasting TCPI=\frac{BAC-EV}{BAC-AC} Use: This is the cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to finish at the original budget. Exam trap: Once the forecast replaces the budget as the goal, the denominator is EAC minus AC, not BAC minus AC. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Table 7-1 and Section 7.4.2.3, and 8th edition Table 5-1. sections.heading: Triangular expected value
sections.text: PMP-TRI TRI Process Estimating t_E=\frac{t_O+t_M+t_P}{3} Use: Add the optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values, then divide by 3. The guide prints this for duration and the same algebra for cost. Exam trap: Do not put a 4 on the most likely value. That weight belongs to the beta form. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Section 6.4.2.4 for duration and Section 7.2 for cost, and the 8th edition three-point duration display. One card covers both because the algebra is the same. This note is original study guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Beta expected value
sections.text: PMP-BETA BETA Process Estimating c_E=\frac{c_O+4c_M+c_P}{6} Use: The 6th edition prints this weighted average for a three-point cost estimate. The same weights are the expected-time form a duration question means by PERT. Exam trap: Dividing by 3 is the triangular card. The 4 belongs on the most likely estimate, not on the optimistic or pessimistic one. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Section 7.2, beta distribution for cost. The 8th edition three-point display prints the triangular form and does not reprint this weighted form. This note is original study guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: PERT standard deviation
sections.text: PMP-SIGMA σ Process Estimating Exam algebra \sigma=\frac{P-O}{6} Use: Subtract the optimistic estimate from the pessimistic estimate and divide by 6. Variance is that result squared. A path standard deviation is the square root of the sum of the activity variances. Exam trap: This is not the expected duration. The triangular and beta averages are other cards. Do not square the range before dividing by 6. The guides print the triangular and beta averages and name PERT. They do not print this standard-deviation line. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Total float
sections.text: PMP-TF TF Process Schedule Exam algebra TF=LS-ES=LF-EF Use: Subtract the early start from the late start, or the early finish from the late finish. On the day-1 network, Activity B is 11 minus 6 and 15 minus 10, both 5 days. Exam trap: Total float is not free float. Free float looks only at the next activity. A negative result means the late date is already before the early date. The 8th edition says the difference between the late date and the early date is total float. Neither edition prints LS minus ES as a line of algebra. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.
sections.excerpt: PMP-TF TF Process Schedule Exam algebra TF=LS-ES=LF-EF Use: Subtract the early start from the late start, or the early finish from the late finish. On the day-1 network, Activity B is 11 minus 6 and 15 minus 10, both 5 days. Exam trap: Total float is not free…

sections.heading: Free float
sections.text: PMP-FF FF Process Schedule Exam algebra FF=ES_{\text{successor}}-EF Use: Subtract this activity's early finish from the earliest early start of the activities that follow it. Exam trap: On a day-1 network, subtract one more day. Activity B finishes on day 10 and Activity D starts on day 16, so 16 minus 10 minus 1 is the figure's 5 days of free float. Late dates belong to total float, not this card. The network figures show Activity B's free float as 5 days. They do not print successor start minus early finish. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Communication channels
sections.text: PMP-CH n Process Communications Exam algebra \text{Channels}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2} Use: n is the number of people. Six people make 6 times 5 divided by 2, which is 15 channels. Exam trap: Do not use n squared, and do not forget to divide by 2. Adding one person adds a channel to every existing person, not a single new line. 6th edition Section 10.1.2.2 and the 8th edition communication requirements name the count of channels and do not print this line. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Expected monetary value
sections.text: PMP-EMV EMV Business Environment Risk \mathrm{EMV}=\sum(P\times\text{monetary outcome}) Use: A chance node is the sum of each probability times its monetary outcome. Subtract an investment that is not already inside those outcomes, the way the decision-tree figure does. Exam trap: Do not choose the branch with the largest single payoff. Weight every outcome by its probability before the branches are compared. PMBOK Guide, 6th edition Figure 11-15 and 8th edition Figure 5-5. The figure computes each chance node as probability times monetary outcome. This note is original study guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Net present value
sections.text: PMP-NPV NPV Business Environment Selection Exam algebra NPV=\sum\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} Use: Discount each cash flow to today and add the results. A single present value is the future amount divided by (1 plus the rate) to the power of the period. When the question says to maximize value, the higher NPV wins. Exam trap: Do not compare undiscounted totals. A larger far-future payoff can lose once it is discounted. NPV is not the benefit-cost ratio. Both guides name net present value as a selection measure and do not print this algebra. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.

sections.heading: Return on investment
sections.text: PMP-ROI ROI Business Environment Selection Exam algebra ROI=\frac{\text{benefit}-\text{cost}}{\text{cost}} Use: Subtract cost from benefit, then divide by cost. Exam trap: ROI is not benefits divided by costs. That quotient is the benefit-cost ratio. A result of 1 is not the same statement as a benefit-cost ratio of 1. The guides name return on investment and do not print this ratio. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.
sections.excerpt: PMP-ROI ROI Business Environment Selection Exam algebra ROI=\frac{\text{benefit}-\text{cost}}{\text{cost}} Use: Subtract cost from benefit, then divide by cost. Exam trap: ROI is not benefits divided by costs. That quotient is the benefit-cost ratio. A result…

sections.heading: Internal rate of return
sections.text: PMP-IRR IRR Business Environment Selection Exam algebra 0=\sum\frac{CF_t}{(1+\mathrm{IRR})^t} Use: IRR is the discount rate that makes net present value zero. Compare it with the hurdle rate in the question. A typical series of cash flows has no closed-form rearrangement. Exam trap: Do not treat IRR as profit divided by cost. That is return on investment. A higher IRR is not automatically the choice when the question says to maximize net present value. The guides name the internal rate of return and do not print a solving formula. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.
sections.excerpt: PMP-IRR IRR Business Environment Selection Exam algebra 0=\sum\frac{CF_t}{(1+\mathrm{IRR})^t} Use: IRR is the discount rate that makes net present value zero. Compare it with the hurdle rate in the question. A typical series of cash flows has no closed-form…

sections.heading: Payback period
sections.text: PMP-PBP PB Business Environment Selection Exam algebra \text{Payback}=\frac{\text{investment}}{\text{annual net cash flow}} Use: When net cash flow is the same every year, divide the investment by that annual amount. When the cash flow changes by year, count the years until the investment is recovered. Exam trap: Payback ignores cash after the investment is recovered. It does not discount unless the question says discounted payback. The guides name payback and do not print this line. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.
sections.excerpt: PMP-PBP PB Business Environment Selection Exam algebra \text{Payback}=\frac{\text{investment}}{\text{annual net cash flow}} Use: When net cash flow is the same every year, divide the investment by that annual amount. When the cash flow changes by year, count…

sections.heading: Benefit-cost ratio
sections.text: PMP-BCR BCR Business Environment Selection Exam algebra BCR=\frac{\text{benefits}}{\text{costs}} Use: Divide benefits by costs. A result above 1 means benefits exceed costs. Exam trap: Do not subtract cost from benefit before dividing. That subtraction is return on investment. A ratio of 1.2 is not a 120 percent return on investment. The 6th edition names the benefit-cost ratio. The 8th edition discusses cost-benefit analysis. Neither prints this quotient. This note is original exam guidance, not a copy of the guide.
